\hypertarget{M01-m1.-marketing-decisions-data-and-ai-assisted-python}{%
\chapter{Marketing Decisions, Data, and AI-Assisted
Python}\label{M01-m1.-marketing-decisions-data-and-ai-assisted-python}}

\noindent A retailer must decide which customers should receive a coupon, how much
inventory to place in each store, and which product descriptions should
appear online. Each decision needs a different analytical object. A
forecast of next week's purchases can inform inventory. A comparison of
purchases with and without a coupon can inform targeting. A summary of
product complaints can identify a service problem. An analysis becomes
useful when its output corresponds to the decision the manager can
actually change.

A managerial objective also requires justification. Before optimizing a
response, identify who selected the end, whose choices the action
changes, and what reasons could justify it to affected people. An
accurate forecast or efficient algorithm can advance an end the firm
ought to reject. Kant's distinction between phenomena and noumena,
developed in §9.41, limits the claim that an empirical representation
exhausts the person represented. Practical judgments about ends,
authority, and obligations require their own arguments.

\hypertarget{M01-from-a-marketing-question-to-an-analytical-object}{%
\section{From a Marketing Question to an Analytical
Object}\label{M01-from-a-marketing-question-to-an-analytical-object}}

\noindent Consider a subscription service deciding whether to offer a renewal
discount. The service observes account tenure, past payments, recent
use, and prior contacts. A descriptive analysis reports renewal rates by
tenure. A predictive analysis estimates the probability that an account
renews under the conditions represented in the training data. A causal
analysis estimates how an offer changes renewal. A decision analysis
combines that change with margins, contact costs, and operational
constraints. These objects can use overlapping data while answering
different questions.

The timing of the decision determines what information is available. If
an account must be selected on Monday morning, a support call made on
Wednesday cannot be a predictor for that selection. A variable can be
strongly associated with an outcome and still be unusable at the
decision time. Write down a forecast origin, an outcome window, and a
feature window before constructing a table. An account-week table and an
account-lifetime table support different forecasts because their rows
and time horizons differ.

For a renewal offer, a useful decision quantity is incremental expected
contribution:

\[
\Delta\pi_i=m_i\{p_i(1)-p_i(0)\}-c_i.
\]

Here \(i\) identifies an account, \(p_i(1)\) and \(p_i(0)\) are its
renewal probabilities with and without the offer, \(m_i\) is
contribution in dollars per retained account over the specified horizon,
and \(c_i\) is the expected incremental cost of making the offer. This
compact expression assumes that the offer's costs can be summarized by
\(c_i\) and that \(m_i\) already reflects relevant variable costs. When
every renewing recipient receives a discount, discount expense depends
on renewal under treatment and should be modeled explicitly.

The difference between the two renewal probabilities matters because
many accounts would renew without assistance. Suppose contribution is
\$100 and contact cost is \$3. Then an account whose renewal probability
rises from 0.90 to 0.91 has incremental expected contribution of \$-2.
An account whose probability rises from 0.40 to 0.50 has contribution of
\$7. Ranking by treated renewal probability chooses the first account;
ranking by incremental contribution chooses the second. Observing only
treated customers would not reveal the untreated probabilities.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_response_vs_value.tex}
\caption{High response and high incremental value can identify different customers.}\label{fig:M01_response_vs_value}
\end{figure}

With contribution and contact cost held fixed, the first account's high
baseline renewal probability reverses its ranking under incremental
value. A response model and a targeting policy therefore need separate
evaluation.

A recommendation also needs a reason why the action ought to be taken. A
profitable renewal rule may impose an unwanted obligation on a customer
or a burden on someone outside the customer table. Identify affected
people, state the principle governing their treatment, and compare a
feasible alternative. An estimate of what a company can achieve supplies
evidence for that argument; the normative premise explains which means
and consequences are justified.

\hypertarget{M01-the-unit-of-observation-determines-the-calculation}{%
\section{The Unit of Observation Determines the
Calculation}\label{M01-the-unit-of-observation-determines-the-calculation}}

\noindent A transaction system often stores one row per product line, while the
marketing question concerns orders or customers. Suppose order O1
contains two product lines, O2 contains one, and O3 contains three.
There are six rows, three orders, and perhaps only two customers.
Counting rows as purchases would report six orders. Averaging customer
attributes over product lines would give more weight to customers with
larger baskets.

A key uniquely identifies the intended unit. At the line level, the key
might be the combination of order ID and line number. At the order
level, it is order ID. At the customer level, it is customer ID. A
useful data contract states the key, allowed duplicates, measurement
units, missing-value codes, and date conventions. It also states whether
a negative quantity represents a return, whether a price includes tax,
and whether canceled orders belong in the analysis.

For line \(\ell\) in order \(o\), gross line sales are quantity times
unit price, \(s_{o\ell}=q_{o\ell}p_{o\ell}\). Order sales are
\(S_o=\sum_\ell s_{o\ell}\), and customer-period sales are the sum
across that customer's eligible orders during the period. These are
identities once the population and variables have been defined. They do
not require a behavioral assumption. The substantive choices enter
through eligibility, returns, discounts, and the observation window.

Joining data can change the population or its weights. A many-to-one
join from order lines to a customer table should add customer attributes
without multiplying the original rows. If the customer table
accidentally contains two records for a customer, every matching order
line appears twice. A program can finish without an error while
overstating sales. Verify the relationship between keys before joining,
and compare row counts and totals afterward.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_join_multiplication.tex}
\caption{A duplicate customer key multiplies transactions in a join.}\label{fig:M01_join_multiplication}
\end{figure}

For a single \$40 order, a customer lookup with two matching records
produces two joined rows and an apparent \$80 total. This error arises
from the structure of the tables. Increasing the sophistication of the
subsequent model cannot repair it.

\hypertarget{M01-python-objects-and-reproducible-calculations}{%
\section{Python Objects and Reproducible
Calculations}\label{M01-python-objects-and-reproducible-calculations}}

\noindent Python stores individual values in objects such as integers,
floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans. A list stores an ordered
collection; a dictionary associates names with values. A function
packages a calculation with explicit inputs and an output. These
distinctions matter when an assistant supplies code: a column of
numeric-looking strings does not behave like a numeric column, and an
empty string does not automatically represent a missing value.

Suppose two orders contain three product lines. Multiplying quantity by
unit price gives line sales; summing within each order gives order
sales. Returning each calculation as a number allows its result to be
checked and reused.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
lines = [
    {"order": "O1", "quantity": 2, "unit_price": 10.0},
    {"order": "O1", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 5.0},
    {"order": "O2", "quantity": 3, "unit_price": 4.0},
]

def line_sales(line):
    return line["quantity"] * line["unit_price"]

order_sales = {}
for line in lines:
    key = line["order"]
    order_sales[key] = order_sales.get(key, 0.0) + line_sales(line)

assert order_sales == {"O1": 25.0, "O2": 12.0}
assert sum(order_sales.values()) == 37.0
\end{Verbatim}

The total is \$37 across two orders, so average order value is \$18.50.
Dividing by the three product lines would instead give average line
sales, \$12.33. Neither denominator is inherently wrong; they describe
different objects. The mistake would be assigning one calculation the
other's interpretation.

A DataFrame provides a tabular interface for larger data. In pandas,
selecting columns, filtering rows, creating variables, grouping
observations, and joining tables are distinct operations. Use explicit
intermediate names when those operations change the unit of observation.
For example, \texttt{eligible\_lines}, \texttt{orders}, and
\texttt{customer\_months} communicate more than repeatedly overwriting
\texttt{df}. The
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/}{pandas
tutorials} provide syntax references; the analytical specification
should determine which operations are needed.

Notebook execution order can hide dependencies. A cell may work because
an earlier interactive command created a variable that is absent from
the saved notebook. Before describing a notebook as reproducible,
restart the kernel and run all cells in order. Store file paths relative
to the project, record package versions, and distinguish source data
from derived outputs. A random seed helps reproduce a simulation or
split, but it does not guarantee identical results across every software
version or computing platform.

\hypertarget{M01-case-study-a-coupon-campaign-specification}{%
\section{Case Study: A Coupon Campaign
Specification}\label{M01-case-study-a-coupon-campaign-specification}}

\noindent A retailer has a monthly contact budget for 5,000 customers. The
proposed campaign offers a discount on the next purchase. The manager
initially asks for ``a model to find our best customers.'' That request
leaves the action, outcome, and objective unresolved. The
highest-spending customers may receive the offer without changing their
behavior; customers likely to respond may buy products with low margins.

A usable specification would identify the decision date, eligible
customer population, offer, evaluation horizon, and objective. One
possibility is to maximize incremental contribution during the next 30
days, subject to the contact limit. Eligibility might require marketing
consent and an active account. The analysis should define contribution
after discounts, returns, fulfillment, and contact costs. It should
identify which customer information existed before assignment and how
untreated outcomes will be measured.

The initial dataset might include customer-level histories and a
randomized pilot. Without such a pilot or another credible design, a
response model can help describe or predict behavior, but the
incremental contribution calculation remains unresolved. A randomized
test can supply the incremental-response evidence needed to decide
whether a larger rollout is profitable.

A specification also needs acceptance criteria. The eligible-customer
table must have one row per customer, no post-assignment features, and
the intended date coverage. A campaign summary must reconcile assigned
counts, contact costs, purchases, and contribution. These checks are
small enough to state before asking an AI assistant to implement the
analysis. They protect the meaning of the result while allowing
flexibility in the code.

\hypertarget{M01-ai-assisted-coding-as-a-sequence-of-verifiable-steps}{%
\section{AI-Assisted Coding as a Sequence of Verifiable
Steps}\label{M01-ai-assisted-coding-as-a-sequence-of-verifiable-steps}}

\noindent An effective coding request names the inputs, output, definitions, and
checks. For the transaction example, ask for a function that accepts
product-line records, validates required fields, aggregates sales by
order, and returns both order totals and an exception report. Provide
the three-line example and its expected \$37 total. Ask the assistant to
explain what happens with a return, a missing order ID, or a duplicated
line.

Generate one analytical transformation at a time when the next step
depends on a definition. Inspect the proposed code before executing it,
especially commands that install software, delete files, upload data, or
invoke an external API. Read error messages as evidence about the code's
assumptions. A type error may reveal numeric values stored as strings; a
merge error may reveal an incorrect key. Repairing the error without
understanding its cause can preserve the underlying analytical mistake.

Verification should use both identities and meaningful counterexamples.
Order totals must sum to the line total for the same eligible rows. A
single known customer should produce a manually calculable summary. An
empty input should have an explicit result. A missing customer lookup
should not silently remove sales. These checks constrain what the
implementation is allowed to do without forcing one particular coding
style.

Keep a short record of consequential AI contributions: the task
requested, important changes to the plan or code, and the checks
performed. A saved conversation alone does not establish correctness.
The record should make it possible to explain why a transformation was
accepted.

\hypertarget{M01-interpreting-and-communicating-a-result}{%
\section{Interpreting and Communicating a
Result}\label{M01-interpreting-and-communicating-a-result}}

\noindent A useful recommendation names the decision, states the relevant estimate
with units and uncertainty, and explains how it changes the action.
``The model has high accuracy'' leaves the manager's decision
unresolved. ``At a \$3 contact cost and the stated contribution
assumptions, contact the customers with positive estimated incremental
contribution, subject to capacity'' connects the analysis to the
objective. The recommendation still needs evidence about how the
probabilities were estimated and whether the policy was evaluated on new
customers or periods.

Results should distinguish observation from assumption. A transaction
total is calculated from recorded eligible rows. A renewal probability
is an estimate. A contribution margin may be supplied by finance. An
untreated outcome for an offered customer is counterfactual. Listing
these roles prevents a spreadsheet or notebook from giving every input
the appearance of equal certainty.

If one customer places four orders and another places one, an
order-weighted mean gives the first customer four times the weight. If
both customers should count equally, calculate each customer's mean
first. If an AI-generated program reports six purchases from six product
lines, inspect whether purchase was defined as a line or an order. If an
offer has a high response rate, ask for the response rate under no offer
before interpreting the response as an effect.

\hypertarget{M01-mhealth-from-food-entries-to-a-decision-table}{%
\section{mHealth: From Food Entries to a Decision
Table}\label{M01-mhealth-from-food-entries-to-a-decision-table}}

\noindent An mHealth product manager must decide which food categories to suggest
when a customer returns to the app. Recent logs reveal repeated
categories, variation across days, and gaps in observation. The
immediate analytical task is to construct a reliable customer history. A
recommendation based on duplicated daily totals or an accidental change
in the customer population can look precise while describing the wrong
behavior.

The released files contain actual 2016 records. User identifiers have
been replaced, birthdays have been replaced with age on January 1, 2016,
and weight fields contain documented random perturbations. The food file
has 13,874,280 entries from 5,908 users. The separate daily file covers
a smaller set of users and dates. Food categories, descriptions, and
calorie fields retain their source values, apart from standardizing
provider references to mHealth. The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/DATA_DICTIONARY.md}{data dictionary}
defines the available fields and unresolved coding conventions. In
particular, \texttt{Weightchange}, \texttt{Goalplan}, and
\texttt{Gender} have undocumented code meanings. None establishes a
treatment, a behavioral goal, or a validated sex variable for an energy
equation.

The working cohort retains every entry for users whose first four
hexadecimal pseudonym digits have a value below 4,096. This fixed rule
reduces memory requirements and preserves within-user histories. Its
realized sample contains 917,153 entries, 370 users, and 76,804 observed
user-days. Ages at the reference date range from 17 to 76. The cohort is
a subset of app users who appear in the released file; it is not a
representative population sample. The adult nutrition sensitivity
analysis in M2 uses a separate age restriction.

A food-entry row records an item, while \texttt{Foodcalories} repeats
the source daily total. On the first eligible user-day selected by the
code below, five entries on July 4 have item calories summing to
1,132.7852. Each row repeats a daily total of 1,132.79. Summing that
repeated field gives 5,663.95, exactly five times the reported daily
total. The small difference between the item sum and one copy of the
daily total is compatible with rounding in this case. Larger
discrepancies elsewhere require investigation.

The daily key is \texttt{(Userid,\ date)}. A left join preserves all
76,804 cohort days, with 37,634 matched days and 39,170 unmatched days
in the separate daily file. Replacing it with an inner join would remove
more than half the cohort days. An unmatched row is therefore a
sample-definition decision, even if the software reports no error.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_mhealth_join.tex}
\caption{A left join preserves observed days while an inner join changes the analysis population.}\label{fig:M01_mhealth_join}
\end{figure}

The two branches retain the same matched records. Only the left-join
branch preserves the unmatched days needed to describe the food-log
cohort. Neither branch supplies unobserved calendar days.

\hypertarget{M01-loading-data-and-constructing-daily-measures}{%
\subsection{Loading Data and Constructing Daily
Measures}\label{M01-loading-data-and-constructing-daily-measures}}

\noindent Use Python 3.13 with NumPy 2.1.3, pandas 2.2.3, PyArrow 19.0.0, SciPy
1.15.3, scikit-learn 1.6.1, and statsmodels 0.14.4 to reproduce the
saved calculations. From the repository root, install the pinned
packages into an environment, verify the release files, and run the
analyses in dependency order:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
python -m pip install -r 03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/requirements.txt
python 03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/download_data.py
python 03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/run_all.py
\end{Verbatim}

The downloader checks the published SHA-256 hashes. The first run reads
the compressed food file in chunks and saves a local Parquet cache;
subsequent runs reuse it. The cache is excluded from Git. Delete the
\texttt{recurring\_examples/cache} directory to force a fresh
derivation. \texttt{common.py} supplies the same sample and measurement
functions to every module. Paths are relative to the script location, so
the saved programs can also be run from another working directory.

For each observed day, category breadth counts distinct recorded
categories, assigning missing labels to \texttt{Unclassified}.
Calorie-share variety uses the sum of included item calories as its
denominator. A negative or missing item calorie value invalidates that
day's share calculation; a nonpositive item sum also makes shares
undefined. These conditions affect calorie-based variety, while the
day's existence can still be used to measure logging. The first reported
daily total is retained only after checking that its nonmissing values
agree within the day.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/common.py}{common.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ common.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Shared input and measurement functions for the eight mHealth examples."""

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib
import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DATA = ROOT.parent / "data"
CACHE = ROOT / "cache"
OUTPUT = ROOT / "results"
SEED = 534
COHORT_THRESHOLD = 4096


def save_result(module, result):
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (OUTPUT / f"{module}.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(result, indent=2, allow_nan=False) + "\n"
    )


def load_food():
    """Keep all rows for users whose first four pseudonym hex digits are <4096."""
    CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    cached = CACHE / "food.parquet"
    metadata = CACHE / "source.json"
    manifest = json.loads((ROOT.parent / "manifest.json").read_text())
    signature = {
        "sha256": manifest["files"]["food_entries.csv.gz"]["sha256"],
        "threshold": COHORT_THRESHOLD,
        "preparation_version": 2,
    }
    if (
        cached.exists()
        and metadata.exists()
        and json.loads(metadata.read_text()) == signature
    ):
        return pd.read_parquet(cached)
    columns = [
        "Userid",
        "Fancydate",
        "Name",
        "Category",
        "Calories",
        "Foodcalories",
        "Budgetcalories",
        "Age_at_2016_01_01",
    ]
    parts = []
    for chunk in pd.read_csv(
        DATA / "food_entries.csv.gz", usecols=columns, chunksize=250000
    ):
        code = chunk.Userid.str.slice(1, 5).map(lambda value: int(value, 16))
        parts.append(chunk.loc[code < COHORT_THRESHOLD].copy())
    food = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
    food["date"] = pd.to_datetime(food.Fancydate)
    food["category"] = food.Category.fillna("Unclassified")
    food["description"] = (
        food.Name.fillna("")
        .str.casefold()
        .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
        .str.strip()
    )
    food.to_parquet(cached, index=False)
    metadata.write_text(json.dumps(signature, indent=2) + "\n")
    return food


def make_daily(food):
    """One row per observed user-day; missing calendar days are not created."""
    keys = ["Userid", "date"]
    grouped = food.groupby(keys, observed=True)
    daily = grouped.agg(
        entries=("Calories", "size"),
        category_count=("category", "nunique"),
        item_calories=("Calories", "sum"),
        food_calories=("Foodcalories", "first"),
        budget_calories=("Budgetcalories", "first"),
        daily_total_versions=("Foodcalories", "nunique"),
        budget_versions=("Budgetcalories", "nunique"),
    )
    daily.loc[daily.daily_total_versions != 1, "food_calories"] = np.nan
    daily.loc[daily.budget_versions != 1, "budget_calories"] = np.nan
    invalid = food.Calories.isna() | food.Calories.lt(0)
    daily["invalid_item_calories"] = invalid.groupby([food.Userid, food.date]).sum()
    categories = food.groupby(keys + ["category"], observed=True).Calories.sum()
    category_totals = categories.groupby(level=keys).transform("sum")
    concentration = (
        (categories / category_totals.where(category_totals > 0))
        .pow(2)
        .groupby(level=keys)
        .sum(min_count=1)
    )
    daily["variety"] = (1 - concentration).where(
        (daily.item_calories > 0) & (daily.invalid_item_calories == 0)
    )
    daily = daily.reset_index().sort_values(keys).reset_index(drop=True)
    assert not daily.duplicated(keys).any()
    assert daily.variety.dropna().between(-1e-10, 1 + 1e-10).all()
    return daily


def make_baskets(food):
    """Distinct observed categories; the missing-category label is not a candidate."""
    selected = food.loc[
        food.category != "Unclassified", ["Userid", "date", "category"]
    ].drop_duplicates()
    return (
        selected.groupby(["Userid", "date"], observed=True)
        .category.agg(lambda values: tuple(sorted(values)))
        .reset_index(name="basket")
    )


def description_holdout(text):
    """A fixed description-level split independent of labels or outcomes."""
    return int(hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:8], 16) % 5 == 0


def load_inputs():
    food = load_food()
    return food, make_daily(food), make_baskets(food)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    food, daily, baskets = load_inputs()
    daily.to_parquet(CACHE / "daily.parquet", index=False)
    baskets.to_parquet(CACHE / "baskets.parquet", index=False)
    result = {
        "rows": len(food),
        "users": int(food.Userid.nunique()),
        "user_days": len(daily),
        "categories": int(food.category.nunique()),
        "missing_category_rows": int(food.Category.isna().sum()),
        "invalid_item_calorie_rows": int(
            (food.Calories.isna() | food.Calories.lt(0)).sum()
        ),
        "days_with_inconsistent_daily_total": int(
            daily.daily_total_versions.ne(1).sum()
        ),
        "days_with_inconsistent_budget": int(daily.budget_versions.ne(1).sum()),
        "nonpositive_recorded_daily_totals": int(daily.food_calories.le(0).sum()),
        "variety_eligible_days": int(daily.variety.notna().sum()),
        "item_total_matches_recorded_total_within_one": int(
            (daily.item_calories - daily.food_calories).abs().le(1).sum()
        ),
    }
    save_result("cohort", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M01-join-validation-and-a-hand-checkable-day}{%
\subsection{Join Validation and a Hand-Checkable
Day}\label{M01-join-validation-and-a-hand-checkable-day}}

\noindent The join declares a one-to-one relationship and records unmatched keys.
The small day-level example checks both candidate aggregations against
the repeated total. Keeping these checks beside the join prevents a
later model from silently inheriting a different denominator.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/m01.py}{m01.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ m01.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Assess the cohort, repeated totals, and the separate daily file."""

import json
import pandas as pd
from common import DATA, load_inputs, save_result

food, daily, baskets = load_inputs()
other = pd.read_csv(DATA / "daily_records.csv.gz", usecols=["Userid", "Fancydate"])
other["date"] = pd.to_datetime(other.Fancydate)
assert not other.duplicated(["Userid", "date"]).any()
joined = daily.merge(
    other[["Userid", "date"]],
    how="left",
    on=["Userid", "date"],
    validate="one_to_one",
    indicator=True,
)
assert len(joined) == len(daily)
example = daily.loc[(daily.entries.between(3, 6)) & daily.food_calories.gt(0)].iloc[0]
rows = food.loc[food.Userid.eq(example.Userid) & food.date.eq(example.date)]
result = {
    "rows": len(food),
    "users": int(food.Userid.nunique()),
    "days": len(daily),
    "matched_days": int(joined._merge.eq("both").sum()),
    "unmatched_days": int(joined._merge.eq("left_only").sum()),
    "example_date": str(example.date.date()),
    "example_entries": len(rows),
    "example_item_sum": float(rows.Calories.sum()),
    "example_daily_total": float(example.food_calories),
    "example_wrong_sum": float(rows.Foodcalories.sum()),
}
save_result("M01", result)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M01-data-cleaning-as-a-sequence-of-decisions}{%
\subsection{Data Cleaning as a Sequence of
Decisions}\label{M01-data-cleaning-as-a-sequence-of-decisions}}

\noindent Structural checks stop calculations that violate their stated
observation unit. A duplicate key in a daily lookup can multiply food
records, so it must be resolved before joining. Review flags serve a
different purpose: they identify observations whose meaning needs
investigation. The cohort contains 52,838 rows equal on the selected
fields of user, day, normalized description, category, and calories.
Those fields omit event timestamps and meal identifiers. Repeated
servings can therefore produce equal rows. Automatically dropping them
would impose an unsupported definition of duplication.

The assessment finds 206 food rows with missing categories, one negative
item calorie value, and 23 days with a nonpositive sum of item calories.
The calorie-share calculation consequently excludes 24 days. By
contrast, 319 days have a nonpositive reported daily total. These counts
differ because the item sum and reported total are separate
measurements. Their discrepancy exceeds one calorie unit on 23,729 days.
These flags can overlap and must not be added as if they represented
disjoint exclusions.

A value outside a chosen review range is evidence for inspection, not
proof of an error. The reported daily calorie median is 1,475.63, and
the range is 0 to 9,190. A review flag below 100 or above 5,000 marks
651 days. Those thresholds are imposed sensitivity choices. They do not
establish nutritional adequacy or identify incorrect reports. Preserve
the released values, add flags, document the rule for each analysis, and
report the resulting sample. M2 compares nutrition-informed
alternatives; M3 repeats a regression after a stated restriction.

A useful AI coding request is: ``Create separate structural checks and
review flags. Stop on a duplicate daily key, preserve repeated food
entries, count overlapping flags separately, and return the retained
sample for each calculation.'' Verify the proposed implementation with a
two-entry day whose repeated total is 100 and whose calorie shares are
0.9 and 0.1. It must produce a daily total of 100 and variety of 0.18. A
gap from January 1 to January 3 must remain a missing January 2
observation. The executable counterexamples are in
\texttt{test\_logic.py}.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/assessment.py}{assessment.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ assessment.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Separate structural failures, review flags, and analysis-specific exclusions."""

import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from common import DATA, load_inputs, save_result


def require_unique(frame, keys):
    if frame[keys].isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("Missing join key")
    if frame.duplicated(keys).any():
        raise ValueError("Duplicate key at the declared observation unit")


def daily_flags(daily):
    flags = pd.DataFrame(index=daily.index)
    flags["invalid_item"] = daily.invalid_item_calories.gt(0)
    flags["nonpositive_item_sum"] = daily.item_calories.le(0)
    flags["nonpositive_daily_total"] = daily.food_calories.le(0)
    flags["missing_daily_total"] = daily.food_calories.isna()
    flags["total_discrepancy_over_one"] = (
        (daily.food_calories - daily.item_calories).abs().gt(1)
    )
    flags["daily_total_below_100_or_above_5000"] = daily.food_calories.lt(
        100
    ) | daily.food_calories.gt(5000)
    return flags


def run_assessment():
    food, daily, baskets = load_inputs()
    assert food.Userid.notna().all() and food.date.notna().all()
    assert food.date.between("2016-01-01", "2016-12-31").all()
    require_unique(daily, ["Userid", "date"])
    # Repeated entries can be legitimate. Flag equality on these fields without deletion.
    fields = ["Userid", "date", "description", "category", "Calories"]
    duplicate_flags = food.duplicated(fields, keep=False)
    flags = daily_flags(daily)
    health = pd.read_csv(
        DATA / "daily_records.csv.gz",
        usecols=["Userid", "Fancydate", "Age_at_2016_01_01", "Currentweight"],
    )
    health = health.loc[health.Userid.isin(food.Userid.unique())]
    require_unique(health, ["Userid", "Fancydate"])
    age_versions = health.groupby("Userid").Age_at_2016_01_01.nunique(dropna=False)
    assert age_versions.eq(1).all()
    result = {
        "food_rows": len(food),
        "daily_rows": len(daily),
        "missing_category_rows": int(food.Category.isna().sum()),
        "rows_equal_on_selected_entry_fields": int(duplicate_flags.sum()),
        "missing_item_calorie_rows": int(food.Calories.isna().sum()),
        "negative_item_calorie_rows": int(food.Calories.lt(0).sum()),
        "flags_by_user_day": {key: int(value) for key, value in flags.sum().items()},
        "recorded_calorie_quantiles": {
            str(q): float(value)
            for q, value in daily.food_calories.quantile(
                [0, 0.01, 0.5, 0.99, 1]
            ).items()
        },
        "matched_daily_file_rows": len(health),
        "fixed_age_min": int(health.Age_at_2016_01_01.min()),
        "fixed_age_max": int(health.Age_at_2016_01_01.max()),
        "nonpositive_weight_rows": int(health.Currentweight.le(0).sum()),
    }
    save_result("assessment", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_assessment()
\end{Verbatim}

"""File output and arithmetic helpers for synthetic lecture examples."""

import csv
import itertools
import json
import math
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def write_csv(name, fields, rows):
    with (ROOT / name).open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        out = csv.writer(f)
        out.writerow(fields)
        out.writerows(rows)


def ols_slope(points):
    xbar = sum(x for x, y in points) / len(points)
    ybar = sum(y for x, y in points) / len(points)
    slope = sum((x - xbar) * (y - ybar) for x, y in points) / sum(
        (x - xbar) ** 2 for x, y in points
    )
    return {"intercept": ybar - slope * xbar, "slope": slope}


def shares(utilities):
    weights = {key: math.exp(val) for key, val in utilities.items()}
    return {key: weight / sum(weights.values()) for key, weight in weights.items()}
\end{Verbatim}

r = {}
lines = [("O1", "C1", 2, 10), ("O1", "C1", 1, 5), ("O2", "C2", 3, 4)]
write_csv(

for order, customer, qty, price in lines:

\hypertarget{M01-mhealth-a-verifiable-monthly-business-review}{%
\section{mHealth: A Verifiable Monthly Business
Review}\label{M01-mhealth-a-verifiable-monthly-business-review}}

\noindent \noindent An mHealth manager needs to decide whether a decline in food
entries warrants attention to customer engagement. Entry counts combine
the number of eligible customers, the length of the reporting month, the
frequency of logging, and the intensity of logging on observed days. A
decline can arise from any of these components. The comparison becomes
interpretable when the eligible population is fixed before the reporting
periods and every component has an explicit denominator.

Define the population as users in the teaching cohort with at least one
observed day before May 1, 2016. All members remain in the May and June
denominators, including those with no logs in a month. A missing day
contributes zero to the indicator for an observed log; its food
consumption remains unobserved. For month \(t\), the number of entries
satisfies the accounting identity

\[
L_t=N D_t p_t a_t,
\]

where \(N\) is the fixed number of eligible users, \(D_t\) is calendar
days in the month, \(p_t\) is observed user-days divided by \(ND_t\),
and \(a_t\) is entries per observed user-day. The identity separates
calendar exposure from logging behavior. It uses counts of records, with
no assumption that an entry represents a purchase or a complete meal.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Quantity & May & June \\
\midrule

Eligible Users & 340 & 340 \\
Calendar User-Days & 10,540 & 10,200 \\
Observed User-Days & 7,082 & 6,331 \\
Observed Logging Fraction & 0.6719 & 0.6207 \\
Entries per Observed Day & 11.7995 & 11.6910 \\
Food Entries & 83,564 & 74,016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The table identifies a 5.12 percentage-point decline in the logging
fraction, alongside a shorter month and a modest decline in entries per
observed day. Changing the denominator to users who happened to log
during June would remove inactive members from the comparison. The
fixed-population result supports investigation of engagement, recording
practices, and seasonality. It supplies no estimate of a campaign effect
or change in nutrition.

An AI-assisted business review should retrieve numerical claims from a
computed evidence file. The file below records the source checksum,
membership rule, observation unit, month, numerator, and denominator. A
useful coding request is: ``Construct the fixed cohort before May, count
distinct user-dates, retain members with zero logs, and verify the
accounting identity separately for each month.'' The independent
calculation must finish before an assistant writes the managerial
explanation.

The \href{https://github.com/takechanman1228/claude-ecom}{claude-ecom
reference} separates numerical computation from a narrative layer for
ecommerce reviews. The mHealth calculation applies that separation to
logging data. Its descriptive evidence file also supplies the
structured-claim checks in M8.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/reporting.py}{reporting.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ reporting.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Compute a verifiable, fixed-cohort mHealth business review locally."""

import json
import pandas as pd
from common import ROOT, load_food, save_result


def monthly_review(food):
    # Fix membership before either reporting month; retain zero-log users.
    members = sorted(food.loc[food.date < "2016-05-01", "Userid"].unique())
    rows = []
    for month in ["2016-05", "2016-06"]:
        period = pd.Period(month, freq="M")
        part = food.loc[
            food.Userid.isin(members) & food.date.dt.to_period("M").eq(period)
        ]
        days = part[["Userid", "date"]].drop_duplicates()
        denominator = len(members) * period.days_in_month
        assert len(days) <= denominator
        rows.append(
            {
                "period": month,
                "eligible_users": len(members),
                "calendar_user_days": denominator,
                "observed_user_days": len(days),
                "users_with_logs": int(days.Userid.nunique()),
                "food_entries": len(part),
                "logging_fraction": len(days) / denominator,
                "entries_per_observed_day": len(part) / len(days),
            }
        )
    manifest = json.loads((ROOT.parent / "manifest.json").read_text())
    return {
        "source_sha256": manifest["files"]["food_entries.csv.gz"]["sha256"],
        "membership": "At least one observed day before 2016-05-01",
        "unit": "eligible user-calendar-day",
        "metric": "logging_fraction",
        "interpretation": "descriptive",
        "periods": rows,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = monthly_review(load_food())
    save_result("reporting", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M01-customer-data-and-the-coding-environment}{%
\section{Customer Data and the Coding
Environment}\label{M01-customer-data-and-the-coding-environment}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team deciding whom to contact needs a defined set
of customer information. Additional fields can increase exposure without
improving the decision. Begin with the unit of analysis, the intended
calculation, and the information available before contact. A transaction
date can be necessary for a forecasting split; a customer's name usually
contributes nothing to that split. A reproducible pipeline should make
these distinctions visible in its input schema.

An AI coding tool can receive information through prompts, uploaded
files, logs, screenshots, or repository access. Generate and debug a
transformation using a small synthetic table when real records are
unnecessary. Before using actual records, establish whether that
environment is authorized for those fields and that purpose. An
assistant's ability to read a file does not establish the firm's
authority to transmit it. Access, processing location, retention, and
permitted uses belong to the specification of the work.

The mHealth exercises provide a concrete comparison. Ages and perturbed
weights support selected teaching calculations, while exact birthdays
are unnecessary. Replacing identifiers and perturbing one measurement do
not establish anonymity for every possible linkage. A useful
implementation loads the minimum required columns, avoids printing
individual histories into logs, and publishes aggregate results with
their denominators. Students can inspect generated code for file
uploads, external API calls, and unnecessary exports before running it.
These checks concern observable data flows and preserve the ability to
reproduce the local analysis.

\hypertarget{M01-a-failed-analysis-can-require-different-evidence}{%
\section{A Failed Analysis Can Require Different
Evidence}\label{M01-a-failed-analysis-can-require-different-evidence}}

\noindent \noindent A manager commissioning an AI-assisted analysis must choose
what to change when the answer remains unreliable. A wrong join requires
a correction to the program. A missing observation requires an
information decision. A poorly defined target requires a clearer
managerial question. These diagnoses lead to different uses of time and
money, even when all three failures initially appear as an
unsatisfactory answer from the same assistant.

The mHealth records make the distinction concrete. Repeated daily totals
can be counted once using the user-day key, and a join can preserve the
intended cohort. Those changes improve calculations on recorded
information. Food consumed without a corresponding log remains
unobserved. Estimating total consumption would require additional
measurement or assumptions linking logging to consumption. An analysis
of recorded food categories can instead proceed with its population and
outcome stated explicitly.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Difficulty & Useful Response & Evidence of Resolution \\
\midrule

Daily totals are repeated across food entries & Correct aggregation at
the user-day level & Reconcile one day by hand and compare totals \\
An item description maps to several categories & Obtain a reference
label or retain the ambiguity & Evaluate separately adjudicated
descriptions \\
Food consumption was never recorded & Collect additional evidence or
define a recorded-behavior outcome & Check the measurement process and
stated population \\
A coupon model predicts response but the decision requires
incrementality & Establish an untreated comparison & Evaluate assignment
and contribution over a common horizon \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

A useful request to a coding assistant states the decision, the
unresolved distinction, and the smallest check that could resolve it.
For example: ``Construct one row per observed user-day, retain unmatched
daily records, and reconcile item calories with one copy of the daily
total. Identify which conclusions would additionally require unrecorded
consumption.'' The request gives the assistant a verifiable task while
keeping the missing-information question visible.

An alternative procedure can also remove a costly intermediate step. If
a campaign decision requires category totals, a validated category
aggregation may avoid generating individual prose summaries that nobody
uses. The required customer protections and analytical meaning remain
fixed. Simplification is valuable when the resulting output still
answers the decision and passes its checks. Reusable functions then
become investments whose subsequent benefits and maintenance costs can
be compared, as in M8, Section 8.17.

\hypertarget{M01-model-versions-and-the-scope-of-an-ai-claim}{%
\section{Model Versions and the Scope of an AI
Claim}\label{M01-model-versions-and-the-scope-of-an-ai-claim}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team considering an AI coding service needs to
know which tasks it performs reliably in the intended workflow. The
statement that a model can produce correct Python leaves several
economically relevant conditions unspecified. A script may solve a
calculation after manual repair while failing the team's automated
parser. It may pass familiar examples while mishandling a new customer
identifier or a changed data schema. These outcomes imply different
verification costs and different feasible uses.

\href{https://hdsr.mitpress.mit.edu/pub/y95zitmz/release/2}{Chen,
Zaharia, and Zou (2024)}, Section 3.5, distinguish directly executable
outputs from correctness after removing surrounding noncode text. Their
March and June 2023 comparisons show why the interface around generated
code belongs in the evaluation. A claim about a particular historical
configuration provides evidence about that configuration. Transferring
it to a replacement requires a comparison on the relevant tasks.

A reproducible claim specifies the model identifier and evaluation date,
system and user prompts, tools, reasoning and sampling settings, token
or cost budget, input version, parsing rule, scoring rule, and
denominator. For an mHealth aggregation, the output contract could
require one row per user-month, preservation of users with no recorded
entries, and reconciliation to independently calculated totals. For
earnings-call extraction, it could require the complete relevant passage
and a distinction between a stated plan and an implemented policy. These
requirements remain meaningful when the model changes.

Retain a fixed set of known failure cases to detect regressions and a
separate supply of fresh cases to assess transfer.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314v2}{LiveBench} and
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07974v2}{LiveCodeBench} motivate
refreshed evaluation with objective scoring. New cases should preserve
the target task mix or report its changes explicitly. Repeated tuning
against the same public answers consumes their value as fresh evidence.
Revalidation is warranted after changes to the model, prompt, tool,
scorer, schema, or supported customer population.

\noindent A model change can alter the behavior of dependent components
even when its own reference score improves. M7 §§7.31--7.32 separate
draft-token verification, answer correctness, and request resolution.
Record target and drafter versions, generation settings, and the
complete attempted-request roster before comparing an updated assistant.

\hypertarget{M01-specifications-independent-checks-and-retained-skills}{%
\section{Specifications, Independent Checks, and Retained
Skills}\label{M01-specifications-independent-checks-and-retained-skills}}

\noindent \noindent A manager who delegates a customer analysis must still define
the decision, the observation unit, and the evidence that would justify
action. Before requesting code, write the required inputs,
transformation, output, and a small calculation that can be checked
independently. If the objective is retention, specify the starting
cohort and horizon. If it is an incremental marketing effect, specify
the treatment comparison and assignment process. A working program can
faithfully implement an unsuitable target.

Compare anonymous outputs using criteria fixed before inspecting their
style. Reopen the saved artifact, run the calculation, and inspect the
result that matters for the decision. An assistant's statement that it
completed a task supplies a claim to verify. A check against
independently calculated totals supplies additional evidence. Record
both execution time and correction effort when comparing workflows.

After assisted work, explain the analytical choice and solve a new small
instance without the assistant. This establishes whether the relevant
skill can be demonstrated at that moment. A long-term claim about
learning requires repeated assessment and a suitable comparison.
\href{https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs193t/cs193t.1272/assignments/1-ai-foundations/}{Stanford
CS193T's AI Foundations activity} motivates explicit decisions about
which skills to preserve; the
\href{https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs193t/cs193t.1272/assignments/6-coding-agents/}{coding-agent
activity} connects a working result to a documented failure or unchecked
component. The source and grader calculations in Sections 5.19 and 5.20
provide hand-checkable instances.

\hypertarget{M01-reproducible-calculations-and-product-recommendations}{%
\section{Reproducible Calculations and Product
Recommendations}\label{M01-reproducible-calculations-and-product-recommendations}}

\noindent \noindent A product manager deciding which concepts warrant human
research needs to understand how an analyst constructed the reported
preference scores. A second analyst may reproduce every number and still
interpret the recommendation incorrectly if the report leaves its
weights or population unclear. The synthetic refill example makes this
distinction visible. Two invented personas have Set 1 expected ratings
of 4.25 and 3.70 on categories one through five. Persona p01 contributes
two identical responses, while persona p02 contributes one. These are
authored responses with imposed similarities; no person or language
model produced them in an observed study.

Giving each persona equal weight yields \((4.25+3.70)/2=3.975\). Giving
each response row equal weight yields \((2\times4.25+3.70)/3=4.066667\).
Both calculations are reproducible, but they answer different questions.
The first treats the two personas as equally represented. The second
gives the persona with more responses a larger share of the result.
Repeating an identical response changes that share without changing
either persona's preference. The observation unit and intended weighting
therefore belong beside the number in a managerial report.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_repeat_weights.tex}
\caption{Identical responses raise the row-weighted mean while both persona ratings remain fixed. The equal-persona mean stays at 3.975 as p01 repeats increase from one to five and p02 supplies one response.}\label{fig:M01_repeat_weights}
\end{figure}

With five identical p01 responses and one p02 response, the row-weighted
mean reaches 4.158333. The equal-persona mean remains 3.975. A figure
whose horizontal axis counts responses and whose vertical axis reports
ratings makes the changed composition explicit. The increasing series
describes an imposed weighting effect; it supplies no evidence of
preference change or additional independent information.

A separate six-concept construction compares pooled and reversed rating
patterns against invented reference counts. The pooled pattern gives
every concept the same mean, so correlation and a unique shortlist
remain undefined. The reversed pattern selects F and E and retains zero
of the reference top two, A and B. An assistant that turns the pooled
result into a launch recommendation has added unsupported meaning even
if it quotes the distribution score correctly. Both candidate patterns
use reference outcomes in their construction. A human study with
separate development and evaluation concepts would be needed to assess
performance on new concepts.

\hypertarget{M01-a-report-with-traceable-numerical-evidence}{%
\subsection{A Report with Traceable Numerical
Evidence}\label{M01-a-report-with-traceable-numerical-evidence}}

\noindent \noindent Recomputing a table can reveal that the saved result no longer
matches its inputs or program. The program below imports the complete
mapping and screening functions in Sections 5.23 and 4.23, recomputes
four saved tables, and stops if any table disagrees. It writes a short
recommendation and a JSON evidence file containing the sample counts,
quantities, missing values, and hashes of the inputs and calculation
files. Independent arithmetic establishes the reference values above.
Agreement between a saved table and the program that created it supplies
a separate consistency check.

Keep the two example folders together within the course checkout. Paths
resolve from the program's location, so changing the terminal directory
does not change which inputs it reads. The output option adjusts
relative links when the report moves. A reader can follow the
recommendation to its evidence file, source program, data dictionary,
inputs, and figure. Record the Python version and command when rerunning
it. The script uses only the standard library and makes no network or
model calls.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Reproducible_Recommendations/reproduce_recommendation.py}{reproduce\_recommendation.py}.
From the course root, run
\texttt{python3\ 03\_Data\_and\_Code/Reproducible\_Recommendations/reproduce\_recommendation.py}.
From its folder, run \texttt{python3\ reproduce\_recommendation.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Recompute a synthetic recommendation and retain its numerical evidence.

Python 3.10+, standard library. No network, model, or editor calls.
The two input constructions are separate; all personas and panels are invented.
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import sys

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = ROOT.parent / "Synthetic_Consumers"
sys.path.insert(0, str(SOURCE))
from anchor_measurement import score_responses, summarize
from concept_screening import evaluate


def load(path):
    return json.loads(path.read_text())


def calculate(source=SOURCE):
    records = score_responses(load(source / "data/anchor_responses.json"))
    concepts = summarize(records)
    screening, details = evaluate(load(source / "data/concept_panels.json"))
    computed = dict(response_ratings=records, concept_ratings=concepts,
                    screening_summary=screening, screening_details=details)
    for name, value in computed.items():
        if load(source / f"results/{name}.json") != value:
            raise ValueError(f"Saved {name} disagrees with a fresh calculation.")
    refill = next(r for r in concepts
                  if r["concept"] == "refill" and r["anchor_set"] == "set_1")
    first = next(r for r in records if r["concept"] == "refill"
                 and r["persona"] == "p01" and r["repeat"] == 1
                 and r["anchor_set"] == "set_1")
    second = next(r for r in records if r["concept"] == "refill"
                  and r["persona"] == "p02" and r["anchor_set"] == "set_1")
    # Hold each persona's rating fixed and vary p01's identical repeat count.
    sensitivity = [dict(p01_repeats=n, p02_repeats=1,
        equal_persona_mean=(first["mean_rating"] + second["mean_rating"]) / 2,
        equal_row_mean=(n * first["mean_rating"] + second["mean_rating"]) / (n + 1))
        for n in range(1, 6)]
    tracked = [source / "data/anchor_responses.json",
               source / "data/concept_panels.json",
               SOURCE / "anchor_measurement.py", SOURCE / "concept_screening.py",
               ROOT / "reproduce_recommendation.py"]
    return dict(scope="Entirely synthetic; no model or customer observations",
        response_mean=first["mean_rating"], response_distribution=first["distribution"],
        equal_persona_mean=refill["mean_rating"],
        equal_row_mean=refill["row_weighted_mean"],
        response_rows=refill["response_rows"], personas=refill["personas"],
        repeat_sensitivity=sensitivity, screening=screening,
        sha256={p.parent.name + "/" + p.name:
                hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in tracked})


def write_report(result, output):
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (output / "evidence.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(result, indent=2, allow_nan=False) + "\n")
    link = lambda path: Path(os.path.relpath(path, output)).as_posix()
    rows = {r["candidate"]: r for r in result["screening"]}
    selected = lambda row: ("unresolved" if row["selected"] is None
                            else ", ".join(row["selected"]))
    pooled, reversed_row = rows["pooled"], rows["reversed"]
    correlation = ("undefined" if pooled["pearson"] is None
                   else f"{pooled['pearson']:.3f}")
    recall = ("undefined" if reversed_row["top_two_recall"] is None
              else f"{reversed_row['top_two_recall']:.0%}")
    lines = ["# Product-Screening Recommendation", "", "By Nathan Yang", "",
        "A product manager must decide which concepts warrant human research. "
        "All inputs below are invented. No model calls or customer study took place.", "",
        "## Response Weights", "",
        f"The refill example has {result['response_rows']} response rows from "
        f"{result['personas']} personas. Equal persona weights give "
        f"{result['equal_persona_mean']:.3f}; equal row weights give "
        f"{result['equal_row_mean']:.6f} on a five-category rating scale.", "",
        "Persona p01's first response has the following imposed category weights.", "",
        "| Rating | Weight |", "| --- | --- |"]
    lines += [f"| {k} | {p:.2f} |"
              for k, p in enumerate(result["response_distribution"], 1)]
    lines += ["", rf"The expected rating is $\sum_{{k=1}}^{{5}}k p_k={result['response_mean']:.2f}$.", "",
        "![Identical repeats raise the row mean while the persona mean stays fixed]("
        + link(ROOT.parents[1] / "06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M01_repeat_weights.png") + ")", "",
        "## Concept Selection", "",
        f"A separate construction compares {pooled['concepts']} invented concepts "
        "with an invented reference panel. The pooled pattern's shortlist is "
        f"{selected(pooled)} and its correlation is {correlation}. "
        f"The reversed pattern selects {selected(reversed_row)}. Its recall of "
        f"the reference top two ({', '.join(reversed_row['reference_top_two'])}) "
        f"is {recall}.", "",
        "These patterns use reference outcomes in their construction. Their results "
        "justify checking ranking errors before funding a human study. They supply "
        "no evidence of actual purchase demand or out-of-sample performance.", "",
        "An assumed research budget of \\$500 and an assumed incentive of \\$25 "
        "per participant allow 20 incentives before recruitment and operating costs. "
        "This arithmetic does not determine an adequate study size.", "",
        "## Reproduction", "",
        "[Numerical evidence](evidence.json) | [Full Python]("
        + link(ROOT / "reproduce_recommendation.py") + ") | [Data dictionary]("
        + link(SOURCE / "DATA_DICTIONARY.md") + ")", "",
        "[Response inputs](" + link(SOURCE / "data/anchor_responses.json")
        + ") | [Concept inputs](" + link(SOURCE / "data/concept_panels.json") + ")", "",
        "From the course root: `python3 "
        "03_Data_and_Code/Reproducible_Recommendations/reproduce_recommendation.py`.", ""]
    (output / "recommendation.md").write_text("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=ROOT / "results")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    write_report(calculate(), args.output.resolve())
    print("Recomputed four saved tables and wrote evidence.json and recommendation.md.")
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M01-the-meaning-of-a-successful-check}{%
\subsection{The Meaning of a Successful
Check}\label{M01-the-meaning-of-a-successful-check}}

\noindent \noindent A calculation check establishes a numerical property under the
specified inputs and rules. A file hash establishes identity. Neither
establishes that invented personas represent actual customers. Review an
AI-written interpretation against the observation unit, weighting rule,
uncertainty, and proposed action. Preserve undefined values as missing;
replacing an unresolved shortlist with an arbitrary alphabetical order
would turn an implementation convention into a substantive
recommendation.

A file conversion also requires its own checks. The report contains
currency, a mathematical expression, a table, and a linked figure.
Reopen the exported document and verify their meaning and destinations.
The inspected
\href{https://github.com/harrywang/suzuri/blob/88f58aae544bdc60d5068e7b5d40a05ca7f1a564/crates/markdown_export/src/preprocess.rs}{Suzuri
0.7.0 source} converts internal wikilinks to display text and records
missing note embeds separately from conversion success. These behaviors
explain why an export can finish while navigation or content remains
incomplete. Standard relative links, explicit missing-file checks, and
inspection of the final document address those questions. The
\href{../07_Labs/Reproducible_Recommendations/README.md}{optional
exercise} distinguishes reproducible course calculations from
editor-specific tests.

\hypertarget{M01-definitions-inference-and-evidence}{%
\section{Definitions, Inference, and
Evidence}\label{M01-definitions-inference-and-evidence}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription manager asks an AI assistant for a cancellation
rate and unresolved requests. Define the customer, subscription,
request, and completed cancellation before counting them. A request
records a communicated intention; a confirmation records a claimed state
transition. Equating these events can raise the reported completion rate
and remove unresolved requests from the service queue.

An ontology specifies classes of objects, relationships among them, and
rules that support additional statements. An account is an object; a
particular cancellation request is another object related to a
subscription and a time. A class such as CancellationRequest can be a
subclass of ServiceRecord. Assigning an event to the first class then
supports membership in the second. A data dictionary supplies names and
units, while an ontology adds relationships and their implications. Both
depend on substantive decisions about what the records mean.

The \href{https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-primer/}{W3C OWL 2 Primer}
distinguishes inference from the absence of information. A domain axiom
saying that the subject of \texttt{requestedBy} is a CancellationRequest
lets a reasoner infer that type when it encounters the relationship. It
need not reject a row that lacks an explicit type. Under an open-world
interpretation, a missing confirmation can remain unknown. A rule
searching a supplied table for requests without confirmations answers a
narrower operational question about the available records.

Data validation instead asks whether the supplied information satisfies
specified requirements. A timestamp requirement can reject a missing
value before applying a reporting cutoff. A confirmation can be checked
for a matching subscription and a time no earlier than its request.
\href{https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/}{SHACL} provides a standard for
expressing graph-validation conditions. Logical inference, validation,
and source verification answer different questions. A logically
consistent set of false statements remains consistent; an inconsistent
classification can reflect an inappropriate axiom or an erroneous
observation.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_cancellation_evidence.tex}
\caption{Cancellation evidence separates event classification, checks on records, and a review decision. A request without an accepted confirmation remains in the review queue.}\label{fig:M01_cancellation_evidence}
\end{figure}

The \href{https://learn-ontology.vercel.app/\#learn}{Ontology
Playground} uses short prediction-and-trace exercises to make rule
implications visible. For a marketing application, state an expected
inference, inspect the facts and rules that produce it, and then
challenge their empirical justification. The complete cancellation
calculation in §2.25 preserves the reporting population, exclusion
reasons, and observation times. Successful code execution establishes
that the implemented calculation ran. Whether the calculation represents
the intended commercial event requires those additional checks.

Predicted acceptance does not establish permission. Preserve the source,
time, scope, and withdrawal conditions of permission records
independently of inferred preferences. Section 9.19 connects these
distinctions to the justification of a firm's conduct.

\hypertarget{M01-information-tools-and-a-verified-analysis}{%
\section{Information, Tools, and a Verified
Analysis}\label{M01-information-tools-and-a-verified-analysis}}

\noindent \noindent A manager considering customer outreach first needs a measure
of recorded activity. A coding assistant can produce a plausible table
while counting food entries as days, omitting customers with no later
records, or including observations beyond the reporting window. Each
error changes the population or quantity relevant to the decision.
Supplying a model with a clear question begins the analysis; the files
it can inspect, operations it can perform, and checks it receives also
affect the result.

An agent harness is the execution system surrounding a model. Its
components include tools, task context, state retained between steps,
resource limits, execution records, verification, and permissions. Li
and coauthors'
\href{../01_Resources/35_Agent_Workflow_Evaluation/README.md}{survey},
especially §§5 and 8, connects these components to reproducible
evaluation. A useful implementation stores the current task definition
and input versions, executes small changes, and retains evidence of
their results. A progress note that says a calculation passed should
link to the calculation and its output. After a reset or interruption,
the assistant can then recover the relevant state without treating its
earlier assertion as proof.

The recurring mHealth task fixes eligibility using food records from
January through June 2016 within the established pseudonym-selected
cohort. The resulting roster contains 358 users. July activity counts
distinct dates from July 1 inclusive to August 1 exclusive. Every roster
user receives 31 possible days. The source contains no
account-enrollment registry; eligibility means observed earlier in this
released file. A zero for July means no recorded food-log day in that
window. It supplies no measurement of food intake on the missing days.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Quantity & July Development Task & August Evaluation Task \\
\midrule

Earlier-period roster users & 358 & 358 \\
Calendar days per user & 31 & 31 \\
Possible user-days & 11,098 & 11,098 \\
Recorded user-days & 6,455 & 6,501 \\
Users with no recorded days & 39 & 41 \\
Mean recorded logging rate & 58.16\% & 58.58\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The mean gives each roster user equal weight. The inputs include
observed boundary dates immediately before and after the target
interval. Excluding those dates and collapsing repeated dates are
separate operations. An inner join to July records would omit the
zero-log users and change the target to activity conditional on having a
July record. Retaining the roster before counting preserves the intended
comparison.

\hypertarget{M01-information-and-feedback-as-separate-choices}{%
\subsection{Information and Feedback as Separate
Choices}\label{M01-information-and-feedback-as-separate-choices}}

\noindent \noindent A controlled comparison can vary a structured data dictionary
and independent development feedback while holding the model and
analytical target fixed. All four configurations receive the core
measurement request, output schema, input files, execution tools,
permissions, and resource caps. The information condition adds organized
definitions of units, eligibility, boundaries, and missingness. The
feedback condition returns discrepancies from a separate development
checker and permits at most two corrections within the common budget. An
improvement in either condition is an empirical question.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M01_workflow_design.tex}
\caption{A two-by-two design holds the model, task, tools, permissions, and resource caps fixed while crossing explicit measurement information with development-check feedback.}\label{fig:M01_workflow_design}
\end{figure}

Use fresh conversations and clean output directories for repeated runs.
Preserve the prompt, model version, visible file list, commands,
feedback, revisions, and final output. Develop with July and score a
frozen program on August. The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows/EXPERIMENT_PROTOCOL.md}{experiment
protocol} separates the public reference files from the files exposed to
the assistant during a measured run. An exported report can describe the
result; the saved inputs and executable calculation establish what was
computed.

\hypertarget{M01-reproduce-the-logging-tasks}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the Logging
Tasks}\label{M01-reproduce-the-logging-tasks}}

\noindent \noindent The task builder verifies the compressed public source
checksum, selects the earlier roster, assigns stable aliases, and
exports only user-day counts and timing metadata. Compact inputs are
included in the repository. Rebuilding them requires the mHealth release
in its documented local data folder. The following program uses Python's
standard library and makes no model calls.

The source count is food rows per user-date. The task interval later
determines which observed dates contribute to logging activity.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows/build_tasks.py}{build\_tasks.py}.
From the repository root:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
cd 03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows
python3 build_tasks.py
\end{Verbatim}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Construct small, reproducible tasks from the released mHealth food file."""
import csv
import gzip
import hashlib
import json
from collections import Counter
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = HERE.parent / "mHealth"


def digest(path):
    with path.open("rb") as stream:
        return hashlib.file_digest(stream, "sha256").hexdigest()


def write_csv(path, fields, rows):
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with path.open("w", newline="") as stream:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=fields, lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def main():
    source = SOURCE / "data/food_entries.csv.gz"
    release = json.loads((SOURCE / "manifest.json").read_text())
    expected = release["files"][source.name]["sha256"]
    if digest(source) != expected:
        raise ValueError("The mHealth release checksum differs.")
    prior_users, counts = set(), Counter()
    with gzip.open(source, "rt", newline="") as stream:
        for row in csv.DictReader(stream):
            user = row["Userid"]
            if int(user[1:5], 16) >= 4096:
                continue
            day = date.fromisoformat(row["Fancydate"][:10])
            if date(2016, 1, 1) <= day < date(2016, 7, 1):
                prior_users.add(user)
            if date(2016, 6, 30) <= day <= date(2016, 9, 1):
                counts[user, day] += 1
    # Eligibility is fixed using January-June records for both later tasks.
    aliases = {u: f"U{i:04d}" for i, u in enumerate(sorted(prior_users), 1)}
    tasks = []
    for month, role in [(7, "development"), (8, "evaluation")]:
        start, end = date(2016, month, 1), date(2016, month + 1, 1)
        task = HERE / "tasks" / role
        spec = {"task_id": role, "start": str(start), "end_exclusive": str(end),
                "eligibility_cutoff_exclusive": "2016-07-01"}
        write_csv(task / "roster.csv", ["user_id"],
                  ({"user_id": u} for u in aliases.values()))
        records = [{"user_id": aliases[u], "date": str(d), "entries": n}
                   for (u, d), n in sorted(counts.items())
                   if u in aliases and start - timedelta(days=1) <= d <= end]
        write_csv(task / "observed_days.csv", ["user_id", "date", "entries"], records)
        (task / "task.json").write_text(json.dumps(spec, indent=2) + "\n")
        tasks.append({**spec, "roster_users": len(aliases), "input_rows": len(records)})
    inputs = sorted((HERE / "tasks").glob("*/*"))
    manifest = {"source": "mHealth teaching release 2026-10-23",
                "source_sha256": expected, "selection": "Pseudonym prefix below 4096; observed January-June 2016",
                "unit": "Observed user-day; entries counts source food rows",
                "tasks": tasks, "model_calls": 0,
                "files": {str(p.relative_to(HERE)): digest(p) for p in inputs}}
    (HERE / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(tasks, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

The reference calculation starts with every roster user and collects a
set of eligible dates. A separate SQL calculation verifies the same
customer-level counts. The generated JSON preserves the denominators and
excluded input-row counts.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows/logging_reference.py}{logging\_reference.py}.
From the repository root:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
cd 03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows
python3 logging_reference.py
\end{Verbatim}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Calculate observed logging days for a fixed earlier-period roster."""
import csv
import json
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def read_csv(path):
    with path.open(newline="") as stream:
        return list(csv.DictReader(stream))


def calculate(roster, records, start, end):
    users = [row["user_id"] for row in roster]
    if not users or len(users) != len(set(users)):
        raise ValueError("The roster must be nonempty with one row per user.")
    days = (end - start).days
    if days <= 0:
        raise ValueError("The end must follow the start.")
    observed = {u: set() for u in users}
    excluded_rows = 0
    for row in records:
        d = date.fromisoformat(row["date"])
        if row["user_id"] not in observed or not start <= d < end:
            excluded_rows += 1
            continue
        # Multiple entries and repeated rows still represent one logged day.
        observed[row["user_id"]].add(d)
    rows = [{"user_id": u, "logged_days": len(observed[u]), "window_days": days,
             "logging_rate": len(observed[u]) / days} for u in users]
    total = sum(r["logged_days"] for r in rows)
    summary = {"roster_users": len(users), "window_days": days,
               "observed_user_days": total, "possible_user_days": len(users) * days,
               "zero_log_users": sum(r["logged_days"] == 0 for r in rows),
               "mean_logging_rate": total / (len(users) * days),
               "excluded_input_rows": excluded_rows}
    return rows, summary


def main():
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    summaries = {}
    for role in ["development", "evaluation"]:
        task = HERE / "tasks" / role
        spec = json.loads((task / "task.json").read_text())
        rows, summary = calculate(read_csv(task / "roster.csv"),
                                  read_csv(task / "observed_days.csv"),
                                  date.fromisoformat(spec["start"]),
                                  date.fromisoformat(spec["end_exclusive"]))
        with (output / f"{role}_reference.csv").open("w", newline="") as stream:
            writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
            writer.writeheader()
            writer.writerows(rows)
        summaries[role] = summary
    (output / "logging_summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summaries, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summaries, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M01-statistical-evidence-in-an-ai-generated-analysis}{%
\section{Statistical Evidence in an AI-Generated
Analysis}\label{M01-statistical-evidence-in-an-ai-generated-analysis}}

\noindent \noindent A manager considering a promotion needs an estimate of
incremental contribution and an account of its uncertainty. An assistant
can produce executable code, a small p-value, and a confident
recommendation while treating transactions from the same store as
independent observations. The program's successful completion
establishes that its instructions ran. The statistical argument also
depends on the assignment process, the observation unit, and the
relationship between the computed quantity and the manager's question.

\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07437}{Miao, Mu, Chen, and Zou's
Fisher-R1 study} evaluates agents on open-ended hypothesis-testing
tasks. On its difficult tasks, Fisher-R1-14B matches the reference
reject/nonreject decision in 65.8\% of single attempts. Requiring a
sufficiently close reference p-value reduces this score to 33.0\%. These
percentages measure agreement with benchmark answers. A false-positive
rate instead requires repeated tests when the null hypothesis is true,
as in the store experiment in Section 6.30.

An analysis request should define the population, intervention or
comparison, outcome, units, and available information. For an
experiment, specify how treatment was assigned. For repeated customer
records, identify which observations belong to the same person. Ask the
assistant to report the retained sample, estimate, uncertainty
calculation, test direction, significance level, and interpretation.
Compare its reported quantities with saved numerical output and inspect
the code that created the sample and standard error.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.50}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.50}}@{}}
\toprule
Assessment & Evidence to Examine \\
\midrule

Execution & The program finishes on the stated inputs and records its
outputs. \\
Statistical method & The estimand, assignment or sampling unit,
dependence, and test match the question. \\
Numerical reporting & Estimates, intervals, p-values, and decisions
agree with the executed calculation. \\
Managerial interpretation & Effect size, costs, customer outcomes, and
the scope of the evidence support the action. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Matching a reference number can coexist with an unsuitable explanation
or an unsupported causal claim. A reference analysis also needs
justification. Several procedures can answer related questions with
different p-values, and an influential observation does not by itself
determine which question the firm should ask. A mean-dollar effect and a
rank-order association concern different economic quantities. Choose the
