def cohort_outcomes(subs, provider, start, horizon, observed_months):
    """Endpoint and continuous retention for one fixed provider cohort."""
    required = {str(pd.Period(start, freq="M") + k) for k in range(horizon + 1)}
    if not required.issubset(set(observed_months)):
        raise ValueError("Cohort horizon extends beyond the observed calendar")
    cohort = set(subs.loc[subs.month.eq(start) & subs.provider.eq(provider), "consumer_id"])
    if not cohort:
        raise ValueError("Empty starting cohort")
    continuous = cohort.copy()
    rows = []
    for k in range(horizon + 1):
        month = str(pd.Period(start, freq="M") + k)
        active = subs.loc[subs.month.eq(month)]
        own = set(active.loc[active.provider.eq(provider), "consumer_id"])
        any_provider = set(active.consumer_id)
        continuous &= own
        row = {"provider": provider, "start_month": start, "month": month,
               "horizon_months": k, "cohort_size": len(cohort),
               "same_provider": len(cohort & own),
               "other_provider_only": len((cohort & any_provider) - own),
               "no_paid_provider": len(cohort - any_provider),
               "continuous_same_provider": len(continuous)}
        assert row["same_provider"] + row["other_provider_only"] + row["no_paid_provider"] == len(cohort)
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def main():
    consumers = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_consumers.csv")
    subs = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_subscriptions.csv.gz")
    dgp = json.loads((SOURCE / "synthetic_dgp.json").read_text())
    months = sorted(dgp["g_trend"])
    n = len(consumers)
    assert n == dgp["n_consumers"] and consumers.consumer_id.is_unique
    assert not subs.duplicated(["consumer_id", "month", "provider"]).any()
    assert subs.consumer_id.isin(consumers.consumer_id).all()
    assert subs.month.isin(months).all() and subs.price.gt(0).all()
    assert subs["new"].isin([True, False]).all()
    assert subs.tier.isin(["basic", "premium"]).all()
    states = {m: {int(i): set(g.provider) for i, g in s.groupby("consumer_id")}
              for m, s in subs.groupby("month")}
    events, monthly, history = [], [], set()
    previous = {}
    for month in months:
        current = states.get(month, {})
        for consumer, providers in current.items():
            old = previous.get(consumer, set())
            for provider in sorted(providers - old):
                events.append({"month": month, "consumer_id": consumer, "provider": provider,
                               "event": acquisition_type(old, providers, consumer in history)})
        group = subs.loc[subs.month.eq(month)]
        monthly.append({"month": month, "population": n, "payers": len(current),
                        "subscriptions": len(group), "adoption": len(current) / n,
                        "multihomers": sum(len(s) > 1 for s in current.values()),
                        "basic_subscriptions": int(group.tier.eq("basic").sum())})
        history.update(current)
        previous = current
    events = pd.DataFrame(events)
    keys = ["month", "consumer_id", "provider"]
    recorded = set(subs.loc[subs["new"], keys].itertuples(index=False, name=None))
    calculated = set(events[keys].itertuples(index=False, name=None))
    assert recorded == calculated
    monthly = pd.DataFrame(monthly)
    monthly["multihoming_given_payment"] = monthly.multihomers / monthly.payers.replace(0, np.nan)
    monthly["basic_subscription_share"] = monthly.basic_subscriptions / monthly.subscriptions.replace(0, np.nan)
    cohort_start, horizon = "2025-01", 12
    assert str(pd.Period(cohort_start, freq="M") + horizon) <= months[-1]
    providers = sorted(subs.loc[subs.month.eq(cohort_start), "provider"].unique())
    cohorts = pd.concat([cohort_outcomes(subs, p, cohort_start, horizon, months)
                         for p in providers], ignore_index=True)
    last_events = events.loc[events.month.eq(months[-1])]
    counts = last_events.event.value_counts().sort_index()
    last = monthly.iloc[-1]
    result = {"data_type": "synthetic", "population": n, "subscription_rows": len(subs),
              "calendar_months": len(months), "last_month": months[-1],
              "last_payers": int(last.payers), "last_subscriptions": int(last.subscriptions),
              "last_adoption": float(last.adoption),
              "last_multihomers": int(last.multihomers),
              "last_multihoming_given_payment": float(last.multihoming_given_payment),
              "last_acquisition_events": int(len(last_events)),
              "last_acquisition_consumers": int(last_events.consumer_id.nunique()),
              "last_acquisition_types": {k: int(v) for k, v in counts.items()},
              "new_flag_verified": True}
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    monthly.to_csv(OUTPUT / "adoption.csv", index=False, float_format="%.8f")
    cohorts.to_csv(OUTPUT / "cohorts.csv", index=False)
    counts.rename_axis("event").rename("events").to_csv(OUTPUT / "acquisition_types.csv")
    (OUTPUT / "retention.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-retention-customer-value-and-choice}{%
\section{Retention, Customer Value, and
Choice}\label{M04-retention-customer-value-and-choice}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription manager can increase measured customer lifetime
value by improving service or by making cancellation harder. Both
mechanisms can raise the probability of another payment. They have
different implications for customer welfare, future trust, and the
sustainability of the relationship. A financial retention model should
therefore distinguish the source of the additional renewal.

A useful comparison holds the final offer fixed and varies the preceding
interaction. One group sees a direct cancellation option. Another can
choose whether to view a retention offer before deciding. Record
cancellation completion, time spent, subsequent charges, refunds, and
informed willingness to continue. Continued payment and a completed
choice are separate outcomes. The model in Section 8.14 provides a
numerical example in which higher renewal raises firm profit while
reducing customer value under explicitly opposed stakes.

The segmentation decision also has distributional consequences. A
cluster defined by earlier spending and visits describes behavioral
similarity. It does not establish an intrinsic customer type or a
justification for restricting access to an essential service. Compare
the proposed treatment with customers' needs and the consequences of
errors. When a segment receives an offer, record who can obtain it, who
is excluded, and whether the exclusion follows the firm's stated
objective.

In a conjoint task, price components and cancellation conditions are
product attributes when they affect the customer's actual choice.
Omitting a mandatory payment from the described price changes the offer
respondents evaluate. The FTC fee rule's current coverage includes
live-event tickets and short-term lodging; applying it requires the
covered transaction and required components. Its scope should be checked
in the
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/rule-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-frequently-asked-questions}{FTC's
rule guidance}.

\hypertarget{M04-ai-services-buyer-burden-and-the-outside-option}{%
\section{AI Services, Buyer Burden, and the Outside
Option}\label{M04-ai-services-buyer-burden-and-the-outside-option}}

\noindent \noindent A firm pricing an analytics service needs to understand the
customer's best alternative. A customer may buy a competing service,
conduct the analysis internally, or leave the decision unchanged. AI
assistance can improve each of those alternatives. A reduction in the
seller's coding cost therefore need not increase the amount a customer
will pay.

Let \(v\) be a customer's monetary-equivalent value of the delivered
analysis over a specified period, \(b\) its setup and verification
burden, and \(u_0\) the net value of its best alternative. Under
quasilinear utility, the customer weakly prefers purchase at price \(p\)
when \(v-p-b\geq u_0\). Its price ceiling is \(v-b-u_0\). All four
objects refer to the same customer and horizon. The burden includes the
customer's required effort after delivery; the outside option already
includes the costs of pursuing that alternative.

Product design can raise this ceiling by making the output more useful
or reducing integration and verification effort. Competitive
improvements raise \(u_0\) and reduce the ceiling, holding the offered
product fixed. A conjoint exercise should represent realistic
alternatives and implementation requirements. Preference estimates
obtained before customers gain access to a substantially improved
alternative may require new validation.

The conditional pricing calculation in M8, Section 8.17, compares this
participation ceiling with the seller's cost recovery requirement. The
interval can disappear even when the seller becomes more productive.
Measuring actual take-up, substitution, and customer effort is necessary
before treating the assumed sales volume as a forecast.

\hypertarget{M04-clustering-mechanisms-that-can-affect-consumer-agency}{%
\section{Clustering Mechanisms That Can Affect Consumer
Agency}\label{M04-clustering-mechanisms-that-can-affect-consumer-agency}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription firm can use research to identify where a
conversion or retention objective may conflict with customers' ability
to understand and revise their choices. The relevant grouping should
distinguish mechanisms that call for different evaluations. Social
endorsement raises questions about credibility and pressure. Defaults
raise questions about informed selection. Exit friction raises questions
about whether a decision to cancel becomes effective. A high response
rate provides little guidance about which of these mechanisms produced
it.

The primary sample contains 48 retrieved papers coded as having a
reported choice concern or potential dual use. Forty-seven are in the
potential-dual-use category; one explicitly discusses constrained
agency. The twelve binary features describe attention, framing, social
cues, emotion and identity, disclosure, personalization, privacy,
defaults and order, exit and search friction, habits and rewards,
financial commitment, and delegated control. The labels are preliminary
AI-assisted annotations, largely based on abstracts, with selected
full-text checks. They have not undergone independent human
adjudication. Potential misuse is an inference about a mechanism and
does not establish author intent.

For papers \(i\) and \(j\), let \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) contain the
mechanisms coded as present. Jaccard distance measures the proportion of
their combined positive features that they do not share:

\[
d_J(i,j)=1-\frac{|A_i\cap A_j|}{|A_i\cup A_j|}.
\]

The numerator counts shared mechanisms and the denominator counts
mechanisms present in either paper. Shared absences do not create
similarity. This matters when most of the twelve codes are zero. Papers
with no positive mechanism are excluded from this comparison, and
unreviewed papers remain outside the analysis. Average linkage merges
groups according to their average pairwise distance. K-means would
impose a different Euclidean representation and objective.

The program evaluates two through eight clusters and selects the
partition with the largest silhouette score. For a paper, the silhouette
compares its mean distance to its own group with the smallest mean
distance to another group, scaled by the larger distance. The selected
four-cluster solution has a mean silhouette of 0.272. Cluster names
describe the profiles after estimation; they are not inputs to the
algorithm.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Profile & Papers & Share of 48 \\
\midrule

Social Influence & 19 & 39.6\% \\
Emotion and Identity & 15 & 31.3\% \\
Disclosure, Framing, and Defaults & 8 & 16.7\% \\
Attention, Search, and Control & 6 & 12.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_agency_clusters.tex}
\caption{Four mutually exclusive clusters contain 19, 15, 8, and 6 papers. The denominator is the 48 retrieved papers coded as potentially relevant to agency concerns.}\label{fig:M04_agency_clusters}
\end{figure}

Social influence is the largest cluster in this selected sample. Every
paper in that group receives the social-cue indicator, and six also
receive the emotion/identity indicator. Emotion/identity is the most
common individual feature across all groups, appearing in 21 of 48
papers. Thus the largest cluster and the most common feature answer
different questions. Clusters partition the papers; feature memberships
overlap. Neither statistic estimates the prevalence or severity of
agency erosion in markets.

Stability checks change the strength of the conclusion. Re-estimation on
200 random 80\% subsamples, holding four clusters fixed, produces a
median adjusted Rand index of 0.794 against the full-sample partition.
Switching to Hamming distance lowers agreement to 0.485. An imposed
stress test that changes one feature per paper yields median agreement
of 0.250. Those values compare partitions, with one indicating identical
grouping and zero corresponding to chance-adjusted agreement. The stress
test is a sensitivity calculation; its feature changes do not represent
an estimated error rate.

Including 36 additional abstract-only risk reviews produces 84 papers
and selects eight clusters, the top of the candidate range. Adding
retrieved protective papers with positive mechanism codes produces 60
papers and selects six clusters. These changes warrant further review
before treating the groups as a stable taxonomy. A manager can still use
the profiles to choose customer-outcome measures: comprehension and
credibility for social influence, informed preferences for emotional
appeals, term recall for disclosure, and successful exit for
cancellation flows.

Reproduction starts with \texttt{coded\_papers.csv} and preserves all
three sample definitions, the code checks, distance calculations, K
selection, paper-level assignments, and sensitivity comparisons. All
feature definitions and status rules appear in the
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Consumer_Agency_Literature/CODEBOOK.md}{codebook}.
Run it from the saved script with the dependencies in the example
folder. Counts and profiles are checked against independent row-wise
totals.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Consumer_Agency_Literature/cluster.py}{cluster.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Cluster coded paper mechanisms; all prevalence estimates condition on the review sample."""
from pathlib import Path
import json
import platform
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import scipy
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, cut_tree
import sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FEATURES = [
    "attention_salience", "framing_reference", "social_cues", "emotion_identity",
    "opacity_disclosure", "personalization", "privacy_control", "defaults_order",
    "exit_search_friction", "habits_rewards", "financial_commitment", "delegation_control",
]
RISK = ["potential_dual_use", "reported_choice_concern"]


def select_sample(data, sample):
    """Never convert uncoded papers into zero-feature observations."""
    risk = data.review_status.isin(RISK)
    if sample == "downloaded_risk":
        mask = risk & data.download_status.eq("downloaded")
    elif sample == "all_reviewed_risk":
        mask = risk
    elif sample == "downloaded_with_protective":
        mask = (risk | data.review_status.eq("protective")) & data.download_status.eq("downloaded")
        # Broad governance/inclusion papers without these mechanisms remain in
        # the review catalog; a zero vector has no positive mechanism to compare.
        mask &= data[FEATURES].sum(axis=1) > 0
    else:
        raise ValueError(sample)
    result = data.loc[mask].sort_values("id").reset_index(drop=True)
    if result[FEATURES].isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("Missing codes require review, not zero imputation")
    if not result[FEATURES].isin([0, 1]).all().all():
        raise ValueError("Mechanism indicators must be binary")
    if (result[FEATURES].sum(axis=1) == 0).any():
        raise ValueError("An uncoded mechanism cannot enter the similarity analysis")
    return result


def partition(matrix, k, metric="jaccard"):
    """Average linkage accepts non-Euclidean distances such as Jaccard."""
    distances = pdist(matrix.astype(bool), metric=metric)
    tree = linkage(distances, method="average")
    labels = cut_tree(tree, n_clusters=[k]).ravel()
    return labels, squareform(distances)


def evaluate_sample(data, name, output):
    sample = select_sample(data, name)
    matrix = sample[FEATURES].to_numpy(dtype=int)
    n = len(sample)
    candidates = []
    for k in range(2, min(8, n - 1) + 1):
        labels, distance = partition(matrix, k)
        sizes = np.bincount(labels)
        candidates.append({"k": k, "silhouette": silhouette_score(distance, labels, metric="precomputed"),
                           "smallest_cluster": int(sizes.min()), "largest_cluster": int(sizes.max())})
    candidates = pd.DataFrame(candidates)
    # This is a declared selection rule, not a claim that nature has K types.
    best = candidates.sort_values(["silhouette", "k"], ascending=[False, True]).iloc[0]
    k = int(best.k)
    labels, _ = partition(matrix, k)
    # Stable presentation IDs: descending size, with original ID breaking ties.
    order = sorted(set(labels), key=lambda c: (-sum(labels == c), c))
    label_map = {c: rank + 1 for rank, c in enumerate(order)}
    sample["cluster"] = [label_map[c] for c in labels]
    counts = sample.groupby("cluster").size().rename("papers").to_frame()
    counts["share"] = counts.papers / n
    profiles = sample.groupby("cluster")[FEATURES].mean()
    counts["most_common_features"] = [
        "; ".join(profiles.loc[c].sort_values(ascending=False, kind="stable").head(3).index)
        for c in counts.index
    ]
    frequency = sample[FEATURES].sum().rename("papers").to_frame()
    frequency["denominator"] = n
    frequency["share"] = frequency.papers / n
    frequency = frequency.sort_values(["papers"], ascending=False, kind="stable")
    # Refit on 80% subsamples, comparing shared rows with the full partition.
    # Quantiles measure conditional algorithm stability, not population uncertainty.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(534)
    stability = []
    for iteration in range(200):
        indices = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=max(k + 1, int(.8 * n)), replace=False))
        new_labels, _ = partition(matrix[indices], k)
        stability.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels[indices], new_labels))
    alternative, _ = partition(matrix, k, metric="hamming")
    # Perturb one coded bit per paper to expose sensitivity to annotation choices.
    # This imposed stress test is not an estimated annotation error distribution.
    perturbation = []
    for iteration in range(200):
        changed = matrix.copy()
        for row in range(n):
            allowed = np.arange(len(FEATURES))
            if changed[row].sum() == 1:
                allowed = allowed[changed[row] == 0]
            column = rng.choice(allowed)
            changed[row, column] = 1 - changed[row, column]
        new_labels, _ = partition(changed, k)
        perturbation.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels, new_labels))
    folder = output / name
    folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)
    sample.to_csv(folder / "assignments.csv", index=False)
    counts.to_csv(folder / "cluster_sizes.csv")
    profiles.to_csv(folder / "cluster_profiles.csv")
    frequency.to_csv(folder / "feature_prevalence.csv", index_label="feature")
    candidates.to_csv(folder / "k_comparison.csv", index=False)
    pd.DataFrame({"adjusted_rand_index": stability}).to_csv(folder / "subsample_stability.csv", index=False)
    assert counts.papers.sum() == n and np.isclose(counts.share.sum(), 1)
    # Independent row-loop count checks the vectorized feature aggregate.
    for feature in FEATURES:
        assert int(frequency.loc[feature, "papers"]) == sum(int(row[feature]) for _, row in sample.iterrows())
    return {"papers": n, "k": k, "silhouette": float(best.silhouette),
            "cluster_counts": {str(c): int(v) for c, v in counts.papers.items()},
            "largest_features": frequency.head(3).reset_index().to_dict("records"),
            "subsample_ari_quantiles": np.quantile(stability, [.1, .5, .9]).tolist(),
            "hamming_ari": float(adjusted_rand_score(labels, alternative)),
            "one_bit_perturbation_ari_quantiles": np.quantile(perturbation, [.1, .5, .9]).tolist(),
            "valid_perturbation_runs": len(perturbation)}


def main():
    data = pd.read_csv(HERE / "coded_papers.csv")
    assert data.id.is_unique and data.doi.is_unique
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    summary = {name: evaluate_sample(data, name, output) for name in [
        "downloaded_risk", "all_reviewed_risk", "downloaded_with_protective"]}
    summary["environment"] = {"python": platform.python_version(), "numpy": np.__version__,
                              "pandas": pd.__version__, "scipy": scipy.__version__, "sklearn": sklearn.__version__}
    (output / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-clustering-cost-and-the-meaning-of-a-segment}{%
\section{Clustering Cost and the Meaning of a
Segment}\label{M04-clustering-cost-and-the-meaning-of-a-segment}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team organizing millions of product or review
vectors may need to repeat clustering as its catalog changes. Lower
computation time can make alternative representations and robustness
checks feasible. The economic value depends on what the groups enable:
inspecting representative complaints, organizing a product taxonomy, or
allocating a fixed amount of human review. A customer-support decision
also requires evidence about how the proposed action changes customer
outcomes. Computational efficiency alone does not identify that
response.

For a fixed representation, the optimization comparison can hold the
observations, feature scale, and number of centers constant. Let
\(z_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be the transformed vector for observation \(i\),
and let \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\) be the centers. The average squared
distance to the nearest center is

\[
Q(\mu)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min_{1\leq j\leq K}\|z_i-\mu_j\|^2.
\]

The denominator is the number of vectors. Each squared norm sums over
the \(d\) coordinates, so the units are squared transformed-feature
units per vector. Lloyd k-means alternates assigning observations to
centers and replacing each center with the mean of its assigned
observations. MiniBatchKMeans updates centers from smaller batches. Both
the stopping rule and the implementation affect the measured cost of
reaching a particular value of \(Q\).

\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501v1}{Bessa, Mazaré, Szilvasy,
Touvron, Picard, Douze, and Jégou (2026)} develop e-means using
exponentially weighted cluster sums and counts. To describe the update
for cluster \(j\) at training step \(t\), let \(s_{jt}\) be the sum of
vectors assigned to that cluster in the current batch and \(n_{jt}\)
their count. Let \(S_{j,t-1}\) and \(N_{j,t-1}\) be the corresponding
weighted quantities carried from earlier steps. With step weight
\(\alpha_t\), the update is

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{jt}&=(1-\alpha_t)S_{j,t-1}+\alpha_t s_{jt},\\
N_{jt}&=(1-\alpha_t)N_{j,t-1}+\alpha_t n_{jt},\\
\mu_{jt}&=S_{jt}/N_{jt},\qquad N_{jt}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The count update gives observations their appropriate influence when
batches contribute different numbers of assignments to a cluster.
Suppose the earlier weighted count is 10 with sum 20, while the current
batch contributes two observations with sum 14. At \(\alpha_t=1/2\), the
updated sum is 17 and the weighted count is 6, giving a center of
\(17/6\approx2.833\). Directly averaging the earlier mean 2 and the
batch mean 7 would give 4.5. That calculation would give the two batch
observations much greater influence per observation. The complete
e-means implementation also specifies initialization, a cooling
schedule, and treatment of unused clusters. In shuffled static training
data, a recent batch refers to training order. It does not imply that
more recent customer behavior receives greater economic importance.

The
\href{https://github.com/owlgebra-ai/faiss/tree/9ecbf0c2a2f4ca7a771b552badc145584b09e1a6/contrib/o_means}{o-means
implementation} adds a two-level approximate assignment method for large
numbers of centers, along with a different closing mean. Its benchmark
evaluates final centers with exact float32 search and compares
quality-adjusted timing on a particular GPU. Approximate assignment can
save computation while missing the nearest center, and implementation
kernels contribute to speed. The reported benefits concern large
dense-vector problems; the code provides no CPU backend. The
\href{../01_Resources/23_Clustering_Optimization/README.md}{source
guide} records the versions and scope. These methods use squared
Euclidean distance. Applying them to the Jaccard mechanism comparison in
Section 4.17 or the affiliation network in Section 5.17 would change the
objective and interpretation.

\hypertarget{M04-final-centers-and-customer-profiles}{%
\section{Final Centers and Customer
Profiles}\label{M04-final-centers-and-customer-profiles}}

\noindent \noindent A cluster profile combines records assigned to the same group.
When centers move during training, a stored assignment may refer to an
earlier center configuration. Aggregating those stored labels can
therefore describe a different partition from the one implied by the
final centers. The
\href{https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/tree/ebab8f784c1d177129602269d5ad966c525fbdcb/contrib/e_means}{Faiss
e-means documentation} distinguishes the labels returned during training
from a new assignment using the fitted centers. The final assignment
requires its own calculation and can add meaningful computation time.

Consider four synthetic scalar observations, \(0,4,5,10\), and final
centers at 2 and 7.5. Suppose the saved labels place the first three
observations in A and the last in B. The midpoint between the centers is
4.75, so observation 5 belongs to B under the final nearest-center rule.
Holding the points and centers fixed, the saved assignment gives mean
squared distance \(93/16=5.8125\). Reassigning the points gives
\(41/8=5.125\). One of four labels changes. A segment mean or count
computed before this check could therefore be inconsistent with the
reported centers.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_centroid_assignments.tex}
\caption{Four constructed scalar observations retain fixed final centers at 2 and 7.5. The final boundary at 4.75 moves observation 5 from A to B. One of four labels changes, reducing mean squared distance from 5.8125 to 5.125. Blue circles and orange squares identify the two groups.}\label{fig:M04_centroid_assignments}
\end{figure}

The following calculation uses exact fractions for both the
weighted-center example and the assignment comparison. Inputs are
imposed scalar values; there are no observed customer outcomes. Its
output preserves each point, center, assignment, and denominator.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Clustering_Optimization/centroid_checks.py}{centroid\_checks.py}.
From its folder, run \texttt{python3\ centroid\_checks.py} using the
standard library.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Exact arithmetic for centroid weighting and stale assignments."""
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path
import json

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def examples():
    # Earlier assignments: ten observations with mean 2.
    # Current batch: two observations with mean 7. Alpha is one-half.
    alpha = F(1, 2)
    total = (1 - alpha) * 20 + alpha * 14
    mass = (1 - alpha) * 10 + alpha * 2
    center = total / mass
    naive = (1 - alpha) * 2 + alpha * 7
    points = [F(0), F(4), F(5), F(10)]
    centers = [F(2), F(15, 2)]
    saved = [0, 0, 0, 1]
    final = [min(range(2), key=lambda j: (x - centers[j])**2)
             for x in points]
    saved_loss = sum((x - centers[j])**2
                     for x, j in zip(points, saved)) / len(points)
    final_loss = sum((x - centers[j])**2
                     for x, j in zip(points, final)) / len(points)
    return {
        "scope": "Constructed scalar examples; no observed customer outcomes",
        "ema_sum": str(total), "ema_mass": str(mass),
        "ema_centroid": str(center), "mean_of_centroids": str(naive),
        "points": [str(x) for x in points],
        "centers": [str(x) for x in centers],
        "saved_labels": saved, "final_labels": final,
        "boundary": str(sum(centers) / 2),
        "changed": sum(a != b for a, b in zip(saved, final)),
        "denominator": len(points),
        "saved_assignment_mse": str(saved_loss),
        "final_assignment_mse": str(final_loss),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = examples()
    (HERE / "results").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (HERE / "results/centroid_checks.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\noindent Clustering can also reduce the work of searching a vocabulary.
The G-MTP architecture reviewed in M7 §7.31 groups 262,144 tokens into
2,048 clusters of 128 and projects onto tokens in 32 selected clusters.
Its roughly 43-fold reduction concerns projection operations. In the
reported mobile NPU comparison, the additional overall speedup is about
1.01 times because projection is only one part of generation. A
computational saving must be evaluated at the boundary of the complete
task. \href{../01_Resources/27_AI_Inference_Efficiency/README.md}{Source
and configuration}.

\hypertarget{M04-comparing-implementations-on-fixed-data}{%
\section{Comparing Implementations on Fixed
Data}\label{M04-comparing-implementations-on-fixed-data}}

\noindent \noindent A team choosing a clustering implementation needs a common
quality measure and a clearly defined timing boundary. The synthetic
comparison fixes 50,000 training vectors, 10,000 independently drawn
test vectors, 32 coordinates, and 64 centers. Eight Gaussian components
have unequal probabilities, with means drawn once from a normal
distribution with standard deviation 1.5 and coordinate noise with
standard deviation 0.8. Training means and standard deviations transform
both samples. The fitted center count deliberately exceeds the number of
generating components: the objective is a compact squared-distance
approximation, and a fitted cluster need not correspond to a distinct
population type.

The data seed is 20261115. For each initialization seed, all three
implementations receive the same 64 sampled training vectors as starting
centers. The comparison uses seeds 11, 23, and 37 and budget settings 2,
5, and 10. A budget denotes a Lloyd iteration cap, a MiniBatch
maximum-passes setting, or e-means epochs. These settings do not imply
equal arithmetic work. MiniBatch uses batches of 256, while e-means
chooses its batch size and step schedule automatically. The saved
recipes identify those choices. A full-distance float64 calculation
assigns every training and test observation to its nearest final center
and computes the same loss for every method.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Method & Budget & Fit (ms) & Evaluation (ms) & Test MSE & Changed Labels
(\%) \\
\midrule

Lloyd & 2 & 13.5 & 150.8 & 10.6496 & 0.000 \\
Lloyd & 5 & 24.0 & 141.1 & 10.5538 & 0.000 \\
Lloyd & 10 & 49.3 & 169.0 & 10.5264 & 0.000 \\
MiniBatch & 2 & 21.8 & 143.4 & 10.5693 & 0.000 \\
MiniBatch & 5 & 48.8 & 140.1 & 10.5530 & 0.000 \\
MiniBatch & 10 & 89.4 & 150.9 & 10.5448 & 0.000 \\
e-means & 2 & 32.0 & 152.0 & 10.5177 & 9.408 \\
e-means & 5 & 57.4 & 144.6 & 10.5030 & 2.384 \\
e-means & 10 & 114.4 & 159.4 & 10.4960 & 1.496 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Each cell is the median across three initializations, conditional on the
fixed data. Test MSE averages squared distance across all 10,000 test
vectors; changed-label percentages use the 50,000 valid saved training
labels in each run. Training is measured after warm-up with one
numerical thread on an ARM64 CPU. The common evaluation includes final
assignments and distances for both samples. Imports, data generation,
scaling, saving outputs, and stability calculations are excluded. These
short elapsed times are specific to the recorded environment and provide
no confidence interval for performance on another machine.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_clustering_cost.tex}
\caption{The horizontal axis is median CPU fitting time in milliseconds; the vertical axis is mean squared distance per held-out vector. Three seeds are summarized for each method and cap. e-means has lower held-out error and longer fit time than Lloyd at each corresponding cap. The shared evaluation time is excluded from the horizontal axis and reported separately in the table.}\label{fig:M04_clustering_cost}
\end{figure}

At the displayed caps, e-means reaches smaller held-out loss and takes
longer to fit than Lloyd. At cap 2, the median e-means saved-label
disagreement is 9.408\%. The common evaluation also takes longer than
fitting in these runs. Both findings matter for implementation: quality,
fitting time, and the cost of producing consistent final profiles enter
the choice. This comparison evaluates complete library implementations
with their recorded settings. It does not isolate the causal
contribution of the exponential update or reproduce the sources' GPU
speedups.

Pairwise adjusted Rand agreement compares the partitions from different
initialization seeds on the same held-out observations. Relabeling
cluster numbers leaves this statistic unchanged. Agreement measures
sensitivity to initialization conditional on the feature representation,
data, and \(K\). Repeatedly selecting configurations using held-out loss
would turn that sample into development data. A subsequent
generalization claim would require a fresh evaluation sample.

The mHealth segments in Section 4.11 use three earlier-window behavioral
features and three centers. Their later logging profiles address
behavioral interpretation. They provide no evidence that GPU search
would improve this small calculation or that a lower clustering loss
would increase the effect of support. A proposed intervention needs an
outcome and comparison tied to the action, while customer choice and
respect for persons remain part of the justification in Marketing
Dialectics. More efficient grouping increases the feasible range of
analyses; the evidence for using a group in a marketing decision must
still be supplied.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Clustering_Optimization/compare_clustering.py}{compare\_clustering.py}.
Install the pinned requirements in an isolated environment as described
in the
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Clustering_Optimization/README.md}{replication
guide}, then run
\texttt{python\ compare\_clustering.py\ -\/-output\ local\_runs}. The
complete program generates the observations, fits each method, scores
final centers, saves every label vector, and calculates aggregate
results.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Compare three CPU implementations on fixed synthetic vectors."""
from pathlib import Path
from time import perf_counter
from itertools import combinations
import argparse
import csv
import hashlib
import json
import platform

import numpy as np
import sklearn
import faiss
from faiss.contrib.e_means import NumpyEmeans
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, MiniBatchKMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
METHODS = ("lloyd", "minibatch", "emeans")


def make_data(n=50000, d=32, seed=20261115):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = rng.normal(0, 1.5, size=(8, d))
    weights = [.40, .20, .12, .10, .08, .05, .03, .02]
    def draw(count):
        group = rng.choice(8, size=count, p=weights)
        return means[group] + rng.normal(0, .8, size=(count, d))
    train, test = draw(n), draw(n // 5)
    mean, scale = train.mean(axis=0), train.std(axis=0)
    return (np.ascontiguousarray((train - mean) / scale, dtype="float32"),
            np.ascontiguousarray((test - mean) / scale, dtype="float32"))


def nearest(x, centers, chunk=512):
    """Score all final centers using direct float64 distances."""
    c = np.asarray(centers, dtype="float64")
    labels, distances = [], []
    for start in range(0, len(x), chunk):
        block = np.asarray(x[start:start + chunk], dtype="float64")
        squared = ((block[:, None, :] - c[None, :, :])**2).sum(axis=2)
        choice = squared.argmin(axis=1)
        labels.extend(choice.tolist())
        distances.extend(squared[np.arange(len(block)), choice].tolist())
    return np.asarray(labels), np.asarray(distances)


def fit(method, x, initial, budget, seed):
    k, d = initial.shape
    start = perf_counter()
    if method == "emeans":
        model = NumpyEmeans(d, k, nepochs=budget, seed=seed)
        centers, saved = model.train(x, initial.copy())
        details = dict(model.recipe)
    else:
        options = dict(n_clusters=k, init=initial.copy(), n_init=1,
                       max_iter=budget, tol=0.0, random_state=seed)
        if method == "lloyd":
            model = KMeans(algorithm="lloyd", **options)
        else:
            model = MiniBatchKMeans(batch_size=256, max_no_improvement=None,
                                   reassignment_ratio=0.01, **options)
        model.fit(x)
        centers, saved = model.cluster_centers_, model.labels_
        details = {"n_iter": int(model.n_iter_)}
        if method == "minibatch":
            details["n_steps"] = int(model.n_steps_)
            details["batch_size"] = 256
    elapsed = perf_counter() - start
    return np.asarray(centers).copy(), np.asarray(saved).copy(), elapsed, details


def write_csv(path, rows):
    with path.open("w", newline="") as stream:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=50000)
    parser.add_argument("--dimensions", type=int, default=32)
    parser.add_argument("--clusters", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, nargs="+", default=[11, 23, 37])
    parser.add_argument("--budgets", type=int, nargs="+", default=[2, 5, 10])
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=HERE / "results")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not (args.rows >= 10 and 1 < args.clusters <= args.rows
            and args.dimensions > 0 and min(args.budgets) > 0):
        parser.error("Require n >= 10, 1 < k <= n, d > 0 and positive budgets")
    if len(set(args.seeds)) != len(args.seeds) or len(set(args.budgets)) != len(args.budgets):
        parser.error("Seeds and budgets must be unique")
    args.output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    train, test = make_data(args.rows, args.dimensions)
    runs, recipes, heldout = [], {}, {}
    faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)
    with threadpool_limits(limits=1):
        # Exclude import and warm-up work from the reported training time.
        warm = train[:max(1000, args.clusters)]
        for method in METHODS:
            fit(method, warm, warm[:args.clusters].copy(), 1, 0)
        for seed in args.seeds:
            rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
            initial = train[rng.choice(len(train), args.clusters, replace=False)]
            for budget in args.budgets:
                for method in rng.permutation(METHODS):
                    name = f"{method}_{seed}_{budget}"
                    centers, saved, seconds, recipe = fit(
                        method, train, initial, budget, seed)
                    start = perf_counter()
                    train_labels, train_d2 = nearest(train, centers)
                    test_labels, test_d2 = nearest(test, centers)
                    evaluation = perf_counter() - start
                    valid = (saved >= 0) & (saved < args.clusters)
                    disagreement = int(np.sum(saved[valid] != train_labels[valid]))
                    runs.append(dict(method=method, seed=seed, budget=budget,
                        train_rows=len(train), test_rows=len(test), dimensions=args.dimensions,
                        clusters=args.clusters, fit_seconds=seconds,
                        evaluation_seconds=evaluation, total_seconds=seconds + evaluation,
                        train_mse=float(train_d2.mean()), test_mse=float(test_d2.mean()),
                        saved_label_rows=int(valid.sum()),
                        saved_label_disagreements=disagreement,
                        saved_label_disagreement_rate=disagreement / valid.sum()))
                    np.savez_compressed(args.output / (name + ".npz"),
                        centroids=centers, saved_labels=saved,
                        train_labels=train_labels, test_labels=test_labels)
                    heldout[method, budget, seed] = test_labels
                    recipes[name] = recipe
                    print(name, round(seconds, 3), round(test_d2.mean(), 4), flush=True)
    summary, stability = [], []
    for method in METHODS:
        for budget in args.budgets:
            subset = [r for r in runs if r["method"] == method and r["budget"] == budget]
            row = dict(method=method, budget=budget, runs=len(subset))
            for field in ["fit_seconds", "evaluation_seconds", "total_seconds", "test_mse",
                          "train_mse", "saved_label_disagreement_rate"]:
                row[field + "_median"] = float(np.median([r[field] for r in subset]))
            summary.append(row)
            for first, second in combinations(args.seeds, 2):
                stability.append(dict(method=method, budget=budget, seed_a=first, seed_b=second,
                    test_rows=len(test), adjusted_rand=float(adjusted_rand_score(
                        heldout[method, budget, first], heldout[method, budget, second]))))
    write_csv(args.output / "runs.csv", runs)
    write_csv(args.output / "summary.csv", summary)
    if stability:
        write_csv(args.output / "stability.csv", stability)
    metadata = dict(data_seed=20261115, synthetic=True, train_rows=len(train), test_rows=len(test),
        dimensions=args.dimensions, clusters=args.clusters, seeds=args.seeds, budgets=args.budgets,
        threads=1, machine=platform.machine(), system=platform.system(),
        python=platform.python_version(), numpy=np.__version__, sklearn=sklearn.__version__,
        faiss=faiss.__version__, train_sha256=hashlib.sha256(train.tobytes()).hexdigest(),
        test_sha256=hashlib.sha256(test.tobytes()).hexdigest(), recipes=recipes,
        timing_scope="Construction and training after warm-up; common final-center evaluation reported separately. Data creation, scaling, imports, artifact saving and stability calculations excluded.",
        budget_scope="KMeans iteration cap, MiniBatchKMeans max_iter with convergence checks disabled, and e-means epochs. These do not imply equal arithmetic work.")
    (args.output / "metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2,
        default=lambda x: x.item() if isinstance(x, np.generic) else str(x)) + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-group-profiles-and-group-response-curves}{%
\section{Group Profiles and Group Response
Curves}\label{M04-group-profiles-and-group-response-curves}}

\noindent \noindent A customer segment groups observed characteristics. A
segment-specific treatment curve asks how the same group responds to
assigned interventions. That comparison needs an assignment design and a
defined target population. Groups used for causal targeting should rely
on pretreatment information; conditioning on a treatment response
changes the comparison.

Partial pooling can stabilize estimates for small groups. M6 Section
6.26 compares common, separate, and hierarchical curves using randomized
synthetic discounts, with full Python and equal-store evaluation.
Personalized discounts additionally require evidence on customer
outcomes and justification for the group definition.

\hypertarget{M04-spatial-relationships-and-segment-definitions}{%
\section{Spatial Relationships and Segment
Definitions}\label{M04-spatial-relationships-and-segment-definitions}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer grouping neighborhoods can use observed attributes,
travel accessibility, or both. Each representation answers a different
question. Areas with similar incomes may face different retail
alternatives because of roads and crossings. Areas connected by transit
can share access despite geographic separation. A graph embedding
incorporates the supplied links and training objective into the
resulting representation; spatial coherence alone does not establish
similar preferences or a useful targeting policy.

The fixed-neighbor comparison in Section 5.21 holds the six locations
and number of selected neighbors constant while changing the distance
definition. Its altered links arise from the representation. The
\href{https://github.com/c2g-dev/city2graph-case-study}{Liverpool
City2Graph case study} extends this issue to attribute clustering and
graph-autoencoder embeddings. An optional comparison should retain the
same observations, preprocessing, cluster count, and evaluation criteria
wherever feasible. Customer outcomes or other independently chosen
evidence are needed to interpret a cluster's marketing meaning.

Group means require the original membership counts when the decision
concerns average customers or total demand. Equal weight for differently
sized segments changes the population receiving weight. The synthetic
network calculation in Section 5.24 retains zone counts, mean zone
revenue, and total revenue separately, with complete Python. A segment
representation should carry the corresponding counts and units through
every later aggregation.

\hypertarget{M04-synthetic-consumers-and-product-concept-screening}{%
\section{Synthetic Consumers and Product Concept
Screening}\label{M04-synthetic-consumers-and-product-concept-screening}}

\noindent \noindent A personal-care firm may have more product ideas than it can
afford to test with a large human panel. A screening procedure must
identify concepts worth further investigation while making mistaken
exclusions visible. Generated consumer responses can organize possible
benefits and objections. Their usefulness for selecting products depends
on how well the resulting measurements distinguish concepts in the
intended customer population.

\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3}{Maier and coauthors} compare
generated purchase-intent responses with 9,300 human responses across 57
U.S. personal-care concept surveys. Their semantic similarity rating
method maps generated text to distributions over five response
categories. Reference statements and text embeddings determine that
mapping. The authors report promising agreement with concept-level human
results and state that they manually optimized the reference sets on the
same surveys. Prospective screening therefore requires new concepts
whose human outcomes remain outside measurement development.

Concept screening and conjoint analysis inform different decisions.
Screening ranks complete descriptions under a specified measurement
procedure. Identifying attribute tradeoffs additionally requires
variation that separates the attributes and an appropriate response
model. A positive response to a high-priced concept does not isolate a
price effect when its other features also differ. Purchase-intent
ratings also require a separate link to observed sales before entering a
revenue forecast.

\hypertarget{M04-distribution-fit-and-concept-selection}{%
\subsection{Distribution Fit and Concept
Selection}\label{M04-distribution-fit-and-concept-selection}}

\noindent \noindent Consider six fictional body-wash concepts, A through F, each
with 100 invented survey ratings. Categories 1--5 represent increasing
purchase intent. Use the stated counts as a common reference and
construct three candidate response patterns to compare distributional
fit with product ranking.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
\toprule
Concept & Counts in Categories 1--5 & Reference Mean \\
\midrule

A & 0, 0, 10, 30, 60 & 4.50 \\
B & 0, 0, 15, 30, 55 & 4.40 \\
C & 0, 0, 20, 30, 50 & 4.30 \\
D & 0, 0, 25, 30, 45 & 4.20 \\
E & 0, 0, 30, 30, 40 & 4.10 \\
F & 0, 0, 35, 30, 35 & 4.00 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pooled pattern assigns every concept the same distribution,
\((0,0,0.225,0.30,0.475)\), with mean 4.25. The reversed pattern gives A
the distribution of F, B the distribution of E, and so forth. The
compressed pattern assigns 80\% weight to the pooled distribution and
20\% to each concept's reference distribution. All three reproduce the
same overall category shares when concepts receive equal weight. Their
implications for choosing products differ sharply.

\Needspace{7\baselineskip}

For concept \(s\), compare reference and candidate cumulative
distributions using

\[
K_s=1-\max_{r\in\{1,\ldots,5\}}\left|F_s^{\mathrm{ref}}(r)-F_s^{\mathrm{cand}}(r)\right|.
\]

The cumulative probability \(F_s(r)\) is the share assigned to category
\(r\) or below. The maximum difference compares cumulative shares on the
ordered categories. The average of \(K_s\) gives each concept equal
weight. Pearson correlation compares concept means, while Spearman
correlation compares their ranks. Selecting two concepts creates a
further decision criterion: the share of the reference top two that the
candidate shortlist retains.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.16}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.18}}@{}}
\toprule
Imposed Pattern & Mean KS Similarity & Mean Absolute Rating Error &
Correlation & Reference Top Two Retained \\
\midrule

Pooled & 0.925 & 0.150 & Undefined & Boundary Tie \\
Reversed & 0.850 & 0.300 & -1.000 & 0 of 2 \\
Compressed & 0.940 & 0.120 & 1.000 & 2 of 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The correlation column reports Pearson correlation; Spearman gives the
same results in this construction. The pooled means are constant, so
both correlations are undefined and every concept ties at the screening
threshold. The reversed pattern selects F and E, excluding both A and B.
The compressed pattern preserves the correct shortlist while shrinking
the difference between A and F from 0.50 to 0.10 rating points. Its
perfect ordering consequently supplies no guarantee that the magnitude
of a rating difference is accurate.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_concept_screening.tex}
\caption{All three imposed candidate patterns match the overall category shares. Across concepts A–F, the reference means fall, the pooled means remain constant, the reversed means rise, and the compressed means fall over a narrower range.}\label{fig:M04_concept_screening}
\end{figure}

The left panel pools the same six equally weighted concepts. The right
panel retains concept identity and uses a 3.9--4.6 vertical scale to
show the differences in mean ratings. The managerial consequence follows
from the intended action: broad distribution fit can coexist with a
shortlist that rejects the strongest concepts. Alphabetical selection
among tied concepts would introduce a decision rule unsupported by the
ratings.

\hypertarget{M04-human-validation-and-missed-concepts}{%
\subsection{Human Validation and Missed
Concepts}\label{M04-human-validation-and-missed-concepts}}

\noindent \noindent A prospective evaluation fixes the target population and
recruitment process before comparing generated and human responses.
Develop anchors on one set of concepts, choose a configuration on
another, and reserve final concepts for evaluating the complete
procedure. Model, prompt, embedding, anchor wording, and screening
threshold all belong to that procedure. Splitting respondents within
familiar concepts answers a narrower question than predicting responses
to new products.

Human validation should include a random sample of concepts that the
screening procedure rejects. Testing only the shortlist leaves promising
exclusions unobserved. Known selection probabilities can support
estimates of screening errors across the original concept pool, with
uncertainty that respects concept and respondent sampling. A manager can
then compare the cost of human validation with the consequences of
advancing weak ideas or discarding strong ones. The synthetic
calculations specify no monetary value for those errors.

\hypertarget{M04-complete-python-evaluation}{%
\subsection{Complete Python
Evaluation}\label{M04-complete-python-evaluation}}

\noindent \noindent The program reads the frozen invented panels and verifies that
all candidate patterns cover the same concepts. It calculates
distribution similarity, mean-rating error, correlations, and shortlist
overlap. A constant score leaves correlation undefined; a tie at the
selection boundary leaves the shortlist unresolved. The reference data
construct the three patterns for an analytical comparison, so these
results are not a test of a trained model on unseen data.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/concept_screening.py}{concept\_screening.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python3\ concept\_screening.py}. Inputs
are in the accompanying \texttt{data} folder; outputs are written to
\texttt{results}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Evaluate three imposed rating patterns on the same six synthetic concepts.

Reference counts are invented surveys, not human observations. Candidate PMFs are
fixed teaching inputs, not fitted predictions. No model calls or dependencies.
"""
import json
from math import isclose, isfinite, sqrt
from pathlib import Path
from statistics import mean

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def validate_pmf(pmf):
    if len(pmf) != 5 or any(not isfinite(x) or x < 0 for x in pmf):
        raise ValueError("A PMF needs five finite nonnegative values.")
    if not isclose(sum(pmf), 1, abs_tol=1e-12, rel_tol=0):
        raise ValueError("Category probabilities must sum to one.")
    return pmf


def mean_rating(pmf):
    return sum((k + 1) * x for k, x in enumerate(validate_pmf(pmf)))


def ks_similarity(left, right):
    validate_pmf(left)
    validate_pmf(right)
    x = y = distance = 0.0
    for a, b in zip(left, right):
        x, y = x + a, y + b
        distance = max(distance, abs(x - y))
    return 1 - distance


def correlation(left, right):
    if len(left) != len(right) or len(left) < 2:
        raise ValueError("Use paired concept scores with at least two concepts.")
    if any(not isfinite(x) for x in [*left, *right]):
        raise ValueError("Correlation requires finite scores.")
    x = [v - mean(left) for v in left]
    y = [v - mean(right) for v in right]
    xx, yy = sum(v * v for v in x), sum(v * v for v in y)
    return None if min(xx, yy) <= 1e-24 else sum(a * b for a, b in zip(x, y)) / sqrt(xx * yy)


def ranks(values):
    """Average ranks for exact ties; scores are ordered from smallest to largest."""
    order = sorted(range(len(values)), key=values.__getitem__)
    result = [None] * len(values)
    first = 0
    while first < len(order):
        last = first + 1
        while last < len(order) and values[order[last]] == values[order[first]]:
            last += 1
        for i in order[first:last]:
            result[i] = (first + 1 + last) / 2
        first = last
    return result


def shortlist(scores, count=2):
    if not 0 < count < len(scores) or any(not isfinite(x) for x in scores.values()):
        raise ValueError("Require finite scores and a shortlist smaller than the roster.")
    ordered = sorted(scores, key=lambda key: (-scores[key], key))
    if isclose(scores[ordered[count - 1]], scores[ordered[count]], abs_tol=1e-12, rel_tol=0):
        return None  # A boundary tie supplies no unique shortlist.
    return ordered[:count]


def evaluate(data):
    ids = [row["concept"] for row in data["reference"]]
    if len(set(ids)) != len(ids):
        raise ValueError("Reference concept identifiers must be unique.")
    observed = {}
    for row in data["reference"]:
        counts = row["counts"]
        if len(counts) != 5 or any(type(x) is not int or x < 0 for x in counts) or sum(counts) == 0:
            raise ValueError("Reference counts need five nonnegative integers and a positive total.")
        observed[row["concept"]] = [n / sum(counts) for n in counts]
    reference_means = {key: mean_rating(observed[key]) for key in ids}
    reference_top = shortlist(reference_means)
    if reference_top is None:
        raise ValueError("The reference needs a unique shortlist for this comparison.")
    summary, details = [], []
    for candidate, predictions in data["candidates"].items():
        if set(predictions) != set(ids):
            raise ValueError("Every candidate must cover exactly the same concept roster.")
        predicted_means = {key: mean_rating(predictions[key]) for key in ids}
        selected = shortlist(predicted_means)
        left, right = [reference_means[k] for k in ids], [predicted_means[k] for k in ids]
        similarities = [ks_similarity(observed[k], predictions[k]) for k in ids]
        summary.append(dict(candidate=candidate, concepts=len(ids),
            mean_ks_similarity=mean(similarities), mean_absolute_rating_error=mean(abs(x-y) for x,y in zip(left,right)),
            pearson=correlation(left, right), spearman=correlation(ranks(left), ranks(right)),
            reference_top_two=reference_top, selected=selected,
            selection_status="boundary_tie" if selected is None else "unique",
            top_two_recall=None if selected is None else len(set(selected) & set(reference_top))/2))
        for i, key in enumerate(ids):
            details.append(dict(candidate=candidate, concept=key, reference_mean=left[i],
                predicted_mean=right[i], ks_similarity=similarities[i],
                reference_distribution=observed[key], predicted_distribution=predictions[key]))
    return summary, details


def main():
    data = json.loads((ROOT / "data/concept_panels.json").read_text())
    summary, details = evaluate(data)
    out = ROOT / "results"
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for name, value in [("screening_summary.json", summary), ("screening_details.json", details)]:
        (out / name).write_text(json.dumps(value, indent=2, allow_nan=False) + "\n")
    for row in summary:
        print(row["candidate"], row["mean_ks_similarity"], row["pearson"], row["selected"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-human-and-synthetic-evidence-for-product-design}{%
\section{Human and Synthetic Evidence for Product
Design}\label{M04-human-and-synthetic-evidence-for-product-design}}

\noindent \noindent A body-wash manager must decide whether to include a premium
feature and how to price the product. Human survey responses cost more
than generated responses. The research budget should reflect which
attribute comparisons each source can support at the required accuracy.
A synthetic respondent can preserve the feature comparison while
reversing the response to price.

\hypertarget{M04-response-features-and-bias-features}{%
\subsection{Response Features and Bias
Features}\label{M04-response-features-and-bias-features}}

\noindent \noindent Four product profiles cross a standard or premium feature with
a low or high price. Code the feature as \(f=-1\) or \(+1\) and price as
\(p=-1\) or \(+1\). An observation is one response at one profile from
one source in a fixed research setting. The response is a stylized
continuous rating score measured in points. The price code identifies
two levels; a price coefficient here is measured per coded unit and is
not an elasticity.

To distinguish customer preferences from source bias, specify the
primary and auxiliary responses as

\[
Y^P=\beta_0+\beta_F f+\beta_P p+e^P,\qquad
Y^A=\beta_0+\beta_F f+\beta_P p+\gamma_0+\gamma_Pp+e^A.
\]

The three \(\beta\) coefficients describe the primary response. The
auxiliary source adds an overall shift \(\gamma_0\) and a price
distortion \(\gamma_P\). Estimation treats these coefficients as
unknown. The exclusion of a separate feature bias supplies the
informative feature comparison.

\begin{assumption}[Response and Bias Structure]
\label{ass:auxiliary-response-design}
The four profiles have the linear conditional means specified above. The response features $(1,f,p)$ and auxiliary bias features $(1,p)$ are known and fixed. The unknown response and bias coefficients are unrestricted. Errors are independent across observations and sources, Gaussian with mean zero, and have known positive source variances $\sigma_P^2$ and $\sigma_A^2$. Sampling costs $c_P$ and $c_A$ are positive and constant across profiles within each source.
\end{assumption}

Under Assumption \ref{ass:auxiliary-response-design}, differences
between auxiliary ratings at the same price remove both bias terms.
Their expected premium-minus-standard contrast is \(2\beta_F\). A
high-minus-low price contrast instead equals \(2(\beta_P+\gamma_P)\), so
auxiliary responses alone do not separate the two price coefficients.
The response-feature space contains three directions; the bias-feature
space overlaps the intercept and price directions.

\hypertarget{M04-preserved-feature-comparisons-and-reversed-price-responses}{%
\subsection{Preserved Feature Comparisons and Reversed Price
Responses}\label{M04-preserved-feature-comparisons-and-reversed-price-responses}}

\noindent \noindent Set the primary coefficients to \((3,0.4,-0.5)\) and the
auxiliary bias coefficients to \((0.8,0.6)\). These are invented inputs,
with no observed human or generated-model responses. The resulting
conditional means are:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrr@{}}
\toprule
Price & Feature & Primary Mean & Auxiliary Mean \\
\midrule

Low & Standard & 3.1 & 3.3 \\
Low & Premium & 3.9 & 4.1 \\
High & Standard & 2.1 & 3.5 \\
High & Premium & 2.9 & 4.3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

At either price, the premium feature raises both sources' expected
ratings by 0.8 points. Raising price reduces the primary rating by 1.0
point and increases the auxiliary rating by 0.2 points at either feature
level. Thus, the model permits synthetic evidence to inform the feature
comparison while reserving the price comparison for human research. A
recommendation about willingness to pay would additionally require the
monetary price difference and a justified mapping from these ratings to
choice.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_auxiliary_contrasts.tex}
\caption{The left panel holds price low and compares standard with premium features: primary means rise from 3.1 to 3.9 and auxiliary means from 3.3 to 4.1. The right panel holds the feature standard and raises price: primary means fall from 3.1 to 2.1 while auxiliary means rise from 3.3 to 3.5. Both panels share the rating scale. All means are invented.}\label{fig:M04_auxiliary_contrasts}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{M04-research-cost-at-a-common-accuracy-target}{%
\subsection{Research Cost at a Common Accuracy
Target}\label{M04-research-cost-at-a-common-accuracy-target}}

\noindent \noindent Compare designs that estimate the same vector
\((\beta_0,\beta_F,\beta_P)\) with expected total squared coefficient
error at most \(\epsilon^2\). The loss is measured in squared rating
points under the fixed attribute coding. It is distinct from prediction
error on an individual response or expected profit from a launch.
\href{https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298}{Jasin,
Lin, and Zhang}, §5.3, derive the optimal continuous allocation for this
design.

Balanced sampling places the same number of observations at each profile
within each source. Define total primary precision \(t=N_P/\sigma_P^2\)
and auxiliary precision \(s=N_A/\sigma_A^2\). Joint weighted least
squares estimates both response and bias coefficients. Under Assumption
\ref{ass:auxiliary-response-design}, its total coefficient MSE is

\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\beta)=\frac{2}{t}+\frac{1}{t+s}.
\]

The intercept and price variances each equal \(1/t\), because the
auxiliary bias confounds those coefficients. Both sources inform the
feature coefficient, whose variance is \(1/(t+s)\). Increasing auxiliary
precision helps the final term while leaving the first two terms
dependent on primary observations.

The relevant relative cost combines response cost and noise variance:

\[
\lambda=\frac{c_A\sigma_A^2}{c_P\sigma_P^2}.
\]

For the normalized target \(\epsilon^2=1\), the optimal precisions are
\(t^*=3\) and \(s^*=0\) when \(\lambda\geq1/3\). For \(0<\lambda<1/3\),
they are

\[
t^*=2+\sqrt{\frac{2\lambda}{1-\lambda}},\qquad
s^*=\sqrt{\frac{2(1-\lambda)}{\lambda}}-1-\sqrt{\frac{2\lambda}{1-\lambda}}.
\]

For a target \(\epsilon^2\), divide these normalized precisions by
\(\epsilon^2\), convert precision to response counts using each source
variance, and round each profile's count upward. Relative to optimized
primary-only sampling, the asymptotic saving is

\[
V(\lambda)=
\begin{cases}
1-\bigl[2-\lambda+2\sqrt{2\lambda(1-\lambda)}\bigr]/3,&0<\lambda<1/3,\\
0,&\lambda\geq1/3.
\end{cases}
\]

As auxiliary information becomes arbitrarily inexpensive, this saving
approaches one third. In this balanced design and equally weighted
coefficient loss, only the feature direction receives usable auxiliary
information. The limiting fraction changes with the design and
objective; counting unconfounded coefficients does not supply a general
cost formula.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_auxiliary_value.tex}
\caption{Under the invented four-profile design, asymptotic cost savings approach 33.33 percent as the relative information cost approaches zero, then decline to zero at one third. A second curve is zero at every cost ratio when auxiliary bias can affect every primary response feature. The zero-cost endpoint denotes a limit.}\label{fig:M04_auxiliary_value}
\end{figure}

Set both error variances to 1, primary cost to 1, auxiliary cost to
0.01, and the MSE target to 0.01. The units of cost are normalized
research-budget units. The continuous design implies a 24.29\%
asymptotic saving. Rounding profile counts gives:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Allocation & Primary Responses & Auxiliary Responses & Cost & Total
MSE \\
\midrule

Primary Only & 300 & 0 & 300.00 & 0.010000 \\
Mixed Sources & 216 & 1,296 & 228.96 & 0.009921 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The mixed design uses 54 primary and 324 auxiliary responses at each
profile. Its 23.68\% cost saving retains the same accuracy requirement.
The rounded construction satisfies the target; it need not be the exact
optimum over finite integer allocations. Model development, validation,
and monitoring costs require separate entries in an operational research
budget.

\hypertarget{M04-python-allocation-and-profile-comparisons}{%
\subsection{Python Allocation and Profile
Comparisons}\label{M04-python-allocation-and-profile-comparisons}}

\noindent \noindent The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/data/parameters.json}{parameter
file} supplies the invented coefficients, variances, source costs, and
accuracy target. The program computes profile means, converts optimal
precision into balanced integer counts, and saves the allocation and
cost curve. A zero cost ratio appears only as the limiting point of the
saved curve. No response records are simulated or sent to an external
model. Run from the repository root:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/allocate_responses.py
\end{Verbatim}

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/allocate_responses.py}{allocate\_responses.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Four invented product profiles and a cost comparison at a common MSE target.

Adaptation of Jasin, Lin, and Zhang (2026), Section 5.3. All parameters are
imposed. Independent Gaussian errors and the specified bias features define
the model; this program calculates analytic moments without collecting data.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import json
from math import ceil, isfinite, sqrt
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def load_parameters(path=ROOT / "data/parameters.json"):
    parameters = json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
    for key in ("primary_variance", "auxiliary_variance", "primary_cost",
                "auxiliary_cost", "mse_target"):
        if not isfinite(parameters[key]) or parameters[key] <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{key} must be finite and positive.")
    if len(parameters["primary_coefficients"]) != 3:
        raise ValueError("Primary coefficients must follow intercept, feature, price.")
    if len(parameters["auxiliary_bias_coefficients"]) != 2:
        raise ValueError("Bias coefficients must follow intercept, price.")
    return parameters


def optimal_precision(lam):
    if not isfinite(lam) or lam <= 0:
        raise ValueError("The information-cost ratio must be finite and positive.")
    if lam >= 1 / 3:
        return 3.0, 0.0
    primary = 2 + sqrt(2 * lam / (1 - lam))
    auxiliary = sqrt(2 * (1 - lam) / lam) - 1 - sqrt(2 * lam / (1 - lam))
    return primary, auxiliary


def calculate(parameters):
    b0, bf, bp = parameters["primary_coefficients"]
    g0, gp = parameters["auxiliary_bias_coefficients"]
    profiles = []
    for price in (-1, 1):
        for feature in (-1, 1):
            primary = b0 + bf * feature + bp * price
            profiles.append(dict(price=price, feature=feature,
                primary_mean=round(primary, 12),
                auxiliary_mean=round(primary + g0 + gp * price, 12)))
    vp, va = parameters["primary_variance"], parameters["auxiliary_variance"]
    cp, ca = parameters["primary_cost"], parameters["auxiliary_cost"]
    target = parameters["mse_target"]
    lam = ca * va / (cp * vp)
    t, s = optimal_precision(lam)
    primary_n = 4 * ceil(t * vp / (4 * target))
    auxiliary_n = 4 * ceil(s * va / (4 * target))
    reference_n = 4 * ceil(3 * vp / (4 * target))
    tp, ta = primary_n / vp, auxiliary_n / va
    cost = cp * primary_n + ca * auxiliary_n
    summary = dict(information_cost_ratio=lam, mse_target=target,
        primary_n=primary_n, auxiliary_n=auxiliary_n,
        primary_per_profile=primary_n // 4, auxiliary_per_profile=auxiliary_n // 4,
        primary_only_n=reference_n, primary_only_cost=cp * reference_n,
        primary_only_mse=3 * vp / reference_n, mixed_cost=cost,
        rounded_saving_fraction=1 - cost / (cp * reference_n),
        asymptotic_saving_fraction=1 - (t + lam * s) / 3,
        primary_precision=tp, auxiliary_precision=ta,
        intercept_variance=1 / tp, price_variance=1 / tp,
        feature_variance=1 / (tp + ta),
        correct_model_mse=2 / tp + 1 / (tp + ta))
    curve = [dict(information_cost_ratio=0.0, saving_fraction=1 / 3,
                  fully_confounded_saving=0.0, limiting_value=True)]
    ratios = [0.000001, 0.00001, 0.0001, 0.0002, 0.0005]
    ratios += [i / 1000 for i in range(1, 401)]
    for ratio in ratios:
        t, s = optimal_precision(ratio)
        curve.append(dict(information_cost_ratio=ratio,
            saving_fraction=1 - (t + ratio * s) / 3,
            fully_confounded_saving=0.0, limiting_value=False))
    return profiles, summary, curve


def write_csv(path, rows):
    with path.open("w", newline="") as stream:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def run(output):
    profiles, summary, curve = calculate(load_parameters())
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    write_csv(output / "profile_means.csv", profiles)
    write_csv(output / "value_curve.csv", curve)
    (output / "allocation.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2, allow_nan=False) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=ROOT / "results")
    run(parser.parse_args().output)
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-stable-segments-and-substantive-meaning}{%
\section{Stable Segments and Substantive
Meaning}\label{M04-stable-segments-and-substantive-meaning}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing manager uses customer-text features to define
segments and allocate service resources. A feature that reconstructs
common wording accurately may contribute little to identifying a
complaint that requires attention. Evaluate the representation against
the intended decision before interpreting its clusters. The synthetic
comparison in §7.39 holds the case population fixed while contrasting
aggregate reconstruction with recall of cases requiring review.

Cluster labels and feature coordinates can change across seeds even when
an objective value changes little. Align cluster memberships or feature
directions under a stated matching rule before comparing repeated fits.
Report the population, preprocessing, number of groups, and matching
criterion. Stable assignments support reproducibility under those
choices; external behaviors or independently coded text provide evidence
for a substantive segment interpretation. A segment name proposed by an
LLM is a hypothesis requiring that evidence.

A high-value segment describes a firm's valuation under a specified
horizon and cost model. It does not establish the customer's preferences
or permission to receive a particular intervention. Keep segment
definitions, predicted responses, customer outcomes, and authorization
records separate when selecting an action.

\hypertarget{M04-demand-information-pricing-and-consumer-surplus}{%
\section{Demand Information, Pricing, and Consumer
Surplus}\label{M04-demand-information-pricing-and-consumer-surplus}}

\noindent \noindent Two restaurant owners are considering a service that improves
their forecasts of local demand. Each owner expects to earn more by
adjusting prices to the information. A separate proposal would choose
both restaurants' prices to maximize their combined profit. The first
comparison changes information; the second changes the pricing
objective. Customer outcomes depend on both choices, so an evaluation
must preserve that distinction.

Suppose the market contains two symmetric restaurants and a
representative consumer who chooses continuous quantities of their
meals. Quantities are measured in meal equivalents per market-day.
Prices and marginal cost are dollars per meal equivalent. A low demand
intercept of 10 and a high intercept of 14 each occur with probability
one half. Marginal cost is 2 at each restaurant. These are synthetic
inputs, with no estimated relationship to a particular restaurant
company.

\hypertarget{M04-demand-and-information}{%
\subsection{Demand and Information}\label{M04-demand-and-information}}

\noindent \noindent Consumer surplus requires a preference model as well as
observed expenditure. Let \(q_i\) denote quantity from restaurant \(i\),
\(p_i\) its price, and \(m\) spending on a numeraire good whose price is
one. Gross utility in dollars is

\[
U(q_1,q_2,m;a)=a(q_1+q_2)
-\frac{q_1^2+2\delta q_1q_2+q_2^2}{2}+m.
\]

The intercept \(a\) measures marginal willingness to pay at zero
quantity. The own-quantity coefficient is normalized to one dollar per
squared meal equivalent, and \(\delta=0.5\) is the relative
cross-quantity coefficient. Positive \(\delta\) makes the restaurant
meals substitutes: consuming more of one lowers marginal willingness to
pay for the other. The consumer maximizes utility subject to expenditure
and nonnegative quantities.

\begin{assumption}[Preferences, Costs, and Timing]\label{ass:pricing-market}
Preferences are quasi-linear with sufficient numeraire wealth and $0\leq\delta<1$. Both restaurants have constant marginal cost $c$, with no fixed costs, capacity limits, or vendor fees. Demand has two equally likely states. Firms observe a common binary signal before setting prices simultaneously; customers choose quantities using the actual state and posted prices. The reported solutions have positive quantities in every positive-probability state-signal cell.
\end{assumption}

Under Assumption \ref{ass:pricing-market}, interior consumer choice
gives inverse demand \(p_i=a-q_i-\delta q_j\). Solving the two equations
gives

\[
q_i=\frac{(a-p_i)-\delta(a-p_j)}{1-\delta^2}.
\]

The own-price derivative is \(-1/(1-\delta^2)\), holding the rival's
price fixed. At equal prices, quantity at each restaurant simplifies to
\(q=(a-p)/(1+\delta)\). The cross-quantity restriction makes utility
strictly concave, which permits an independent calculation of consumer
choice, including quantity corners when checking alternative prices.

Let \(r\) be the probability that the common signal correctly identifies
the state. Equal prior probabilities and symmetric signal errors imply
that, after a low signal,

\[
\widehat a_L=r a_L+(1-r)a_H.
\]

After a high signal, \(\widehat a_H=r a_H+(1-r)a_L\). A signal with
\(r=0.5\) supplies no demand information, so both forecasts equal 12. At
\(r=1\), the forecast equals actual demand. The expected squared
intercept error falls from 4 to 0, in squared dollars per squared meal
equivalent. No learning algorithm or estimation sample is needed for
these stipulated forecasts.

\hypertarget{M04-independent-and-joint-pricing}{%
\subsection{Independent and Joint
Pricing}\label{M04-independent-and-joint-pricing}}

\noindent \noindent Each independent owner chooses a price to maximize
\(E[(p_i-c)q_i\mid Z]\), where \(Z\) is the observed signal.
Differentiating with respect to the owner's price and using linear
demand gives

\[
2p_i-\delta p_j=(1-\delta)\widehat a+c.
\]

At a symmetric equilibrium, the independent price is therefore

\[
p^N(\widehat a)=\frac{(1-\delta)\widehat a+c}{2-\delta}.
\]

Each owner accounts for its own lost sales when raising price. Joint
maximization also accounts for sales transferred to the other
restaurant. Maximizing their combined conditional profit gives the
