final rule} introduced a limited circumvention exemption for diagnosis,
maintenance, and repair of retail-level commercial food-preparation
equipment. Its effective date is October 28, 2024, as stated on page
85437; the relevant provision appears on pages 85448--85449.
Announcement timing, the legal effective date, and actual adoption of
new repair practices are distinct dates. A change in an ordering
indicator can arise through several channels described in Section 2.16.

The weekly country data permit a concrete calculation of the comparison
that a difference-in-differences design would use. Retain the 12 common
weekly snapshots before October 28 and the 12 after the implementation
week. Exclude that week from the pre/post means. Require at least 2,000
US records and 500 records in each comparison country. These imposed
thresholds retain all 24 pre/post weeks for the USA, Canada, and the UK
in this window. Compute each weekly percentage from its numerator and
denominator, then weight weeks equally.

For comparison country \(c\), the descriptive contrast is

\[
\widehat D_c=(\overline p_{US,post}-\overline p_{US,pre})
 -(\overline p_{c,post}-\overline p_{c,pre}).
\]

Here \(p\) is the percentage of observed records reporting
unavailability. The contrast has percentage-point units. A causal
interpretation would require the US outcome to follow the comparison
country's change in the absence of the policy, together with comparable
measurement, a suitable exposure definition, and no consequential
spillovers or simultaneous country-specific changes. The national policy
supplies one treated country. Repeated stores and weeks do not create
additional independent policy assignments.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Country & Pre-Period Mean (\%) & Post-Period Mean (\%) & Change
(Percentage Points) \\
\midrule

USA & 14.80 & 16.87 & +2.07 \\
Canada & 6.09 & 7.52 & +1.42 \\
UK & 19.36 & 8.06 & -11.29 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The US-minus-Canada contrast is +0.65 percentage points. The US-minus-UK
contrast is +13.37 points. The UK pre-period contains a large temporary
rise in recorded unavailability; its subsequent decline dominates the
second contrast. The time paths therefore matter for selecting a
comparison, even when a regression can readily produce a coefficient.
Canadian record counts are constant at 1,428 in this window. That
regularity calls for checking the source's refresh process alongside the
apparent stability of the percentage. A constant count alone does not
establish a stale feed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_mcbroken_policy.tex}
\caption{Weekly recorded unavailability varies sharply in the UK before the US policy date. The country paths expose the sensitivity of a pre/post contrast to the chosen comparison.}\label{fig:M06_mcbroken_policy}
\end{figure}

These data support an evaluation of a proposed policy comparison. The
positive contrasts do not establish that the exemption worsened
availability. Stronger evidence would connect a stable set of outlets to
policy exposure, actual repair adoption, verified mechanical
interruptions, and comparable collection times. Pre-treatment event
coefficients can diagnose particular discrepancies, while a
nonsignificant pre-trend test supplies no proof of the counterfactual
assumption. Customer demand, service hours, and repair implementation
would further distinguish an operational policy effect from a change in
the ordering measure.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source: \href{../03_Data_and_Code/McBroken/policy.py}{policy.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ policy.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Calculate descriptive country contrasts around the October 2024 exemption."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def main():
    data = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/policy_window.csv")
    assert not data.duplicated(["country", "event_week"]).any()
    data["percent"] = 100 * data.n_broken / data.n_checked
    # These are sensitivity screens, not a claim of representative coverage.
    data = data[data.n_checked.ge(data.country.map({"USA": 2000, "UK": 500, "CA": 500}))]
    wide = data.pivot(index="event_week", columns="country", values="percent")
    common = wide[["USA", "UK", "CA"]].dropna()
    pre = common.loc[common.index < 0].mean()
    post = common.loc[common.index > 0].mean()  # omit the implementation week
    if len(common.loc[common.index < 0]) != 12 or len(common.loc[common.index > 0]) != 12:
        raise ValueError("Expected 12 common pre weeks and 12 common post weeks")
    change = post - pre
    table = pd.DataFrame({"pre_percent": pre, "post_percent": post,
                          "change_pp": change})
    contrasts = {c: float(change.USA - change[c]) for c in ["CA", "UK"]}
    results = ROOT / "results"
    results.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    table.to_csv(results / "policy_means.csv", index_label="country")
    (results / "policy.json").write_text(json.dumps({
        "effective_date": "2024-10-28", "pre_weeks": 12, "post_weeks": 12,
        "omitted_week": 0, "weighting": "Equal weight per common weekly snapshot",
        "us_change_minus_comparator_change_pp": contrasts,
        "interpretation": "Descriptive contrasts; parallel counterfactual trends and stable measurement are not established."}, indent=2) + "\n")
    figure = r"""\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[width=12.5cm,height=6.7cm,xmin=-12,xmax=12,ymin=0,ymax=100,
 xlabel={Weeks Relative to October 28, 2024},ylabel={Unavailable (\%)},
 xtick={-12,-8,-4,0,4,8,12},legend style={at={(0.98,0.98)},anchor=north east}]
"""
    for country, style in [("USA", "IlliniBlue,mark=*"),
                           ("CA", "IlliniOrange,dashed,mark=square*"),
                           ("UK", "Storm,dotted,mark=triangle*")]:
        points = " ".join(f"({i},{v:.6f})" for i, v in common[country].items())
        figure += f"\\addplot[{style},mark size=1.4pt] coordinates {{{points}}};\n"
    figure += r"\legend{USA,Canada,UK}" + "\n"
    figure += r"\draw[Storm,dashed] (axis cs:0,0)--(axis cs:0,100);" + "\n"
    figure += "\\end{axis}\n\\end{tikzpicture}\n"
    (ROOT.parents[1] / "06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M06_mcbroken_policy.tex").write_text(figure)
    print(table.to_string())
    print(json.dumps(contrasts, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-experimental-objectives-and-customer-outcomes}{%
\section{Experimental Objectives and Customer
Outcomes}\label{M06-experimental-objectives-and-customer-outcomes}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing experiment identifies a response to the assigned
intervention for the represented population. The choice of outcome
determines what success means. An experiment that ranks interfaces by
completed renewals can reliably select a profitable interface while
remaining silent about whether customers wanted the additional
subscription. Randomization addresses the comparison between assigned
procedures; customer value requires an appropriate outcome and its own
measurement.

For a cancellation experiment, define eligibility before assignment and
retain every assigned customer in the primary denominator. Include a
direct-choice benchmark and record the final payment status over a fixed
horizon. Also measure completion time, refunds, unwanted charges, and
customers' informed willingness to continue. Conditioning only on
customers who reach the last page can remove the people most affected by
a difficult interface. Report that intermediate reach rate separately.

The procedure includes the customer's opportunity to refuse optional
retention content. If a customer must first undergo the intervention to
discover how to decline it, the refusal path changes the treatment
itself. A comparison of optional and compulsory interaction can
therefore require different treatment definitions even when the last
screen is identical. Describe the complete assigned sequence before
interpreting the estimated effect.

Under the model in Section 8.14, firm and customer interests are opposed
for the same renewal. Accurate experimentation then helps the firm
select the procedure with the largest customer loss within the available
set. This conditional result follows from the stakes and objective. When
a better product increases both willingness to pay and firm profit, the
same experiment can instead select a mutually beneficial change. The
empirical task is to measure the consequences that distinguish those
settings.

\hypertarget{M06-earnings-calls-a-public-clarification-and-the-event-window}{%
\section{Earnings Calls: A Public Clarification and the Event
Window}\label{M06-earnings-calls-a-public-clarification-and-the-event-window}}

\noindent \noindent A communications manager wants to understand whether pricing
language changed around a public clarification.
\href{https://www.wendys.com/blog/wendys-digital-news-update}{Wendy's
February 27, 2024 statement} described intended uses of digital menu
boards and rejected the interpretation that the company planned higher
prices at its busiest times. That dated company statement supplies an
observable event. It does not establish realized prices or customer
responses.

Define a before window from 90 through one calendar day before the
statement and an after window from one through 90 days after it. Exclude
calls on the event day because within-day ordering is unavailable. Use
calls with observed text and report both all available firms and firms
appearing in both windows. The comparison is the change in the fraction
of calls containing core language. A separate firm-equal calculation
first averages calls within firm and period, then averages those firm
rates, so extra captured calls do not increase a firm's weight.

In the common-firm comparison group, each window contains one call from
each of 27 firms. Core occurrences fall from five to two, while the
number of positive calls remains two in each window. Incidence therefore
remains 2/27, or 7.41\%. In the full available comparison sample, the
apparent call rate falls from 2/27 to 2/34 as coverage expands. These
are distinct sources of an apparent change: repeated language within
calls and the number of observed calls.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_calls_windows.tex}
\caption{For the same 27 comparison firms and 27 calls per 90-day window, core occurrences fall from five to two while two calls contain a match in each period. Call incidence remains 7.41 percent. The event day is excluded.}\label{fig:M06_calls_windows}
\end{figure}

The event is shared public information, and the supplied comparison
group identifies an industry classification. Its firms have not been
verified as unexposed to the event. Earnings-call timing, business
conditions, and disclosure choices also vary. Even a measured change in
disclosure would leave adoption and customer effects as separate
outcomes. A causal design would need a specified exposure, a defensible
counterfactual disclosure path, stable measurement, and uncertainty that
accounts for repeated firms. Matching firm coverage addresses
composition alone.

The program repeats the descriptive calculation with 60-, 90-, and
120-day windows and reports counts, call-weighted rates, and firm-equal
rates. Compare these prespecified windows before writing an explanation
for a selected result. Reconcile the numerator and denominator
separately, then identify the evidence needed for any causal claim.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/event_windows.py}{event\_windows.py}.
From \texttt{03\_Data\_and\_Code/Earnings\_Calls}, run
\texttt{python\ event\_windows.py}. Python, pandas, and NumPy are
required; the committed metadata supply all inputs.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Describe call-level language around a public clarification; no causal effect."""
import pandas as pd
from assessment import HERE, load_checked


def compare_windows(calls, event='2024-02-27', days=90):
    date = pd.Timestamp(event)
    d = calls.loc[calls.text_observed].copy()
    delta = (d.call_date - date).dt.days
    # Exclude the event day because within-day ordering is unavailable.
    d = d.loc[delta.between(-days, -1) | delta.between(1, days)].copy()
    d['period'] = d.call_date.gt(date).map({False: 'before', True: 'after'})
    common = d.groupby('ticker').period.nunique()
    common = common[common.eq(2)].index
    rows = []
    for sample, panel in [('available_calls', d), ('firms_in_both_windows', d[d.ticker.isin(common)])]:
        for (group, period), part in panel.groupby(['group', 'period']):
            rows.append({'window_days': days, 'sample': sample, 'group': group,
                         'period': period, 'firms': part.ticker.nunique(),
                         'calls': len(part), 'positive_calls': int(part.has_core.sum()),
                         'core_matches': int(part.n_core.sum()),
                         'share_percent': 100 * part.has_core.mean(),
                         'firm_equal_share_percent': 100 * part.groupby('ticker').has_core.mean().mean()})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def main():
    calls, _, _, _ = load_checked()
    results = pd.concat([compare_windows(calls, days=n) for n in [60, 90, 120]])
    results.to_csv(HERE / 'results/event_windows.csv', index=False)
    print(results[results.window_days.eq(90)].round(4).to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    (HERE / 'results').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-model-improvements-and-reusable-analytical-workflows}{%
\section{Model Improvements and Reusable Analytical
Workflows}\label{M06-model-improvements-and-reusable-analytical-workflows}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team must decide whether to buy access to a newer
model, invest in a tested code library, or use both. A comparison
between its old setup and a new setup that changes both components
cannot isolate their separate contributions. A factorial comparison
crosses model version with library access and evaluates every condition
using a common task population and acceptance rule.

Consider a synthetic table with 100 assigned tasks in each of four
conditions. Each task requires a correct customer-level analysis within
the same deadline and resource limits. The rubric checks aggregation,
available information, and the managerial interpretation. An unfinished
task counts as a failure. The counts below are constructed teaching
inputs; they are neither measured model performance nor results of a
conducted experiment.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrr@{}}
\toprule
Model & Library & Assigned Tasks & Passing Tasks & Pass Rate \\
\midrule

Earlier & Absent & 100 & 60 & 60\% \\
Earlier & Present & 100 & 70 & 70\% \\
Newer & Absent & 100 & 65 & 65\% \\
Newer & Present & 100 & 85 & 85\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Let \(q_{m\ell}\) denote the fraction of all assigned tasks passing,
where \(m=1\) selects the newer model and \(\ell=1\) supplies the
library. The model comparison depends on library access:
\(q_{10}-q_{00}=0.05\) without it and \(q_{11}-q_{01}=0.15\) with it.
The library comparison is ten percentage points with the earlier model
and twenty with the newer model. Their interaction is

\[
\delta=(q_{11}-q_{10})-(q_{01}-q_{00})=0.10.
\]

The positive interaction means that the imposed library gain is larger
with the newer model. The joint change from 60\% to 85\% is twenty-five
percentage points. It can be decomposed as a five-point model change
followed by a twenty-point library change, or a ten-point library change
followed by a fifteen-point model change. Neither path supplies a unique
allocation of the interaction to one component.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_ai_factorial.tex}
\caption{The library raises the pass rate by ten points with the earlier model and twenty with the newer model. All four rates are synthetic.}\label{fig:M06_ai_factorial}
\end{figure}

In an empirical study, randomize teams or independent analytical
projects to the four conditions, with blocking on task difficulty where
useful. If several outputs come from one team, their number does not
establish the number of independent assignments. Shared helpers and
learning can spill across conditions. A team that first sees the library
may carry its knowledge into a later nominally unassisted task. Separate
teams or a justified design for carryover is needed before interpreting
a crossover comparison.

Use fresh tasks, permit a competent baseline to solve the same problem,
and record actual resource consumption alongside the common ceiling. The
library's setup and maintenance cost enters the investment comparison
even if library construction occurs before randomization. A success on
familiar datasets measures execution within that scope. Transfer to a
different schema or task family requires additional tasks. A revised
prompting or search procedure is a further treatment dimension; changing
it simultaneously with both factors would again prevent attribution.

\hypertarget{M06-reproduce-the-four-condition-comparison}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the Four-Condition
Comparison}\label{M06-reproduce-the-four-condition-comparison}}

\noindent \noindent Run
\texttt{python3\ 03\_Data\_and\_Code/AI\_Workflows/factorial.py} from
the repository root. Python 3.10 or later suffices; no packages or model
account are required. The program writes one CSV row per condition and a
JSON of percentage-point contrasts. Exact rational arithmetic checks the
two paths to the joint change. The code operates on the imposed counts
and supplies no sampling uncertainty or empirical efficacy claim.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Workflows/factorial.py}{factorial.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Construct a synthetic model-by-library comparison; no model APIs are called."""
import csv
import json
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results"


def contrasts(rates):
    """Keys are (model, library), each coded 0 or 1; values are pass fractions."""
    if set(rates) != {(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)}:
        raise ValueError("All four conditions are required")
    return {
        "model_without_library": rates[1, 0] - rates[0, 0],
        "model_with_library": rates[1, 1] - rates[0, 1],
        "library_with_earlier_model": rates[0, 1] - rates[0, 0],
        "library_with_newer_model": rates[1, 1] - rates[1, 0],
        "interaction": rates[1, 1] - rates[1, 0] - rates[0, 1] + rates[0, 0],
        "joint_change": rates[1, 1] - rates[0, 0],
    }


def main():
    # Imposed counts: 100 assigned tasks in every cell. An unfinished task fails.
    # All cells use the same task population, rubric, deadline, and resource limits.
    passes = {(0, 0): 60, (0, 1): 70, (1, 0): 65, (1, 1): 85}
    rates = {key: Fraction(count, 100) for key, count in passes.items()}
    effects = contrasts(rates)
    # Two independent paths from the initial cell to the final cell must agree.
    assert effects["joint_change"] == Fraction(25, 100)
    assert effects["joint_change"] == (
        effects["model_without_library"] + effects["library_with_newer_model"]
    )
    assert effects["joint_change"] == (
        effects["library_with_earlier_model"] + effects["model_with_library"]
    )
    assert effects["interaction"] == Fraction(10, 100)
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    with (OUT / "factorial_cells.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(["model", "library", "assigned", "passed", "pass_fraction"])
        for (model, library), passed in passes.items():
            writer.writerow([model, library, 100, passed, float(rates[model, library])])
    result = {
        "scope": "Constructed counts; no observed AI performance or causal estimate.",
        "units": "percentage points in the fraction of all assigned tasks passing",
        "contrasts_pp": {key: float(100 * value) for key, value in effects.items()},
    }
    (OUT / "factorial_results.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-conversion-returns-and-customer-intent}{%
\section{Conversion, Returns, and Customer
Intent}\label{M06-conversion-returns-and-customer-intent}}

\noindent \noindent An online retailer choosing between promotional messages needs
to measure the consequences after checkout. A message that produces more
orders can also produce more reversals if customers commit before
resolving uncertainty. Define the treatment as the assigned message, the
population as eligible visitors, and the initial outcome as purchases
within a prespecified window. Subsequent returns, complaints, and
retained purchases provide additional outcomes over a longer horizon.

\href{https://doi.org/10.1177/00222437231180494}{The Effects of Pressure
and Self-Assurance Nudges on Product Purchases and Returns in Online
Retailing} reports a randomized field experiment. The available abstract
describes stronger purchase responses to pressure nudges alongside more
returns, while self-assurance produces a different balance. The evidence
motivates evaluating net sales and customer outcomes together. The full
text was not retrieved for this collection, so the abstract supports the
directional comparison; exact effect sizes and implementation conditions
require the complete study.

For a cancellation intervention, the population can instead be customers
who start an exit request. Record the request before assigning any
lawful alternative interface so that treatment does not determine
inclusion in the denominator. Measure successful cancellation, time,
later charges, and whether any accepted retention offer matches stated
intent. A comparison that conditions on post-treatment completion can
exclude the consumers most affected by friction. Consumer understanding
should be measured separately from continued payment.

A policy evaluation adds another source of variation. A rule that takes
effect in one jurisdiction can motivate a difference-in-differences
design, but coverage, preexisting trends, and firm-wide interface
changes must be assessed. If a platform changes its interface
everywhere, untreated jurisdictions may also receive the new design. The
comparison must therefore follow actual exposure, including firms
outside the adopting jurisdiction that receive the same interface
change. The existing policy-comparison code in Section 6.16 supplies the
corresponding timing and comparison-group checks; the
\href{../01_Resources/13_Consumer_Agency_and_Recent_Research/Policy/README.md}{cancellation
source record} supplies the legal distinctions.

\hypertarget{M06-experimental-evidence-and-ai-assisted-decisions}{%
\section{Experimental Evidence and AI-Assisted
Decisions}\label{M06-experimental-evidence-and-ai-assisted-decisions}}

\noindent A firm can reuse randomized comparisons to train a model that proposes
new interventions. Angelopoulos, Lee, and Misra's \emph{Causal
Alignment} applies this idea to email subject lines, with human review
and evaluation in new campaigns. The training signal inherits the
outcome used to rank alternatives. A causal effect on clicks therefore
remains an effect on clicks, even when a more effective generator makes
that effect easier to reproduce. Customer understanding, refusal, and
benefit require corresponding measures and reasons for the proposed
action.
\href{../01_Resources/16_AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/README.md}{Research
guide}.

The selection of an action also depends on its anticipated deployment
setting. Farrell, Korganbekova, and Misra's \emph{Robust A/B Decisions}
evaluates policies under uncertainty about future outcome distributions.
Its conservative treatment of the selected payoff does not add customer
outcomes that were absent from the objective. Marketing Dialectics,
Sections 9.14--9.18, connects these decisions to personalized pricing,
current policy discussions, and a reproducible comparison of profit and
customer surplus.

\hypertarget{M06-discount-depth-and-the-causal-response-curve}{%
\section{Discount Depth and the Causal Response
Curve}\label{M06-discount-depth-and-the-causal-response-curve}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer choosing a discount needs to know how another
percentage point changes profit. A larger discount can increase
purchases while reducing the margin on every unit sold. The relevant
response can therefore rise and then fall. A coefficient near zero can
conceal economically important differences between moderate discounts
and either extreme.

Let \(A\) denote the discount in percentage points, so \(A=20\) means a
20 percent discount. Let \(Y(a)\) be profit in dollars per eligible
customer over the promotion week if that customer receives discount
\(a\). Eligibility is determined before the offer. The population curve
\(\theta(a)=E[Y(a)]\) compares the same population at different
discounts; subtracting \(\theta(a_0)\) gives the effect relative to a
specified reference discount. All curves and observations in Sections
6.22--6.26 are synthetic.

Consider the imposed response

\[
\theta(a)=10+0.4a-0.01a^2,\qquad 0\leq a\leq40.
\]

Profit reaches \$14 at a 20 percent discount and equals \$10 at both
endpoints. If discounts are randomized uniformly over this range,
symmetry makes the population linear-regression slope zero. The fitted
constant is \$38/3, or approximately \$12.67. The nonlinear response
still varies by \$4 per customer. This projection calculation concerns
the uniform-randomization benchmark; the observational sample below
follows a different assignment distribution.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_discount_response.tex}
\caption{A known synthetic profit curve peaks at a 20 percent discount. Its best linear projection under uniform randomized discounts is horizontal at approximately 12.67 dollars.}\label{fig:M06_discount_response}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Figure description.} The horizontal axis varies the discount
from 0 to 40 percentage points while holding the target population and
promotion horizon fixed. The blue curve reaches \$14 at 20. The orange
dashed line is the best linear projection under a uniform discount
distribution. A zero linear slope coexists with a substantial nonlinear
response.

DoubleML's partially linear regression specification places a constant
coefficient on treatment while allowing flexible covariate adjustment.
That specification answers a different question from estimating an
unrestricted curve. Under misspecification, the projection's weighting
matters; its coefficient need not equal a simple average derivative.
Nonparametric double-machine-learning methods also exist.
\href{https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/models.html}{DoubleML
models}; \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.03036}{Colangelo and Lee}.

\hypertarget{M06-adjustment-for-selected-discount-intensity}{%
\section{Adjustment for Selected Discount
Intensity}\label{M06-adjustment-for-selected-discount-intensity}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose customers with stronger expected demand tend to
receive larger discounts. Comparing their observed profits with those of
low-discount customers mixes the discount response with differences in
demand. Let \(X\) contain observed characteristics recorded before the
offer. The conditional outcome mean is \(\mu(x,a)=E[Y\mid X=x,A=a]\),
and \(\pi(a\mid x)\) is the conditional density of the discount. A
density has units of inverse percentage points; it is distinct from the
probability of observing one exact value of a continuous treatment.

A causal interpretation requires a well-defined intervention,
consistency, and conditional mean independence of potential outcomes and
assigned discounts given \(X\). Each dose under consideration also needs
sufficient conditional support for the target population. These
conditions exclude unmeasured common causes of discount assignment and
profit. Randomization within the relevant population can provide this
independence by design.

To average over a common population, define \(m(a)=E_X[\mu(X,a)]\) and
\(f_A(a)=E_X[\pi(a\mid X)]\). The doubly robust adjusted outcome is

\[
\xi_i=\widehat m(A_i)+\frac{\widehat f_A(A_i)}{\widehat\pi(A_i\mid X_i)}
\left[Y_i-\widehat\mu(X_i,A_i)\right].
\]

The first term averages predicted profit over the target population. The
second corrects its residual using the relative frequency of the
customer's assigned dose. Under identification and regularity
conditions, the population conditional mean \(E[\xi\mid A=a]\) equals
\(\theta(a)\) when either nuisance function is correct. If the outcome
model is correct, the residual has conditional mean zero. If the density
model is correct, the density ratio changes the covariate distribution
among customers receiving dose \(a\) back to the target distribution,
canceling the outcome-model error.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00747}{Kennedy, Ma, McHugh, and Small}.

Five-fold cross-fitting estimates each customer's nuisance predictions
using the other four folds. A local linear regression then smooths the
adjusted outcomes across discounts. Cross-fitting limits reuse of the
same outcome for fitting and evaluation. Valid confidence intervals
require additional conditions on estimation errors and smoothing bias.
The name double machine learning alone does not establish double
robustness; that property depends on the score and the nuisance
functions it uses.

\hypertarget{M06-a-known-population-and-four-model-specifications}{%
\subsection{A Known Population and Four Model
Specifications}\label{M06-a-known-population-and-four-model-specifications}}

\noindent \noindent The simulated population contains equal shares of two observed
types, \(X=-1\) and \(X=1\). Each sample fixes 1,200 customers of each
type. Discount assignment and realized profit satisfy

\[
Z=\log\!\left(\frac{A}{40-A}\right)=0.9X+\eta,
\qquad Y=10+0.4A-0.01A^2+2X+\varepsilon,
\]

where \(\eta\) is normal with standard deviation 0.9 and \(\varepsilon\)
is independent normal noise with standard deviation 1. The \(2X\) term
affects both observed profits and the selection problem. Equal target
shares make its population average zero. Outcomes are measured once per
customer, all rows are retained, and no missing values are imposed. The
logistic transformation keeps discounts strictly between 0 and 40.

The correctly specified outcome regression includes a quadratic in
discount and the observed type. Its misspecified counterpart omits type.
The correctly specified density regression fits the transformed discount
on type and estimates its normal residual scale, including the
transformation's Jacobian when calculating the density of \(A\). Its
misspecified counterpart omits type. Target standardization uses the
known equal type shares. These transparent parametric nuisance models
isolate the statistical argument; they do not compare commercial
software packages.

Across 200 independently generated samples of 2,400 customers, the
average root mean squared error over the 29 equally weighted doses from
6 through 34 is:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrr@{}}
\toprule
Outcome Model & Density Model & RMSE (USD) & Coverage (\%) \\
\midrule

Correct & Correct & 0.099 & 90.7 \\
Correct & Omits Type & 0.058 & 85.7 \\
Omits Type & Correct & 0.312 & 96.7 \\
Omits Type & Omits Type & 1.335 & 6.4 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Correctness refers to the data-generating specification. The reported
errors include sampling variation and the bias from a fixed
two-percentage-point smoothing bandwidth. The doubly robust population
identity does not require finite-sample errors to be identical when
either model is correct. In this design, density correction introduces
enough variation that the correctly specified outcome model with unit
weights has the lowest average RMSE. Neither this ranking nor the
coverage rates establish performance in a different population.

The reference sample's cross-fitted partially linear coefficient is
\$0.0028 per percentage point. Its small magnitude reflects the
inadequacy of a constant slope for this symmetric response. It does not
imply that changing discount depth has a negligible effect.

\hypertarget{M06-overlap-weight-concentration-and-missing-confounders}{%
\section{Overlap, Weight Concentration, and Missing
Confounders}\label{M06-overlap-weight-concentration-and-missing-confounders}}

\noindent \noindent A common discount grid requires evidence about both customer
types at each proposed dose. Observing many low discounts among one type
and many high discounts among the other can leave the counterfactual
comparisons poorly represented. Reducing the standard deviation of
\(\eta\) from 0.9 to 0.22 concentrates customers near type-specific
discounts while keeping the same causal profit curve.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_dose_overlap.tex}
\caption{Conditional discount densities for two observed customer types under broader and weaker overlap, plotted on identical axes.}\label{fig:M06_dose_overlap}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Figure description.} Each panel plots the discount density for
type minus one as a solid blue curve and type plus one as a dashed
orange curve. The horizontal axis is discount in percentage points. Both
panels use the same vertical scale in density per percentage point.
Lower assignment noise concentrates each type around a different
discount. Mathematical positivity remains, but the observed sample
offers little information about the opposite type at many doses.

The weight-based effective sample size is
\((\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\). It measures concentration among
observed weights. In the reference sample with broader overlap, the
largest estimated weight is 169.9 and the effective sample size is 125.5
out of 2,400. With weaker overlap, almost all observed weights are close
to one-half and the effective sample size is approximately 2,400. The
rare cross-type observations that would receive enormous weights are
largely absent. A high effective sample size therefore does not
establish adequate support. Conditional densities, dose-by-type counts,
and the proposed decision range remain necessary checks.

When the outcome model omits type and the density specification is
correct, capping weights at five raises the broader-overlap reference
error from \$0.532 to \$0.634. Capping reduces weight concentration but
changes the residual correction. It can remove the cancellation of
outcome-model error that supplies double robustness. In the
weaker-overlap sample, the error is \$1.825 with or without the cap.
These are comparisons within one fixed sample. They motivate sensitivity
analysis without selecting a threshold after seeing which estimate is
preferred.

An unobserved common cause creates a separate problem. Add an
independent type \(U\in\{-1,1\}\) with equal shares to both assignment
and profit: \(Z=0.9X+0.8U+\eta\) and \(Y=\theta(A)+2X+2U+\varepsilon\).
Even exact knowledge of \(E[Y\mid A,X]\) identifies an adjusted
association when \(U\) remains omitted. Bayes' rule gives
\(E[U\mid Z,X]=\tanh\{0.8(Z-0.9X)/0.9^2\}\). Standardizing this observed
regression over \(X\) differs from the causal curve by as much as
\$1.666 on the 6--34 grid. Better nuisance prediction cannot remove this
identification failure. Measuring \(U\) or obtaining a credible
alternative design changes the available comparison.

\hypertarget{M06-interval-coverage-and-reproducible-estimation}{%
\section{Interval Coverage and Reproducible
Estimation}\label{M06-interval-coverage-and-reproducible-estimation}}

\noindent \noindent A confidence interval at one prespecified dose addresses a
narrower event than covering the entire response curve. The program
reports conditional HC0 standard errors for the local linear regression,
holding the fitted adjusted outcomes fixed. These approximate standard
errors omit first-stage uncertainty and smoothing bias. Their nominal 95
percent label is evaluated against the known curve across repeated
samples.

With both nuisance models correctly specified, mean pointwise coverage
is 90.7 percent, while all 29 points lie inside their respective
pointwise intervals in 42.5 percent of samples. The latter event has no
nominal 95 percent guarantee because these are pointwise intervals. The
former comparison directly shows undercoverage of the pointwise
procedure in this design. Each dose has 200 simulated coverage
indicators; its Monte Carlo standard error is
\(\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/200}\). Correlated doses within a
sample do not supply independent repetitions. The saved coverage table
retains each dose's rate and simulation uncertainty.

The fixed bandwidth creates a finite-resolution teaching comparison.
Consistency for an unrestricted curve requires an appropriate bandwidth
sequence and regularity conditions. In applied work, inference must
address the sampling unit, nuisance estimation, smoothing, and any
search over doses. Refitting the whole pipeline in a bootstrap can
assess some sources of uncertainty under suitable conditions; it does
not resolve missing confounders or unsupported extrapolation. Selecting
the maximum of an estimated curve also selects estimation noise,
motivating independent policy evaluation.

Run the calculation from its example directory:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
cd 03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response
python dose_response.py --output local_runs --repetitions 200
\end{Verbatim}

The output includes synthetic customer records, all four fitted curves,
coverage by dose, weight diagnostics, and the exact hidden-confounder
comparison. Seeds, units, sample sizes, dependencies, and commands are
recorded in the
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/README.md}{example guide}.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/dose_response.py}{dose\_response.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Synthetic discount curves, cross-fitting, overlap, and interval evaluation.

Run: python dose_response.py --output results --repetitions 200
All doses are percentage points; profit is dollars per eligible customer.
The target population places equal weight on X=-1 and X=1.
"""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse
import json
import platform
import numpy as np

GRID = np.linspace(6, 34, 29)
SETTINGS = [(True, True), (True, False), (False, True), (False, False)]


def truth(a):
    return 10 + 0.4 * np.asarray(a) - 0.01 * np.asarray(a) ** 2


def generate(n=2400, seed=20261118, sigma=0.9):
    """Equal numbers of each observed type; no exclusions or missing rows."""
    if n % 2:
        raise ValueError("n must be even")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = rng.permutation(np.repeat([-1.0, 1.0], n // 2))
    z = 0.9 * x + rng.normal(0, sigma, n)
    a = 40 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
    y = truth(a) + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return x, a, y


def outcome_features(x, a, correct=True):
    t = (np.asarray(a) - 20) / 10
    columns = [np.ones_like(t), t, t * t]
    if correct:
        columns.append(np.broadcast_to(x, t.shape))
    return np.column_stack(columns)


def treatment_features(x, correct=True):
    return np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x]) if correct else np.ones((len(x), 1))


def density(a, mean, sigma):
    """Logistic-normal density on (0,40), including its Jacobian."""
    a = np.asarray(a)
    z = np.log(a / (40 - a))
    return (np.exp(-0.5 * ((z - mean) / sigma) ** 2)
            / (np.sqrt(2 * np.pi) * sigma) * 40 / (a * (40 - a)))


def pseudo_outcome(x, a, y, outcome_correct=True, gps_correct=True, cap=None, seed=71):
    """Five folds; train each nuisance only on the other four folds.

    Standardization uses the stated equal-type target population. The wrong
    outcome model omits X; the wrong dose model omits X on the logit scale.
    cap is a fixed maximum weight, not an estimated quantile.
    """
    fold = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(np.arange(len(y)) % 5)
    xi, raw_weight = np.empty_like(y), np.empty_like(y)
    for k in range(5):
        tr, te = fold != k, fold == k
        b = np.linalg.lstsq(outcome_features(x[tr], a[tr], outcome_correct), y[tr], rcond=None)[0]
        mu = outcome_features(x[te], a[te], outcome_correct) @ b
        marginal_mu = sum(outcome_features(g, a[te], outcome_correct) @ b for g in [-1, 1]) / 2
        z = np.log(a[tr] / (40 - a[tr]))
        design = treatment_features(x[tr], gps_correct)
        c = np.linalg.lstsq(design, z, rcond=None)[0]
        sigma = np.sqrt(np.mean((z - design @ c) ** 2))
        observed_mean = treatment_features(x[te], gps_correct) @ c
        conditional = density(a[te], observed_mean, sigma)
        marginal = sum(density(a[te], treatment_features(np.full(te.sum(), g), gps_correct) @ c,
                               sigma) for g in [-1, 1]) / 2
        raw_weight[te] = marginal / conditional
        weight = raw_weight[te] if cap is None else np.minimum(raw_weight[te], cap)
        xi[te] = marginal_mu + weight * (y[te] - mu)
    return xi, raw_weight


def smooth(a, y, grid=GRID, bandwidth=2.0):
    """Local linear Gaussian smoother and conditional HC0 standard error.

    This standard error holds fitted pseudo-outcomes fixed. It omits nuisance
    estimation and smoothing bias; its coverage is evaluated, never presumed.
    """
    delta = np.asarray(a)[:, None] - np.asarray(grid)[None, :]
    w = np.exp(-0.5 * (delta / bandwidth) ** 2)
    s0, s1, s2 = w.sum(0), (w * delta).sum(0), (w * delta**2).sum(0)
    determinant = s0 * s2 - s1**2
    if np.any(determinant <= 1e-14):
        raise ValueError("Insufficient local variation at an evaluation dose")
    linear_weights = w * (s2 - delta * s1) / determinant
    slope_weights = w * (delta * s0 - s1) / determinant
    estimate = linear_weights.T @ y
    slope = slope_weights.T @ y
    residual = y[:, None] - estimate - delta * slope
    se = np.sqrt(((linear_weights * residual) ** 2).sum(0))
    return estimate, se


def plr_slope(x, a, y):
    """Cross-fitted Robinson partialling-out slope, with binary-X nuisances."""
    fold = np.random.default_rng(71).permutation(np.arange(len(y)) % 5)
    ra, ry = np.empty_like(a), np.empty_like(y)
    design = treatment_features(x)
    for k in range(5):
        tr, te = fold != k, fold == k
        ra[te] = a[te] - design[te] @ np.linalg.lstsq(design[tr], a[tr], rcond=None)[0]
        ry[te] = y[te] - design[te] @ np.linalg.lstsq(design[tr], y[tr], rcond=None)[0]
    return float(ra @ ry / (ra @ ra))


def hidden_confounding(grid=GRID):
    """Exact observable-data regression with an omitted independent U in {-1,1}.

    Z=.9X+.8U+Normal(0,.9), Y=truth(A)+2X+2U+noise. Bayes' rule gives
    E[U|Z,X]=tanh(.8*(Z-.9X)/.9**2). Both observable nuisance functions could
    be known exactly and adjustment for X would still miss the causal curve.
    """
    z = np.log(grid / (40 - grid))
    observed = truth(grid) + sum(2 * np.tanh(0.8 * (z - 0.9 * g) / 0.9**2)
                                for g in [-1, 1]) / 2
    return observed


def save_table(path, columns, rows):
    np.savetxt(path, np.asarray(rows), delimiter=",", header=",".join(columns), comments="", fmt="%.10g")


def run(output, repetitions=200):
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    x, a, y = generate()
    save_table(output / "customers.csv", ["type", "discount_pp", "profit_usd"], np.c_[x, a, y])
    reference, curve_columns, curves = [], ["discount_pp", "truth_usd"], [GRID, truth(GRID)]
    for oc, gc in SETTINGS:
        name = f"outcome_{int(oc)}_density_{int(gc)}"
        xi, w = pseudo_outcome(x, a, y, oc, gc)
        est, se = smooth(a, xi)
        reference.append({"model": name, "rmse_usd": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((est-truth(GRID))**2))),
                          "weight_max": float(w.max()), "ess_rows": float(w.sum()**2/(w@w))})
        curve_columns.extend([name, name + "_conditional_se"])
        curves.extend([est, se])
    save_table(output / "curves.csv", curve_columns, np.column_stack(curves))
    evaluation, point_rows = [], []
    for oc, gc in SETTINGS:
        cover, whole, rmse, bias = [], [], [], []
        for r in range(repetitions):
            xr, ar, yr = generate(seed=10000+r)
            xi, _ = pseudo_outcome(xr, ar, yr, oc, gc)
            est, se = smooth(ar, xi)
            error = est - truth(GRID)
            hit = np.abs(error) <= 1.96 * se
            cover.append(hit); whole.append(hit.all())
            rmse.append(np.sqrt(np.mean(error**2))); bias.append(error)
        point_cover = np.mean(cover, axis=0)
        evaluation.append({"outcome_correct": oc, "density_correct": gc,
                           "mean_rmse_usd": float(np.mean(rmse)),
                           "mean_pointwise_coverage": float(point_cover.mean()),
                           "whole_grid_coverage_of_pointwise_intervals": float(np.mean(whole))})
        for dose, coverage, mean_bias in zip(GRID, point_cover, np.mean(bias, axis=0)):
            point_rows.append([int(oc), int(gc), dose, coverage,
                               np.sqrt(coverage*(1-coverage)/repetitions), mean_bias])
    save_table(output / "coverage.csv", ["outcome_correct", "density_correct", "discount_pp",
               "pointwise_coverage", "monte_carlo_se", "mean_bias_usd"], point_rows)
    overlap = []
    for sigma in [0.9, 0.22]:
        xx, aa, yy = generate(sigma=sigma)
        for cap in [None, 5.0]:
            xi, w = pseudo_outcome(xx, aa, yy, False, True, cap=cap)
            estimate, _ = smooth(aa, xi)
            used = w if cap is None else np.minimum(w, cap)
            overlap.append({"sigma": sigma, "cap": cap, "max_raw_weight": float(w.max()),
                            "ess_rows": float(used.sum()**2/(used@used)),
                            "rmse_usd": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((estimate-truth(GRID))**2)))})
    dose = np.linspace(1, 39, 153)
    save_table(output / "overlap.csv", ["discount_pp", "broad_minus", "broad_plus", "narrow_minus", "narrow_plus"],
               np.c_[dose, density(dose, -.9, .9), density(dose, .9, .9),
                     density(dose, -.9, .22), density(dose, .9, .22)])
    save_table(output / "hidden_confounding.csv", ["discount_pp", "causal_profit_usd", "adjusted_association_usd"],
               np.c_[GRID, truth(GRID), hidden_confounding()])
    report = {"seed": 20261118, "n": len(y), "repetitions": repetitions,
              "python": platform.python_version(), "numpy": np.__version__,
              "grid_pp": [6, 34, 1], "bandwidth_pp": 2.0,
              "reference": reference, "plr_slope_usd_per_pp": plr_slope(x, a, y),
              "simulation": evaluation, "overlap": overlap,
              "hidden_confounding_max_bias_usd": float(np.max(np.abs(hidden_confounding()-truth(GRID)))),
              "scope": "Synthetic fixed-design evaluations. Intervals are conditional HC0 pointwise approximations; no simultaneous-band guarantee."}
    (output / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results")
    parser.add_argument("--repetitions", type=int, default=200)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.repetitions < 2:
        parser.error("Use at least two independent repetitions")
    run(args.output, args.repetitions)
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-store-decisions-and-partial-pooling}{%
\section{Store Decisions and Partial
Pooling}\label{M06-store-decisions-and-partial-pooling}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer may need a different discount for each store, while
some stores supply only a small number of customers. Separate estimates
then have high sampling variation. A common curve can conceal persistent
differences across stores. Partial pooling estimates a common response
together with regional and store deviations, shrinking the deviations
according to a penalty selected using validation outcomes.

The synthetic comparison has 20 stores nested in four regions. Each
region contains stores with 12, 25, 60, 150, and 300 customers, giving
2,188 observations. Discounts are independently randomized between 5 and
35 within every store. Profit equals a quadratic response with imposed
region and store coefficient deviations plus independent noise with a
\$3 standard deviation. Randomization removes the need for confounder
adjustment in this comparison, allowing differences in pooling to
determine the estimation tradeoff.

Write \(B(a)=(1,t,t^2-0.75)'\), where \(t=(a-20)/10\). The fitted curve
for store \(s\) in region \(r\) is

\[
\widehat\theta_s(a)=B(a)'(\widehat\beta+\widehat b_r+\widehat c_s).
\]

The coefficients minimize the sum of squared customer residuals plus
\(\lambda_r\sum_r\|b_r\|^2+\lambda_s\sum_s\|c_s\|^2\). Global
coefficients are unpenalized. Five-fold validation within every store
selects each penalty from 1, 10, and 100, averaging validation squared
error equally across stores. Both selected penalties equal 100. The
final fit uses every observation. The known response curves enter only
the evaluation, with equal weight on each store and each of 29 doses
from 6 through 34.

All entries below are curve RMSE in dollars per customer. Parentheses
give the number of stores.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Store Sample & Complete & Separate & Partial \\
\midrule

All (20) & 0.968 & 0.936 & 0.512 \\
12 or 25 Customers (8) & 0.954 & 1.376 & 0.666 \\
150 or 300 Customers (8) & 1.084 & 0.376 & 0.349 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Partial pooling has the lowest aggregate error in this one simulated
dataset. Individual stores can favor a different estimator. Store 4,
with 300 customers, has separate-fit RMSE of \$0.249 and partial-pooling
RMSE of \$0.550. Pooling trades variation against bias toward shared
coefficients, so a large aggregate improvement does not establish
improvement at every store.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_store_pooling.tex}
\caption{Known, separately fitted, and partially pooled discount curves for one small store and one large store on common axes.}\label{fig:M06_store_pooling}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Figure description.} Store 0 has 12 customers and Store 4 has
300. Solid blue curves show their known synthetic responses, gray dashed
curves show separate quadratic fits, and orange dash-dotted curves show
partial pooling. Both panels share discount and profit scales. Shrinkage
improves the small store's curve while moving the large store's estimate
farther from its known response.

An observational extension would require adjustment for assignment
within the relevant target groups. A group-specific curve averages
covariates within that group and uses the corresponding marginal
treatment density. Smoothing a population-standardized adjusted outcome
within stores generally changes the intended estimand. The reviewed
\texttt{drcurves} implementation performs group-specific standardization
before hierarchical smoothing. Group curves still require credible
within-group support; pooling cannot supply an unobserved counterfactual
without additional modeling assumptions.
\href{https://github.com/raz1470/continuous-dr-learner/blob/72115789652127cc2a89eb960d829d2cc513d9cb/src/drcurves/nuisance.py}{Pinned
implementation}.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/store_pooling.py}{store\_pooling.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Randomized synthetic discounts: separate, complete, and partial pooling.

Twenty stores nested in four regions; equal-store evaluation on a common grid.
Only observed validation outcomes select penalties. Known curves score the fits.
"""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse
import json
import numpy as np


def basis(a):
    t = (np.asarray(a) - 20) / 10
    return np.column_stack([np.ones_like(t), t, t*t - 0.75])


def design(a, store):
    b = basis(a)
    region = store // 5
    return np.column_stack([b] + [b*(region == r)[:, None] for r in range(4)]
                           + [b*(store == s)[:, None] for s in range(20)])


def fit(a, store, y, region_penalty, store_penalty):
    d = design(a, store)
    penalty = np.r_[np.zeros(3), np.full(12, region_penalty), np.full(60, store_penalty)]
    return np.linalg.solve(d.T @ d + np.diag(penalty), d.T @ y)


def generate(seed=20261119):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sizes = np.tile([12, 25, 60, 150, 300], 4)
    region = np.array([[-.6, -.5, .1], [-.2, .4, -.1], [.2, -.2, -.1], [.6, .3, .1]])
    coefficient = (np.array([13.25, 0, -1]) + np.repeat(region, 5, axis=0)
                   + rng.normal(size=(20, 3)) * [.6, .5, .3])
    store = np.repeat(np.arange(20), sizes)
    a = rng.uniform(5, 35, len(store))  # Randomized independently within every store.
    y = np.sum(basis(a) * coefficient[store], axis=1) + rng.normal(0, 3, len(a))
    fold = np.concatenate([rng.permutation(np.arange(n) % 5) for n in sizes])
    return a, store, y, coefficient, fold


def run(output):
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    a, store, y, coefficient, fold = generate()
    candidates = []
    for rp in [1., 10., 100.]:
        for sp in [1., 10., 100.]:
            prediction = np.empty_like(y)
            for k in range(5):
                tr, te = fold != k, fold == k
                beta = fit(a[tr], store[tr], y[tr], rp, sp)
                prediction[te] = design(a[te], store[te]) @ beta
            loss = np.mean([np.mean((y[store == s]-prediction[store == s])**2) for s in range(20)])
            candidates.append((loss, rp, sp))
    loss, rp, sp = min(candidates)
    partial = fit(a, store, y, rp, sp)
    complete = np.linalg.lstsq(basis(a), y, rcond=None)[0]
    grid, rows, errors = np.arange(6., 35.), [], []
    for s in range(20):
        selected = store == s
        separate = np.linalg.lstsq(basis(a[selected]), y[selected], rcond=None)[0]
        target = basis(grid) @ coefficient[s]
        predictions = [basis(grid) @ complete, basis(grid) @ separate,
                       design(grid, np.full(len(grid), s)) @ partial]
        errors.append([selected.sum()] + [np.mean((p-target)**2) for p in predictions])
        rows.extend(np.c_[np.full(len(grid), s), grid, target, *predictions].tolist())
    errors = np.array(errors)
    np.savetxt(output / "stores.csv", np.c_[store, store//5, a, y, fold], delimiter=",", comments="",
               header="store,region,discount_pp,profit_usd,validation_fold", fmt="%.10g")
    np.savetxt(output / "store_curves.csv", rows, delimiter=",", comments="",
               header="store,discount_pp,truth,complete,separate,partial", fmt="%.10g")
    np.savetxt(output / "pooling_cv.csv", candidates, delimiter=",", comments="",
               header="equal_store_validation_mse,region_penalty,store_penalty", fmt="%.10g")
    results = {}
    for name, selected in [("all_stores", np.ones(20, bool)), ("small_stores_n_le_25", errors[:, 0] <= 25),
                           ("large_stores_n_ge_150", errors[:, 0] >= 150)]:
        results[name] = dict(zip(["complete", "separate", "partial"],
                                np.sqrt(errors[selected, 1:].mean(0)).tolist()))
    report = {"seed": 20261119, "observations": len(y), "stores": 20, "regions": 4,
              "region_penalty": rp, "store_penalty": sp, "validation_mse": loss,
              "rmse_usd": results, "scope": "One synthetic randomized dataset; no confidence intervals or general dominance claim."}
    (output / "pooling_summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results")
    run(parser.parse_args().output)
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-continuous-treatment-and-parallel-trends}{%
\section{Continuous Treatment and Parallel
Trends}\label{M06-continuous-treatment-and-parallel-trends}}

\noindent \noindent A store panel can sometimes support a comparison of profit
changes across discount intensities. If an unobserved store
characteristic enters profit additively with the same coefficient in
both periods, differencing removes that component. Time-varying demand
shocks, changing loadings on the characteristic, and dose choices
responding to expected profit changes require further justification.

Ordinary parallel trends can identify treatment-on-the-treated level
effects relative to no treatment for particular dose groups. Comparing
those effects across dose groups also compares populations that may have
different gains from treatment. Interpreting the slope across doses as a
causal response generally requires stronger restrictions. Pretreatment
patterns can reveal some failures, but a flat placebo curve does not
prove the required post-treatment comparison. The appropriate design
depends on the assignment process and the target effect.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02637v8}{Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and
Sant'Anna, December 2025 version}.

For a marketing panel, specify the offer date, anticipation period,
customer or store assignment unit, and any other interventions changing
alongside the discount. Keep repeated units in the same nuisance-fitting
fold and use inference suited to the assignment and dependence
structure. If the existing mHealth logs do not record randomized
notification intensity, a causal notification-response curve requires an
additional design. Logging frequency by itself describes observed
behavior and cannot substitute for an assigned intervention.

\hypertarget{M06-fixed-experimental-designs-and-auxiliary-responses}{%
\section{Fixed Experimental Designs and Auxiliary
Responses}\label{M06-fixed-experimental-designs-and-auxiliary-responses}}

\noindent \noindent A firm planning product research can choose both the profiles
shown and the source supplying each response. When response features,
bias features, variances, and sampling costs are known, the information
supplied by another response is determined by its source and profile.
The realized rating need not change that information calculation. This
makes a design fixed before data collection a useful benchmark.

\href{https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298}{Jasin,
Lin, and Zhang}, Theorem 1, show that such a fixed allocation attains
the minimum leading sampling cost as the coefficient-MSE target
approaches zero in their linear Gaussian model. The objective requires
accuracy uniformly over the unknown response and bias coefficients. The
result permits lower-order differences at finite accuracy. Their pilot
extension estimates unknown noise variances; it retains known response
and bias features.

The distinction from an adaptive marketing experiment follows from the
information structure and objective. A nonlinear choice model can make
information depend on unknown parameters. An online promotion experiment
can value revenue earned during learning as well as a final estimate. An
unknown bias dictionary requires evidence about which source comparisons
remain valid. These changes require their own allocation analysis.
\href{M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md}{Section 4.24} provides the
fixed-design calculation, and
\href{M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md}{Section 7.37} shows what
happens when its bias restriction fails. Synthetic ratings alone do not
establish an intervention's causal effect on human purchasing.

\hypertarget{M06-factorial-comparisons-of-coding-workflows}{%
\section{Factorial Comparisons of Coding
Workflows}\label{M06-factorial-comparisons-of-coding-workflows}}

\noindent \noindent A firm deciding whether to improve task documentation or
introduce automated feedback needs evidence about their separate
contributions. Changing both at once can establish the effect of the
combined procedure under a credible comparison, while leaving each
component's contribution unresolved. The mHealth design in §1.17 crosses
information and feedback at a fixed model version. Each repeated run
receives a clean state, and the order of the four configurations is
randomized within a repetition to reduce systematic timing differences.

Let \(q_{cf}\) denote the probability of a valid complete output on the
fixed evaluation task when explicit context has value \(c\in\{0,1\}\)
and development feedback has value \(f\in\{0,1\}\). Validity is defined
by the independently maintained output checks. The contribution of
context depends on whether feedback is supplied. The interaction records
the difference between those contributions:

\[
\Delta_{CF}=(q_{11}-q_{01})-(q_{10}-q_{00}).
\]

A positive interaction means that context has a larger effect on
valid-output probability when feedback is available, under this model,
task, and resource policy. A negative interaction means that its
measured contribution is smaller. Neither sign by itself identifies why
the components interact. The execution records can suggest a mechanism,
such as a checker exposing a misunderstood date boundary; a targeted
intervention is needed to separate that mechanism from competing
explanations.

Count timeouts and missing files as unsuccessful assigned attempts.
Preserve paired repetitions and record costs even when no valid output
is produced. Fresh conversations limit carryover from prior feedback,
while random order alone does not remove provider updates or
human-review learning. Hold the model version fixed, blind reviewers to
the configuration where feasible, and record disruptions. Five
repetitions per cell on one August workload assess repeat-run variation
conditional on that workload. A claim about marketing analysis generally
requires independent tasks drawn from the intended deployment setting.

An execution record is diagnostic evidence. It can show that a file was
unavailable, a tool failed, or an incorrect output passed a narrow
checker. Those observations do not identify the causal effect of
replacing the model or changing the tool. The component intervention and
its comparison define that question. The public
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows/EXPERIMENT_PROTOCOL.md}{protocol}
supplies the recording requirements without presuming a measured gain.

\hypertarget{M06-store-assignment-and-false-discoveries}{%
\section{Store Assignment and False
Discoveries}\label{M06-store-assignment-and-false-discoveries}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer considering a promotion needs evidence that
incremental customer contribution covers its cost. Suppose the promotion
is assigned to stores, while the data contain one outcome for each
customer. Local demand can move many customers' outcomes together.
Treating every customer as an independent experimental unit can then
produce a precise-looking estimate even when the number of independently
assigned stores is modest.

To isolate this problem, consider a synthetic experiment with 40 stores
and 20 customers per store. Exactly half the stores receive the
promotion. The outcome is net contribution per customer in dollars,
which can include losses. The promotion has zero effect for every
customer. Keeping that truth fixed allows repeated experiments to
measure how often each test incorrectly reports an effect.

The variance calculation uses the following restrictions.

\begin{assumption}\label{ass:balanced-store-assignment}
There are $G$ independent stores, with an even $G\geq4$, and $m\geq2$ customers in every store. Exactly $G/2$ stores are assigned to treatment uniformly at random, independently of potential outcomes. Every customer's outcome is observed, and assignment has no spillovers across stores.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}\label{ass:store-null-outcomes}
For store $g$ and customer $j$, potential outcomes satisfy $Y_{gj}(1)=Y_{gj}(0)=\mu+u_g+e_{gj}$. Store shocks are independent normal draws with variance $\sigma^2\rho$; customer shocks are independent normal draws with variance $\sigma^2(1-\rho)$. The two shock families are independent, with $0\leq\rho<1$ and $\sigma^2>0$.
\end{assumption}

Here \(\mu\) is mean customer contribution, \(u_g\) is a shared store
shock, and \(e_{gj}\) is an individual customer shock. The within-store
correlation is \(\rho\), and each customer's marginal outcome variance
is \(\sigma^2\). Set \(\mu=100\), \(\sigma^2=800\), \(G=40\), and
\(m=20\). These are illustrative parameters, with Gaussian support on
the real line.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_store_assignment.tex}
\caption{The promotion is assigned to 20 of 40 stores. Each store supplies 20 customer outcomes sharing a store shock. Comparing average store means retains the same customer-average point estimate because store sizes are equal.}\label{fig:M06_store_assignment}
\end{figure}

The difference between treated and control store means estimates the
same contrast as the difference between all treated and control customer
outcomes under the equal-size restriction. Its sampling variance under
Assumptions \ref{ass:balanced-store-assignment} and
\ref{ass:store-null-outcomes} is

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\tau)=\frac{4\sigma^2}{G}
\left(\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{m}\right).
\]

The store shock survives averaging over customers, while the individual
component falls with \(m\). An independence calculation using \(Gm\)
customers would instead use \(4\sigma^2/(Gm)\). The ratio of the true
variance to that benchmark is \(1+(m-1)\rho\). At \(\rho=0.3\), the
ratio is 6.7. Additional customer observations reveal the store mean
more precisely while leaving the number of independently assigned stores
unchanged.

The program compares two-sided Welch tests using customer rows or store
means. Each procedure computes the same point estimate, then estimates
variance and reference degrees of freedom using its respective
observation unit. Aggregation to store means is appropriate for the
equal-size setup here. Unequal store sizes require an explicit choice
between a customer-weighted and a store-weighted target and an estimator
suited to that design.

\hypertarget{M06-a-fixed-experiment-and-repeated-null-comparisons}{%
\subsection{A Fixed Experiment and Repeated Null
Comparisons}\label{M06-a-fixed-experiment-and-repeated-null-comparisons}}

\noindent \noindent In the first generated experiment at \(\rho=0.3\), both
methods estimate an increase of \$4.334 per customer. The customer-row
test reports \(p=0.0287\); the store-mean test reports \(p=0.3446\). The
first dataset is retained by its position in the seeded run, without
searching for a significant result. The true intervention effect remains
zero.

The broader comparison generates 4,000 independent experiments at each
correlation. Each experiment redraws stores and customers, randomly
assigns half the stores, and tests one prespecified outcome at
\(\alpha=0.05\). The same underlying Gaussian draws and assignments are
reused across correlations to make those comparisons paired. The
rejection fractions describe repeated sampling and assignment under this
simulation; they are not exact conditional randomization-test
probabilities for one fixed dataset.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Within-Store Correlation & Customer-Row Rejection Rate & Store-Mean
Rejection Rate \\
\midrule

0.0 & 5.20\% & 4.975\% \\
0.1 & 24.20\% & 4.950\% \\
0.3 & 44.90\% & 4.700\% \\
0.5 & 55.00\% & 4.775\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M06_null_calibration.tex}
\caption{Rejection fractions across 4,000 zero-effect experiments at each correlation. Customer-row inference increasingly rejects the true null as within-store correlation rises; store-mean inference stays near the nominal 5\% level. Bars are Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo rejection fractions.}\label{fig:M06_null_calibration}
\end{figure}

The customer-row test allows unequal variances across treatment arms,
yet it omits the covariance among customers sharing a store. Allowing
heteroskedasticity therefore does not solve this dependence problem. The
store-mean test remains close to its nominal level across these Gaussian
settings. Its Monte Carlo intervals describe uncertainty in an estimated
rejection fraction; the intervals do not describe the dispersion of
customer outcomes or uncertainty about one promotion effect.

A firm's assistant should identify assignment and dependence before
inspecting which procedure produces significance. Evaluate a proposed
test on newly generated data with a known null, then examine power under
a specified nonzero effect. Reporting only the most favorable outcome or
stopping after a favorable interim result changes the testing procedure.
The single-outcome calculation here leaves those choices fixed; the
experimental plan in Section 6.3 must address them when they occur.

\hypertarget{M06-reproduce-the-experiments}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the
Experiments}\label{M06-reproduce-the-experiments}}

\noindent \noindent Run
\texttt{python3\ 03\_Data\_and\_Code/Statistical\_Inference/store\_randomization.py}
from the repository root. The program saves the simulation parameters,
rejection counts, Monte Carlo intervals, the first result at each
correlation, and the first customer-level dataset at \(\rho=0.3\). The
analytical variance provides a separate comparison with the empirical
dispersion of estimated effects.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/store_randomization.py}{store\_randomization.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Evaluate false-positive rates with a store-randomized zero-effect promotion."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUTPUT = ROOT / "results"
SEED = 20261125
REPETITIONS = 4000
STORES = 40
CUSTOMERS = 20
VARIANCE = 800.0
CORRELATIONS = (0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5)
ALPHA = .05


def welch(a, b):
    """Treat rows as experiments and columns as independent observations."""
    a, b = np.atleast_2d(a), np.atleast_2d(b)
    if min(a.shape[1], b.shape[1]) < 2:
        raise ValueError("Each arm needs at least two independent observations")
    v0, v1 = a.var(axis=1, ddof=1) / a.shape[1], b.var(axis=1, ddof=1) / b.shape[1]
    se = np.sqrt(v0 + v1)
    if np.any(se == 0):
        raise ValueError("A positive contrast variance is required")
    df = (v0 + v1) ** 2 / (v0 ** 2 / (a.shape[1]-1) + v1 ** 2 / (b.shape[1]-1))
    effect = b.mean(axis=1) - a.mean(axis=1)
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(effect / se), df)
    return effect, se, df, p


def compare_methods(outcomes, treated):
    """Equal store sizes make both point estimates identical."""
    r, g, m = outcomes.shape
    if treated.shape != (r, g) or g % 2 or not np.all(treated.sum(axis=1) == g//2):
        raise ValueError("Exactly half the stores must receive the promotion")
    customer0 = outcomes[~treated].reshape(r, g//2*m)
    customer1 = outcomes[treated].reshape(r, g//2*m)
    store_means = outcomes.mean(axis=2)
    store0 = store_means[~treated].reshape(r, g//2)
    store1 = store_means[treated].reshape(r, g//2)
    return {"customer_rows": welch(customer0, customer1),
            "store_means": welch(store0, store1)}


def wilson(successes, total):
    """Monte Carlo uncertainty for a rejection fraction, not an effect interval."""
    z = stats.norm.ppf(.975)
    p = successes / total
    center = (p + z*z/(2*total)) / (1 + z*z/total)
    half = z * np.sqrt(p*(1-p)/total + z*z/(4*total*total)) / (1 + z*z/total)
    return float(center-half), float(center+half)


def simulate(repetitions=REPETITIONS, stores=STORES, customers=CUSTOMERS, seed=SEED):
    if repetitions < 2 or stores < 4 or stores % 2 or customers < 2:
        raise ValueError("Use two repetitions, an even store count >=4, and >=2 customers")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Shared Gaussian draws and assignments make the rho comparisons paired.
    store_shock = rng.normal(size=(repetitions, stores, 1))
    customer_shock = rng.normal(size=(repetitions, stores, customers))
    order = np.argsort(rng.random((repetitions, stores)), axis=1)
    treated = np.zeros((repetitions, stores), dtype=bool)
    treated[np.arange(repetitions)[:, None], order[:, :stores//2]] = True
    summaries, examples, first_data = [], [], None
    for rho in CORRELATIONS:
        # Potential outcomes are identical under promotion and control.
        y = (100 + np.sqrt(VARIANCE*rho)*store_shock
             + np.sqrt(VARIANCE*(1-rho))*customer_shock)
        results = compare_methods(y, treated)
        if not np.allclose(results["customer_rows"][0], results["store_means"][0]):
            raise AssertionError("Equal-size point estimates differ")
        for method, (effect, se, df, p) in results.items():
            rejected = int((p < ALPHA).sum())
            low, high = wilson(rejected, repetitions)
            summaries.append({"rho": rho, "method": method, "repetitions": repetitions,
                "rejections": rejected, "rejection_rate": rejected/repetitions,
                "mc_ci_low": low, "mc_ci_high": high, "mean_effect_dollars": effect.mean(),
                "empirical_effect_sd": effect.std(ddof=1), "mean_reported_se": se.mean(),
                "theoretical_effect_sd": np.sqrt(4*VARIANCE/stores*(rho+(1-rho)/customers)),
                "design_effect": 1+(customers-1)*rho})
            critical = stats.t.ppf(.975, df[0])
            examples.append({"rho": rho, "method": method, "repetition": 0,
                "effect_dollars": effect[0], "se_dollars": se[0], "df": df[0],
                "p_value": p[0], "ci_low": effect[0]-critical*se[0],
                "ci_high": effect[0]+critical*se[0]})
        if rho == .3:
            first_data = pd.DataFrame({"store": np.repeat(np.arange(stores), customers),
                "customer": np.tile(np.arange(customers), stores),
                "assigned_promotion": np.repeat(treated[0].astype(int), customers),
                "contribution_dollars": y[0].ravel()})
    return pd.DataFrame(summaries), pd.DataFrame(examples), first_data


def main():
    summary, examples, data = simulate()
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    summary.to_csv(OUTPUT / "null_calibration.csv", index=False)
    examples.to_csv(OUTPUT / "first_experiment.csv", index=False)
    data.to_csv(OUTPUT / "synthetic_store_customers.csv", index=False)
    setup = {"seed": SEED, "repetitions_per_rho": REPETITIONS, "stores": STORES,
             "customers_per_store": CUSTOMERS, "treated_stores": STORES//2,
             "outcome_variance": VARIANCE, "mean_contribution_dollars": 100,
             "true_effect_dollars": 0, "within_store_correlations": CORRELATIONS,
             "alpha": ALPHA, "hypotheses_per_experiment": 1,
             "outcome": "synthetic net contribution per customer in dollars",
             "model_api_calls": 0}
    (OUTPUT / "simulation.json").write_text(json.dumps(setup, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(summary[["rho", "method", "rejections", "rejection_rate", "mean_reported_se"]]
          .to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M06-prompt-effects-workflow-changes-and-the-outcome-scale}{%
\section{Prompt Effects, Workflow Changes, and the Outcome
Scale}\label{M06-prompt-effects-workflow-changes-and-the-outcome-scale}}

\noindent \noindent A manager choosing an analysis workflow wants to know whether
a worked example becomes less useful when the assistant can execute
code. The comparison depends on the definition of improvement. An
increase from 80\% to 90\% success removes half the failures; an
increase from 98\% to 99\% removes the same fraction. Their
percentage-point effects differ even though their proportional
reductions in failure agree.

In the published coding benchmark, each prompt-by-workflow cell pools
7,200 runs over six models, 40 tasks, and three languages. The example
supplies related code on separate data. The common task statement
already specifies the target, method, and output in both prompt
conditions.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Workflow & No Example & One Example & Gain (pp) & Baseline Failures
Removed \\
\midrule

Chatbot & 81.49\% & 85.90\% & 4.42 & 23.86\% \\
Self-Repair & 92.40\% & 94.18\% & 1.78 & 23.40\% \\
Agent & 96.97\% & 97.76\% & 0.79 & 26.15\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Let \(q_{ea}\) denote the observed success fraction with example status
\(e\in\{0,1\}\) and workflow \(a\). The example's percentage-point gain
is \(100(q_{1a}-q_{0a})\). To express the same improvement relative to
the available failures, calculate

\[
r_a=\frac{q_{1a}-q_{0a}}{1-q_{0a}}.
\]

The denominator is the no-example failure fraction. The ratio is
undefined if that fraction is zero. The agent's smaller percentage-point
gain coexists with a slightly larger proportional reduction in failures.
The difference between its example gain and the chatbot's gain is
\(-3.625\) percentage points. That additive interaction describes a
particular outcome scale and does not establish a general technological
substitution between prompting and execution.

The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Agent_Workflows/benchmark_evidence.py}{complete
program in Section 1.19.1} calculates each contrast from the published
integer counts. Repeated runs share tasks and datasets. Confidence
intervals for generalization across tasks should preserve that
dependence, as the authors' task-cluster intervals do. Recomputing a
binomial interval over 43,200 independent observations would answer a
different sampling question.

For an original course comparison, hold the core specification and
independent-check instruction fixed while changing the opportunities to
execute and revise. Record actual calls, feedback, stopping decisions,
and resource use. These complete workflow conditions still differ in
several operational features. A separate factorial comparison, such as
Section 6.29, is needed to isolate the effect of a particular
information or feedback component. Use synthetic practice inputs for
live model calls, then evaluate the frozen program locally on the
mHealth task without exposing the final answers.

\hypertarget{M06-statistical-detection-and-a-profitable-campaign}{%
\section{Statistical Detection and a Profitable
Campaign}\label{M06-statistical-detection-and-a-profitable-campaign}}

\noindent \noindent A promotion can change purchases detectably while losing
money. Suppose a randomized campaign assigns one million independent
customers to each arm. Purchases occur for 100,000 control customers and
101,000 treated customers. The estimated lift is 0.1 percentage points,
with a two-sided pooled proportion-test p-value of 0.0187. Its
approximate 95\% interval is 0.0167 to 0.1833 percentage points. These
hypothetical counts supply evidence of a positive purchase effect under
independent assignment, complete observation, and one prespecified
comparison.
