and suppresses the distinction between a small gain and losing access.

The discount-only alternative makes the objection concrete. It preserves
the L price reduction, increases profit by \$0.1167 per eligible person
relative to uniform pricing, and leaves H's offer unchanged. Choosing
the segmented schedule instead earns an additional \$1.9667 per eligible
person. That opportunity cost is relevant to the firm's reasons, but it
does not establish that imposing H's burden is necessary for service
viability. The synthetic zero-cost model establishes a feasible
comparison within its own setting; an empirical assessment must include
fixed costs, capacity, and investment incentives.

A contractualist argument now requires a defended principle. Consider a
principle allowing firms to exploit a customer's urgent need whenever
doing so raises expected profit, even when a viable less burdensome
offer exists. A person facing a serious avoidable deprivation has a
strong reason to reject that principle. The competing objection must
identify the people whose legitimate interests would be impaired by the
alternative and the seriousness of that impairment. Additional
shareholder income does not acquire unlimited moral weight because many
shareholders receive it. Equally, a dollar loss to a comfortable
customer cannot simply be relabeled an essential deprivation. The facts
about need must be established.

A defensible conclusion is conditional and forceful: when the higher
price exploits serious need, the lower offer remains viable, and no
comparably serious countervailing burden is shown, the seller ought to
adopt the less burdensome offer. Refusing to examine need while
declaring the pricing rule justified would exclude the very facts on
which the objection depends. Scanlon's water-owner example makes a
related distinction between a person's weak bargaining position and the
strength of their claim to reasonable terms.
\href{https://e-edu.nbu.bg/pluginfile.php/314831/mod_resource/content/0/scanlon_5.1-3.pdf}{Scanlon,
\emph{What We Owe to Each Other}, chapter 5, especially p.~192}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_pricing_incidence.tex}
\caption{Synthetic pricing incidence separates the majority’s modest gain from H’s larger loss and compares both with a profitable discount-only alternative.}\label{fig:M09_pricing_incidence}
\end{figure}

Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/assess_personalized_pricing.py}{assess\_personalized\_pricing.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Exact synthetic incidence: one purchase opportunity, dollars, zero cost.

Python 3.10+, standard library; imports the adjacent pricing example.
Run: python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/assess_personalized_pricing.py
"""
import json
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path
from evaluate_pricing import GROUPS, best_uniform, demand, evaluate, surplus

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def calculate():
    base = best_uniform(list(GROUPS.values()))
    segmented = {g: best_uniform([cell]) for g, cell in GROUPS.items()}
    policies = {"uniform": {g: base for g in GROUPS},
                "segmented": segmented,
                "discount_only": {g: min(p, base) for g, p in segmented.items()}}
    totals, incidence = {}, []
    for policy, prices in policies.items():
        totals[policy] = {"prices": prices, **evaluate(prices, base)}
        for g, (weight, lo, hi) in GROUPS.items():
            q0, q1 = demand(base, lo, hi), demand(prices[g], lo, hi)
            delta = surplus(prices[g], lo, hi) - surplus(base, lo, hi)
            incidence.append({"policy": policy, "group": g,
                              "population_share": weight, "price": prices[g],
                              "surplus_change_per_group_member": delta,
                              "population_surplus_contribution": weight * delta,
                              "lost_purchase_share_within_group": max(F(0), q0-q1),
                              "population_lost_purchase_share": weight * max(F(0), q0-q1)})
    return {"data_type": "Synthetic uniform valuations; all eligible people included",
            "benchmark_price": base, "policies": totals, "incidence": incidence,
            "foregone_profit_from_cap_per_eligible":
                totals["segmented"]["profit_per_eligible_customer"] -
                totals["discount_only"]["profit_per_eligible_customer"],
            "moral_scope": "Amounts inform reasons; no numerical moral verdict"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = ROOT / "scanlon_results"
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (out / "incidence.json").write_text(json.dumps(calculate(), indent=2,
        default=lambda x: {"exact": str(x), "decimal": float(x)}) + "\n")
\end{Verbatim}

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-dubuxe9s-mobile-targeting-case-and-kantian-authority}{%
\section{Dubé's Mobile Targeting Case and Kantian
Authority}\label{M09-dubuxe9s-mobile-targeting-case-and-kantian-authority}}

\noindent \noindent A theater can use a person's current location and past visits
to choose a coupon. Dubé, Fang, Fong, and Luo (2017) study two competing
theaters using a randomized mobile promotion experiment. Their
historical-visit classification uses at least 90 minutes of dwell time
and a preceding two-month window; the sample contains 18,000 subscribers
across 36 cells. Promotional voucher purchases and control-group
inferred visits are different measurement procedures. The authors
acknowledge that vouchers were not observed at redemption and that the
untreated control also lacks an SMS promotion. These details matter when
interpreting a purchase response as a price effect or a completed movie
visit.
\href{https://www.fox.temple.edu/sites/fox/files/competitive-price-targeting-pub.pdf}{Published
article, §§3--4}.

\hypertarget{M09-what-the-published-game-establishes}{%
\subsection{What the Published Game
Establishes}\label{M09-what-the-published-game-establishes}}

\noindent \noindent Table 9 reports expected revenue per messaged consumer for
each combination of targeting choices. Reconstructing the best responses
from its rounded entries yields one pure-strategy equilibrium: both
theaters select behavioral targeting. Compared with uniform pricing,
theater A gains RMB 0.019 and theater B gains RMB 0.035 per messaged
consumer, approximately 0.97\% and 1.20\%. Theater A's advantage over a
geobehavioral deviation when B uses behavioral targeting is only RMB
0.001 in the rounded table. The paper reports a 40\% posterior
probability that this deviation would improve A's profit. The rounded
optimum is consequently distinct from certainty about the strategic
ranking. \href{https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2017.1042}{Dubé et al.,
Table 9 and discussion, p.~965}.

A Nash equilibrium describes incentives given the modeled strategies and
payoffs. The customer's authority over the use of location history is
absent from this payoff matrix. Reconstructing the equilibrium therefore
cannot settle that authority. Nor does a modeled softening of price
competition establish an unlawful agreement. The same arithmetic can
appear in an analysis of independent strategic conduct, and a legal case
needs evidence about how the firms actually coordinate or compete.

Run from the repository root:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/reconstruct_competitive_targeting.py
\end{Verbatim}

The program reads \texttt{competitive\_payoffs.json}, which transcribes
the 16 rounded payoff pairs from Table 9. It reconstructs the
published-table calculation; it does not re-estimate demand or reproduce
posterior uncertainty from individual records.\footnote{The
  \href{https://services.informs.org/dataset/mksc/download.php?doi=mksc.2017.1042}{INFORMS
  download terms}, checked November 26, 2026, permit verification of the
  main results using the same data and models. They restrict other uses
  without author or data-originator permission and direct follow-up
  articles correcting central results to \emph{Marketing Science}. These
  conditions narrow independent reuse and publication routes for
  critical assessment; they do not prohibit every critical replication.}

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/reconstruct_competitive_targeting.py}{reconstruct\_competitive\_targeting.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Best responses from published rounded Table 9, not microdata replication.

Python 3.10+, standard library. Units are RMB revenue per messaged consumer.
Run: python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/reconstruct_competitive_targeting.py
"""
import json
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def calculate():
    source = json.loads((ROOT / "competitive_payoffs.json").read_text())
    names = source["strategies"]
    a = [[F(cell[0]) for cell in row] for row in source["payoffs"]]
    b = [[F(cell[1]) for cell in row] for row in source["payoffs"]]
    n = len(names)
    best_a = {names[j]: [names[i] for i in range(n)
                         if a[i][j] == max(a[k][j] for k in range(n))] for j in range(n)}
    best_b = {names[i]: [names[j] for j in range(n)
                         if b[i][j] == max(b[i])] for i in range(n)}
    equilibria = [(names[i], names[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)
                 if names[i] in best_a[names[j]] and names[j] in best_b[names[i]]]
    return {"source": source["source"], "units": source["units"],
            "best_responses_A": best_a, "best_responses_B": best_b,
            "pure_equilibria_from_rounded_payoffs": equilibria,
            "behavioral_vs_uniform_revenue_gains":
                {"A": a[2][2]-a[0][0], "B": b[2][2]-b[0][0]},
            "relative_gains": {"A": a[2][2]/a[0][0]-1, "B": b[2][2]/b[0][0]-1},
            "A_behavioral_vs_geobehavioral_gap_when_B_behavioral": a[2][2]-a[3][2],
            "scope": "Static estimated game; no posterior draws, privacy values, or permission measure"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = ROOT / "scanlon_results"
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (out / "competitive_targeting.json").write_text(json.dumps(calculate(), indent=2,
        default=lambda x: {"exact": str(x), "decimal": float(x)}) + "\n")
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M09-specify-the-maxim-before-judging-the-practice}{%
\subsection{Specify the Maxim Before Judging the
Practice}\label{M09-specify-the-maxim-before-judging-the-practice}}

\noindent \noindent Consider the hypothetical maxim: use a customer's location
history to increase revenue while concealing a material use that the
customer would otherwise have a meaningful opportunity to refuse. The
moral objection concerns the deliberate defeat of informed choice. Under
Kant's Formula of Humanity, treating someone merely as a means concerns
how their rational agency enters the action, not merely whether the firm
obtains a benefit. A transaction can benefit both parties while
deception prevents one party from authorizing a material feature of it.
Kant's discussion of false promising also makes the agent's reliance on
another person's mistaken understanding relevant to universalization.
\href{https://www.earlymoderntexts.com/assets/pdfs/kant1785.pdf}{Kant,
\emph{Groundwork}, second section, Academy 4:421--430}.

The published payoff table does not establish that the hypothetical
concealment occurred. A factual assessment would examine notices,
permissions, data provenance, secondary uses, retention, and the
possibility of refusing tracking while obtaining service. An opt-in
program offering understandable discounts and usable alternatives poses
a different maxim. Profit seeking and differentiated prices alone are
insufficient to establish treatment merely as a means. The criticism
becomes strongest when it identifies an actual mechanism that bypasses
deliberation or exploits dependence, and then demonstrates that a
feasible practice respects those capacities.

A company could answer that location targeting provides valuable
discounts and more relevant offers. That defense supports a benefit
claim. To support a claim of permissible conduct, it must also explain
the authority to use the information and the treatment of people who
decline. Making benefits conditional on avoidable surrender of control
can itself be objectionable when the person lacks a reasonable
alternative. An offered discount does not purchase an unrestricted moral
license over the recipient's history.

\hypertarget{M09-reasons-for-restricting-independent-scrutiny}{%
\subsection{Reasons for Restricting Independent
Scrutiny}\label{M09-reasons-for-restricting-independent-scrutiny}}

\noindent \noindent People affected by a pricing recommendation have reasons to
want independent examination of the evidence used to justify it. A
restriction requiring permission for additional analysis or narrowing
the outlet for a corrective result places control over scrutiny with
parties connected to the original research. Authors and data providers
may invoke privacy, contractual obligations, or protection against
misleading reuse. Each reason should be connected to the particular
restriction it is claimed to justify.

Privacy can support removing identifiers, secure access, or review for
disclosure risk. Those measures do not by themselves require control
over a critic's conclusion or choice of publication venue. If a narrower
safeguard protects the relevant interests while permitting competent
independent assessment, a broader restriction faces a reasonable
objection from affected people and researchers. The ethical criticism
concerns whether the restriction is necessary and proportionate to a
defensible purpose. Its existence alone does not establish that the
underlying analysis is wrong.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-pricing-evidence-in-a-u.s.-antitrust-case}{%
\section{Pricing Evidence in a U.S. Antitrust
Case}\label{M09-pricing-evidence-in-a-u.s.-antitrust-case}}

\noindent \noindent An investigator considering a firm that uses individualized
pricing needs to identify the conduct said to restrict competition. A
paper on profitable targeting can supply hypotheses, estimands, and
methods for evaluating effects. Publication, citation, or adoption of
the method supplies no inference that its authors or users joined an
unlawful scheme. The legal comparison must concern the defendant's
conduct, the relevant market, and the claimed injury.

\hypertarget{M09-agreement-exclusion-and-differential-prices}{%
\subsection{Agreement, Exclusion, and Differential
Prices}\label{M09-agreement-exclusion-and-differential-prices}}

\noindent \noindent Section 1 of the Sherman Act requires concerted conduct. In
\emph{Bell Atlantic v. Twombly}, 550 U.S. 544, 553--557 (2007), the
Court distinguishes parallel behavior from facts plausibly suggesting
agreement. For a shared pricing service, relevant evidence could include
agreements to exchange competitors' sensitive nonpublic data,
commitments governing recommendations, communications about pricing, and
mechanisms discouraging independent reductions. A vendor's presence or
correlated prices alone does not decide the issue.
\href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/05-1126.ZO.html}{\emph{Twombly},
majority opinion}.

Section 2 requires monopoly power and exclusionary conduct for a
monopolization claim. \emph{Verizon v. Trinko}, 540 U.S. 398, 407
(2004), explains why monopoly pricing by itself is insufficient. A
theory involving targeted exclusion must establish its own mechanism and
legal requirements; a high personalized price does not supply them.
Robinson--Patman has a different scope: its price-discrimination
provisions concern qualifying sales of commodities and competitive
injury, with defenses including cost justification and meeting
competition. Recruitment services and movie admissions do not become
covered commodities simply because their prices differ across customers.
\href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/02-682}{\emph{Trinko}};
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/advice-guidance/competition-guidance/guide-antitrust-laws/price-discrimination-robinson-patman-violations}{FTC
guidance}.

Ezrachi and Stucke (2017) distinguish algorithms that carry out an
existing agreement, a common intermediary, predictable strategic
responses, and autonomous learning. Their taxonomy helps organize
competing mechanisms and the evidence each requires. The possibility of
tacit coordination creates a policy question where existing agreement
requirements may leave a gap. It does not convert every independent
pricing algorithm into an established Section 1 violation.
\href{https://illinoislawreview.org/print/vol-2017-no-5/artificial-intelligence-collusion/}{``Artificial
Intelligence \& Collusion,'' §§III--IV}.

\hypertarget{M09-a-hypothetical-investigation}{%
\subsection{A Hypothetical
Investigation}\label{M09-a-hypothetical-investigation}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose competing service firms use a common vendor. The
allegation is that they agree to pool recent confidential transaction
data and accept recommendations that suppress independent price cuts.
Request the contracts, feature definitions, data timestamps, pricing
logs, overrides, and communications. Preserve version histories so that
a recommendation can be linked to the information available when it was
made. Compare the alleged arrangement with a feasible world in which
each firm chooses independently using its own permitted information and
lawful public information.

Estimate net prices, quantities, entry, switching, and customer-specific
burdens under that comparison. Randomized price variation can identify
demand responses in its support; identifying the effect of the
challenged coordination requires variation or structural restrictions
tied to that conduct. If adoption responds to declining demand, a
before-and-after price comparison mixes the conduct with the adoption
decision. If rival responses spill into control markets, treating those
controls as unaffected can conceal part of the effect. Firm or market
clustering and pre-specified subgroup definitions should follow the
actual assignment and dependence structure.

Flexible customer effects require particular care. A stable pre-conduct
customer effect can control legitimate heterogeneity. A model that
explains every post-adoption price increase through newly fitted
customer types may absorb the mechanism under investigation. Similarly,
post-conduct willingness to pay can reflect reduced alternatives caused
by the alleged arrangement. Holding that state fixed in the lawful
counterfactual would preserve part of the alleged harm. Assess feature
timing, overlap, invariance, rival substitution, and fit across
competing counterfactual models. This is a specified risk of an
analytical design, not a universal defect of flexible demand models.

The RealPage litigation supplies a documented example of allegations
about nonpublic information and pricing alignment. DOJ's November 24,
2025 Competitive Impact Statement describes those allegations and
proposed restrictions on runtime inputs, model training, and
price-alignment features. The DOJ case page checked November 26, 2026
continues to label the RealPage document a proposed final judgment and
separately lists an entered Greystar judgment dated March 2, 2026. A
proposal and an entered judgment have different status; neither is a
finding that any firm using Dubé or Misra's methods violated the law.
\href{https://www.justice.gov/atr/case/us-and-plaintiff-states-v-realpage-inc}{DOJ
case record};
\href{https://www.justice.gov/atr/media/1419471/dl?inline=}{RealPage
Competitive Impact Statement, §§II--III}.

\hypertarget{M09-revenue-overcharge-and-excluded-customers}{%
\subsection{Revenue, Overcharge, and Excluded
Customers}\label{M09-revenue-overcharge-and-excluded-customers}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose an invented service market would sell 100 units at a
lawful counterfactual price of \$100, while the challenged conduct
yields 92 sales at \$120. Assume for the arithmetic that the entire \$20
price difference is attributable to the challenged conduct. Revenue
rises from \$10,000 to \$11,040. The signed invoice difference on the 92
actual purchases is \$1,840. Revenue growth of \$1,040 subtracts the
\$800 associated with eight fewer units at the benchmark price; it
understates that invoice difference.

For actual purchased quantities \(q_i\) and prices \(p_i\), the relevant
arithmetic is

\[
D=\sum_i q_i(p_i-p_i^{\mathrm{lawful}}).
\]

The counterfactual \(p_i^{\mathrm{lawful}}\) is the price for the same
relevant transaction absent the challenged unlawful conduct. A
revenue-maximizing uniform monopoly price from §9.17 is not
automatically that benchmark. At \$110, the illustrative invoice
difference falls to \$920; at \$120 it is zero. Eight excluded purchases
also matter for welfare and a Scanlonian assessment, but their lost
surplus cannot be recovered from invoice arithmetic without further
information about valuations and alternatives. Legal standing and
available relief require separate analysis.

\emph{Brunswick v. Pueblo Bowl-O-Mat}, 429 U.S. 477, 489 (1977),
requires injury of the kind antitrust law protects against that flows
from the anticompetitive aspect of the conduct. \emph{Comcast v.
Behrend}, 569 U.S. 27, 35--38 (2013), requires the damages model in that
class-certification setting to match the accepted liability theory.
Together they discipline the move from an observed loss to a legally
attributable damages claim.
\href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/429/477}{\emph{Brunswick}};
\href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/11-864}{\emph{Comcast}}.

Run from the repository root:

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/compare_pricing_damages.py
\end{Verbatim}

The program checks the revenue decomposition and varies the assumed
lawful price. All values are synthetic; the output is untrebled
arithmetic under explicit counterfactuals.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/compare_pricing_damages.py}{compare\_pricing\_damages.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Synthetic invoice arithmetic under an assumed lawful price counterfactual.

One period, identical service units, USD. No actual firm, violation, or damages estimate.
Run: python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/compare_pricing_damages.py
"""
import json
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def calculate(but_for_price=F(100), paid_price=F(120),
              actual_units=92, but_for_units=100):
    if min(but_for_price, paid_price, actual_units, but_for_units) < 0:
        raise ValueError("Prices and quantities must be nonnegative.")
    gap = paid_price - but_for_price
    revenue_change = paid_price*actual_units - but_for_price*but_for_units
    return {"assumed_lawful_but_for_price": but_for_price, "paid_price": paid_price,
            "actual_units": actual_units, "assumed_but_for_units": but_for_units,
            "signed_invoice_difference": gap * actual_units,
            "revenue_change": revenue_change,
            "quantity_component_at_but_for_price": but_for_price*(actual_units-but_for_units),
            "unserved_units": max(0, but_for_units-actual_units)}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = {"data_type": "Invented invoices and counterfactuals, not estimated damages",
               "central": calculate(),
               "benchmark_sensitivity": {str(p): calculate(F(p)) for p in [95, 100, 110, 120]},
               "scope": "Attribution to unlawful conduct must be established separately; no trebling"}
    out = ROOT / "scanlon_results"
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (out / "damages.json").write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2,
        default=lambda x: {"exact": str(x), "decimal": float(x)}) + "\n")
\end{Verbatim}

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-antitrust-institutions-and-reasonable-rejection}{%
\section{Antitrust Institutions and Reasonable
Rejection}\label{M09-antitrust-institutions-and-reasonable-rejection}}

\noindent \noindent A person facing coordinated prices can object that nominal
choice among sellers no longer provides meaningful independent
alternatives. The burden includes the extra payment, time spent
searching, and the possibility of losing access. A Scanlonian argument
asks whether a principle permitting that coordination can be justified
to people in that position compared with feasible rules protecting
independent choice. The strength of the objection depends on the good,
the person's circumstances, and the available alternatives. Market
participation gives a firm information about demand; it does not erase
the participant's standing to demand reasons.

\hypertarget{M09-connect-each-legal-requirement-to-a-reason}{%
\subsection{Connect Each Legal Requirement to a
Reason}\label{M09-connect-each-legal-requirement-to-a-reason}}

\noindent \noindent The agreement requirement separates a firm's independent
decisions from a restriction jointly imposed by competitors. A
contractualist argument for rules against coordinated extraction appeals
to each person's interest in meaningful alternatives and fair terms of
cooperation. The firms' objections may invoke service costs, useful
forecasting, security, and investment. Those interests support examining
less restrictive arrangements, such as analytics using a firm's own
data, while preserving the ability to offer independent discounts.
Whether a particular arrangement is lawful still depends on the
governing doctrine and evidence.

Causal attribution and damages requirements also protect persons. A
customer has a reason to seek a remedy for an attributable loss.
Workers, owners, and other customers of an accused firm have reasons to
reject sanctions based on unsupported accusations or losses caused by
unrelated events. A rigorous counterfactual protects both positions.
This does not require customers to prove every moral concern through a
completed lawsuit; it explains why suspicion, a moral objection, a
pleading, a liability finding, and a damages award carry different
evidentiary burdens.

An aggregate welfare improvement supplies a further objection to
consider, rather than an automatic answer. A large number of modest
benefits may coexist with serious avoidable harm to an identifiable
person. Conversely, preventing every differentiated price could remove
discounts or make valuable service unviable. Compare principles that
specify permissible information, customer authority, price safeguards,
and opportunities for redress. The relevant question is whether anyone
has a reasonable objection to the general rule in light of the
alternatives, including people excluded from the transaction data.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_antitrust_reasons.tex}
\caption{Legal proof and moral justification have related but distinct premises. The diagram connects an attributable competitive injury and a feasible remedy to the burdens of affected people, while retaining evidentiary safeguards for an accused firm.}\label{fig:M09_antitrust_reasons}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{M09-a-worked-argument-for-a-remedy}{%
\subsection{A Worked Argument for a
Remedy}\label{M09-a-worked-argument-for-a-remedy}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose an investigation establishes an agreement suppressing
independent discounts, a resulting \$20 overcharge, and a feasible
remedy allowing useful forecasting while ending the restrictive
exchange. The factual premise identifies the coordinated restriction and
attributable burden. The normative premise is that firms ought to
preserve meaningful independent alternatives when restricting them
imposes avoidable substantial burdens and no comparably serious interest
requires the restriction. The conclusion is that the firms ought to end
the restrictive arrangement and support an appropriate remedy for
attributable harm. A legal remedy additionally requires the court's
findings and the applicable remedial standards.

The strongest defense would identify a concrete benefit that depends on
the challenged feature, explain why a less restrictive arrangement
cannot provide it, and state who would bear the burden of removal. The
response should evaluate that claim with cost, service, and market
evidence. If the feature merely increases extraction while the useful
forecasting remains available without it, the proposed defense fails on
its own necessity premise. If removal would cause serious service
losses, the principle or remedy requires further comparison. Reasonable
rejection is a discipline of giving and answering reasons; it is not a
numerical loss threshold or an unconditional personal veto.

\hypertarget{M09-legal-permission-and-what-a-firm-ought-to-do}{%
\subsection{Legal Permission and What a Firm Ought to
Do}\label{M09-legal-permission-and-what-a-firm-ought-to-do}}

\noindent \noindent U.S. antitrust law does not prohibit every form of unilateral
exploitation. That legal boundary can leave a pricing practice open to a
powerful moral objection. A seller may comply with the agreement
requirement while using inferred urgency to impose an avoidable burden
on someone with weak alternatives. The person can reasonably demand a
justification even when a Section 1 case fails. Equally, a Kantian
objection to concealed tracking does not supply the missing agreement
element.

Institutional reform must also answer objections. A proposed rule could
require documented independent pricing, a usable option to refuse
secondary data use, preservation of decision logs, and accessible
complaint handling. Students should specify who pays the compliance
cost, whether the rule preserves useful discounts, how the affected
person can challenge errors, and whether the remedy reaches those
excluded from buying. The moral case for reform draws on these reasons.
It cannot be established solely by the profitability of the practice or
by the fact that existing law permits it.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-logical-consequence-and-a-defensible-recommendation}{%
\section{Logical Consequence and a Defensible
Recommendation}\label{M09-logical-consequence-and-a-defensible-recommendation}}

\noindent \noindent A firm asks whether a successful analytical result justifies
deploying a pricing system. The result may establish accurate purchase
predictions, a causal revenue gain, or a conditional welfare comparison.
A recommendation adds a claim about the action the firm ought to take.
Its credibility depends on the premises connecting these objects and the
reasons supporting those premises. Critical analysis should expose that
connection precisely enough for an affected person to challenge it.

\hypertarget{M09-validity-soundness-and-evidential-support}{%
\subsection{Validity, Soundness, and Evidential
Support}\label{M09-validity-soundness-and-evidential-support}}

\noindent \noindent A deductively valid argument preserves truth: true premises
cannot yield a false conclusion. Soundness requires both validity and
true premises. Consider the argument, ``Every revenue-increasing
practice ought to be adopted; this practice increases revenue; therefore
it ought to be adopted.'' The inference is valid under the stated
meanings. Its first premise grants priority to revenue regardless of
other people's burdens and requires an ethical defense. Precise evidence
for the revenue premise leaves that defense open.

MacFarlane examines the principles connecting facts about logical
consequence to norms governing belief and reasoning. The course
application separates a valid inference from entitlement to accept its
premises. When a conclusion conflicts with strong evidence, revising a
premise may be appropriate. Treating every implication of an accepted
model as an established fact would skip that assessment.
\href{https://johnmacfarlane.net/normativity_of_logic.pdf}{MacFarlane,
2004, §§2--4}.

Empirical support also requires attention to the form of the claim. A
confidence interval is a sampling procedure with stated coverage under
its assumptions. It does not guarantee that its realized endpoints
contain the parameter. An ordinary empirical conclusion may remain
defeasible because further evidence can change its support. Requiring an
impossible deductive guarantee would misdescribe that conclusion. The
appropriate criticism identifies the unsupported strengthening, such as
turning an imprecise average estimate into categorical reassurance for
every household.

\hypertarget{M09-the-question-and-the-meaning-of-its-terms}{%
\subsection{The Question and the Meaning of Its
Terms}\label{M09-the-question-and-the-meaning-of-its-terms}}

\noindent \noindent An analyst can assemble an accurate answer to a question that
omits the decisive issue. ``Which customers accept a higher price?''
leaves the reason for accepting unresolved. Urgent need, valuable
service, and weak alternatives can each matter for the customer's
objection. ``Does an average electricity-price estimate differ from
zero?'' leaves open a question about household exposure to future cost
recovery. State the question answered by the result and the additional
question required by the proposed decision.

Ciardelli, Groenendijk, and Roelofsen distinguish information conveyed
from issues raised by an expression. Koralus and Mascarenhas examine
reasoning that interprets premises as questions and answers. Their work
motivates asking which alternatives an inquiry keeps open and when a
partial answer is treated as complete. Applying that discipline to a
managerial brief does not establish a psychological mechanism in a
particular analyst or AI system.
\href{https://fdslive.oup.com/www.oup.com/academic/pdf/openaccess/9780198814788.pdf}{Ciardelli,
Groenendijk, and Roelofsen, 2018, §§2.3--2.5};
\href{https://doi.org/10.1111/phpe.12029}{Koralus and Mascarenhas, 2013,
§§1--2}.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.50}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.50}}@{}}
\toprule
Expression in an Argument & Distinction That Requires Support \\
\midrule

High willingness to pay & Ability to pay, benefit, and acceptable
treatment are separate claims. \\
Continued subscription & The recorded state may coexist with attempted
withdrawal or an obstructed exit. \\
Average revenue per kWh & Household bills also depend on quantities,
charges, customer class, and timing. \\
No operating facility added & Earlier commitments or failed projects can
still create exposure; actual exposure needs evidence. \\
A feasible customer option & Availability, knowledge, practical ability,
and authority to use the option differ. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The same words must retain the same meaning through an argument. A
question's wording alone does not establish that different customers
understand it alike. Conversely, different wording can express the same
issue. Record the operational definition and examine how the
classification changes under defensible alternatives. Calling a purchase
``consent'' incorporates a substantive interpretation that a transaction
count does not independently verify.

Possibility, actuality, knowledge, permission, and obligation also
require separate premises. A procedure can be technically feasible while
unauthorized. A person can have a formal option without knowing how to
exercise it. An action can be permissible without being required. The
statement that an action is permissible is a necessary condition of its
being obligatory in ordinary duty reasoning; permission alone supplies
no obligation. Specify the relevant sense of ``can,'' ``may,'' and
``ought'' before drawing a conclusion.

\hypertarget{M09-compatibility-identification-and-valuation}{%
\subsection{Compatibility, Identification, and
Valuation}\label{M09-compatibility-identification-and-valuation}}

\noindent \noindent The price construction in §6.38 grants exact agreement with
the historical joint law and obtains different intervention effects. It
isolates the additional assumption needed to turn representation into
identification. The valuation construction in §4.29 grants the purchase
effects themselves and holds the ordinal ranking fixed, yet obtains
opposite consumption gains. It isolates a second premise: how much the
ranked outcomes are worth. Resolving the first problem would leave the
second as a separate question.

A useful sensitivity analysis changes one maintained restriction at a
time and records what conclusion survives. Removing a restriction
enlarges the class of compatible models; adding evidence or a defensible
restriction can narrow it. Check that the restricted class remains
nonempty. An inconsistent set of assumptions and observations supports
no feasible economic explanation. Narrow bounds obtained by imposing a
strong restriction should retain that restriction beside the conclusion.

Statistical precision concerns variation in an estimator under a
specified sampling design. Identification concerns what the observable
law and maintained restrictions determine. Ethical justification
concerns reasons for a principle governing action. A narrow standard
error can coexist with an unidentified target or an indefensible
objective. The analyst should identify which problem an additional
observation, model restriction, or normative argument actually resolves.

\hypertarget{M09-construct-and-repair-an-argument}{%
\subsection{Construct and Repair an
Argument}\label{M09-construct-and-repair-an-argument}}

\noindent \noindent Begin with a claim narrow enough to test, identify its
premises, and search for a counterexample that preserves them. The five
steps in §1.20 provide a repeatable sequence. A counterexample can
reveal an invalid deduction; its relevance to the actual setting
requires further investigation. A criticism should say which of those
tasks it has completed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_argument_revision.tex}
\caption{An argument moves through claim definition, premises, counterexample, assessment of the missing premise, and a revised conclusion.}\label{fig:M09_argument_revision}
\end{figure}

The five boxes distinguish defining the claim, exposing premises,
constructing a counterexample, assessing an additional premise, and
revising the conclusion. The return arrow makes the revision explicit.
Factual and causal premises need evidence; normative premises require
reasons. The same sequence applies to the initial recommendation and its
criticism.

For the electricity case, take the proposed inference from a
statistically insignificant average-price result to reassurance about
household costs. A counterexample can preserve nonrejection while
allowing an economically meaningful effect, or preserve a flat unit
price while household charges rise. Sections 6.33--6.35 and 9.27 give
the source assessment and complete calculations. The missing premises
concern test sensitivity, the mapping from the measured outcome to
household costs, the relevant population, and the time horizon. The
defensible conclusion retains the uncertainty and the actual outcome
measured.

The critic must apply the same discipline to a stronger accusation. An
insensitive test does not prove a positive effect or show that low power
uniquely caused the observed nonsignificance. A hypothetical cancelled
project does not establish contamination of the study's actual controls.
A public statement exceeding its evidence does not establish deliberate
deception. Establishing those conclusions requires evidence on effects,
project histories, or intent. The supported criticism can still be
consequential: an institution using unresolved evidence to dismiss a
material concern owes affected people a better justification.

\hypertarget{M09-from-a-conditional-result-to-an-ought-conclusion}{%
\subsection{From a Conditional Result to an Ought
Conclusion}\label{M09-from-a-conditional-result-to-an-ought-conclusion}}

\noindent \noindent Consider a hypothetical personalized price for an essential
service. Suppose the analysis reliably predicts acceptance, and
independent evidence shows that some buyers face urgent need, weak
alternatives, and a substantial burden. Suppose a feasible pricing rule
could meet legitimate operating needs while imposing a smaller burden.
These factual premises make the person's objection relevant even when
acceptance is instrumentally rational.

A proposed normative principle is that a firm ought to justify avoidable
substantial burdens to the people who bear them, comparing feasible ways
of meeting legitimate needs. A Scanlonian assessment asks whether those
people could reasonably reject the principle permitting the practice
relative to the alternative principle. Buyers' reasons must be assessed
alongside the interests of other customers, workers, and providers. The
conclusion under the stated circumstances is that predicted acceptance
alone supplies an inadequate justification for the more burdensome rule.
A recommendation to adopt the alternative additionally depends on the
evidence and reasons supporting its feasibility and comparative burdens.
\href{https://e-edu.nbu.bg/pluginfile.php/314831/mod_resource/content/0/scanlon_5.1-3.pdf}{Scanlon,
\emph{What We Owe to Each Other}, chapter 5, §§1--3}.

The same structure connects dynamic-pricing communication and
data-center reassurance. Acceptance of a favorable description leaves
the accuracy and completeness of that description to be examined.
Agreement with a prestigious source leaves the support for its inference
to be examined. In each setting, name the people affected, the decision
being justified, the alternatives available, and the premise that
converts the analytical result into permission to act.

\hypertarget{M09-evidence-and-reasons-that-would-change-the-conclusion}{%
\subsection{Evidence and Reasons That Would Change the
Conclusion}\label{M09-evidence-and-reasons-that-would-change-the-conclusion}}

\noindent \noindent A strong criticism identifies a meaningful route to revision.
For the common-price example, valid randomized observations at the
missing group--price combinations would distinguish the two specified
models. For the valuation example, independent evidence supporting the
monetary value gaps and procedural burdens could narrow the welfare
conclusion. For the electricity case, a credible design, sufficiently
informative uncertainty bounds, matched household outcomes, and
documented cost-allocation protections could support a more reassuring
interpretation within their scope.

Normative conclusions also remain answerable to reasons. A necessary
security measure, an unavailable alternative, or a serious burden
imposed on other people can change the justification of a proposed rule.
The analyst should assess these objections in their strongest supported
form. Critical analysis earns its force by stating what follows, why it
follows, and what would require changing the conclusion.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-phenomena-noumena-and-the-ends-of-analysis}{%
\section{Phenomena, Noumena, and the Ends of
Analysis}\label{M09-phenomena-noumena-and-the-ends-of-analysis}}

\noindent \noindent A pricing system can predict a person's purchase with great
accuracy while leaving the justification for imposing that price
unresolved. A utility study can estimate an average outcome while
leaving residents' claims to information, participation, and protection
unanswered. These are fundamental questions about what an analysis is
for and what authority its results possess. Ease of observation gives a
quantity a practical advantage in research; it supplies no independent
reason to let that quantity determine the ends of the inquiry.

\hypertarget{M09-empirical-knowledge-and-its-limits}{%
\subsection{Empirical Knowledge and Its
Limits}\label{M09-empirical-knowledge-and-its-limits}}

\noindent \noindent Kant distinguishes objects as they appear under the conditions
of human cognition from things considered independently of those
conditions. Phenomena are objects of possible experience, whose
investigation can produce genuine empirical knowledge. The distinction
is more demanding than a separation between superficial appearances and
a hidden variable waiting to be estimated.

In the negative sense, a noumenon is a thing considered apart from our
sensible mode of intuition. In the positive sense, it would be an object
of a nonsensible intuition. Kant denies that human theoretical cognition
possesses the intellectual intuition needed for that positive use. The
concept has a limiting role: empirical cognition does not establish a
complete account of things as they are independently of its conditions.
These distinctions appear in the \emph{Critique of Pure Reason},
B306--B311, within ``The Ground of the Distinction of All Objects in
General into Phenomena and Noumena.''
\href{../01_Resources/15_Marketing_Dialectics/01_Kant_Primary_Texts/public_domain_texts/Kant_CritiqueOfPureReason_Meiklejohn1855.html}{Kant,
primary text}.

Acknowledging noumena therefore changes the ambition of the analytical
claim. A model can represent behavior under specified conditions without
exhausting the person represented. Larger samples and more flexible
functions can improve that empirical representation. They supply no
warrant for claiming theoretical knowledge of a noumenal self or for
equating the person with the fitted representation. The precise
relationship between appearances and things in themselves is disputed in
Kant scholarship; the course use relies on the stated limit of
theoretical cognition.

\hypertarget{M09-unmeasured-experience-and-practical-standing}{%
\subsection{Unmeasured Experience and Practical
Standing}\label{M09-unmeasured-experience-and-practical-standing}}

\noindent \noindent An unrecorded household charge, an undocumented constraint, or
an unasked question about comprehension remains an empirical object of
inquiry. Interviews, contracts, observation, and experiments may supply
evidence about it. Qualitative evidence also belongs to experience.
Adding such evidence can correct an impoverished analysis, while the
distinction between phenomena and noumena addresses a different limit.
Calling an omitted variable noumenal would conceal the opportunity to
investigate it.

Kant's practical philosophy supplies a separate argument for treating
persons as ends and understanding ourselves as agents deliberating under
reasons. The \emph{Groundwork}'s humanity formulation, 4:428--429,
places constraints on using people merely as means. Its third section,
4:451--453, discusses the sensible and intelligible standpoints. A
statistical model of conduct and a practical account of what is owed to
the person have different roles. The moral principle requires
philosophical justification; it is not deduced solely from a gap in
empirical knowledge.
\href{../01_Resources/15_Marketing_Dialectics/01_Kant_Primary_Texts/public_domain_texts/Kant_Groundwork_Abbott.html}{Kant,
\emph{Groundwork}, sections II--III}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_phenomena_noumena.tex}
\caption{Empirical investigation, Kant’s limiting concept of noumenon, and practical justification answer distinct questions about a marketing decision.}\label{fig:M09_phenomena_noumena}
\end{figure}

The four upper boxes distinguish established findings, recognized
empirical gaps, unanticipated issues, and acknowledged epistemic limits.
An arrow shows how recognizing an unexpected issue can make it a
question for further investigation. The separate limit box gives the
negative concept of noumenon its role. The lower box asks about ends,
authority, and obligations through a distinct practical argument. No
arrow converts a missing measurement into knowledge of noumena or a
moral duty.

\hypertarget{M09-when-analytical-success-conceals-an-unjustified-objective}{%
\subsection{When Analytical Success Conceals an Unjustified
Objective}\label{M09-when-analytical-success-conceals-an-unjustified-objective}}

\noindent \noindent Marketing analytics often begins with a measurable response
and a firm-selected objective. The critical question is what happens
when that practical starting point becomes the entire account of the
decision. Predicting acceptance can then stand in for examining consent;
estimating willingness to pay can stand in for considering burdens;
maximizing revenue can stand in for defending the objective. The
philosophical error occurs in those substitutions. Their validity
requires premises beyond the success of the calculation.

The pricing studies examined in §§9.14--9.18 and §§9.34--9.39 provide
specific arguments and findings to assess. Retain their welfare results
and safeguards while asking whether the proposed decision rule gives
adequate weight to customers' standing and alternatives. A reported
customer-surplus loss is morally relevant evidence even when the pricing
algorithm works as intended. Describing the same person more flexibly
through unobserved heterogeneity does not itself answer that person's
objection to how the firm treats them.

The electricity case presents a related problem in public
interpretation. A measured average can inform one empirical question. It
supplies no reason to treat residents' claims to explanation or
participation as exhausted by that statistic. Nearby residents need not
first demonstrate a precisely estimated injury to ask for reasons
concerning a proposed involuntary exposure. Whether a particular
safeguard is warranted depends on the relevant circumstances and a
defended principle of justification.

These criticisms concern the arguments, objectives, and uses of
particular studies. Institutional affiliation supplies no substitute for
examining those objects. The transferable lesson applies whenever a
commercially useful representation acquires authority over questions its
evidence and premises leave unresolved.

\hypertarget{M09-deliberate-about-ends-before-optimizing-means}{%
\subsection{Deliberate About Ends Before Optimizing
Means}\label{M09-deliberate-about-ends-before-optimizing-means}}

\noindent \noindent A responsible analysis begins by identifying the proposed end
and the people whose choices or obligations the decision would change.
Ask who chose that end, what authority permits pursuing it, and which
reasons could justify it to affected people. Then determine the
empirical evidence needed to assess feasible actions and consequences.
Better information can alter the practical judgment, while the choice of
a worthy end requires reasons that computation alone does not supply.

Kantian respect and Scanlonian justification approach this problem
through distinct arguments. Kant examines maxims, autonomy, and treating
persons as ends. Scanlon asks whether principles can be justified to
people with reasons for rejecting them. Neither account makes an
observed purchase or a high prediction score a sufficient justification
for treatment. Scanlon's reasons are not thereby identified with Kantian
noumena; the connection concerns the limits of reducing practical
justification to recorded behavior.
\href{https://e-edu.nbu.bg/pluginfile.php/314831/mod_resource/content/0/scanlon_5.1-3.pdf}{Scanlon,
\emph{What We Owe to Each Other}, chapter 5}.

For a pricing proposal, the analyst might recommend a less burdensome
rule, further evidence, a restriction on data use, or abandonment of an
objectionable objective. The recommendation should identify the factual
premises and philosophical reasons supporting it. An effective algorithm
can advance an end the firm ought to reject. Recognizing that
possibility changes the task before a line of optimization code is
written.

\hypertarget{M09-the-known-to-be-the-never-known}{%
\subsection{The ``Known to Be the Never
Known''}\label{M09-the-known-to-be-the-never-known}}

\noindent \noindent An analyst can recognize a boundary of knowledge without
possessing the positive knowledge that lies beyond it. The phrase
``known to be the never known'' directs attention to that situation. An
unknown unknown concerns an issue the analyst has not yet recognized.
Discovering it may make it an ordinary question for investigation. An
acknowledged epistemic limit instead rests on an argument about why a
specified kind of inquiry cannot supply the proposed knowledge.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Epistemic Situation & Marketing Application & Appropriate Response \\
\midrule

Known knowns & A supported empirical finding within its stated
population and conditions. & Retain its evidence, scope, and possibility
of correction. \\
Known unknowns & A recognized question about comprehension, an
unrecorded charge, or a policy response. & Seek evidence or state the
remaining uncertainty. \\
Unknown unknowns & An overlooked mechanism or affected group. & Broaden
inquiry and revise the question when the issue emerges. \\
Acknowledged limits of knowledge & In Kant's account, theoretical
cognition of things independently of our sensible conditions. &
Recognize the limit and restrain claims that exceed it. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The word ``never'' requires a specified scope and a justified boundary.
Kant's restriction concerns human theoretical cognition under its
sensible conditions. It is not a prediction that a currently missing
dataset will remain unavailable forever. Nor does it identify a hidden
preference, a person's complete inner nature, or a particular injury
beyond the evidence. Acknowledging the boundary preserves the
distinction between thinking a limit and knowing the positive content
beyond it.
\href{../01_Resources/15_Marketing_Dialectics/01_Kant_Primary_Texts/public_domain_texts/Kant_CritiqueOfPureReason_Meiklejohn1855.html}{Kant,
\emph{Critique of Pure Reason}, B306--B311}.

Statistical identification supplies a useful comparison with a narrower
scope. In §6.38, no amount of data restricted to the specified
historical joint law distinguishes the two intervention effects. The
restriction can be established by construction. New experimental
information can change that conclusion because it changes the available
observable law. This is a conditional identification limit, whose
mathematical basis differs from Kant's account of cognition. Stating the
scope prevents a temporary evidence gap from being called an absolute
impossibility.

Questions about what a firm ought to do occupy another role. Their
failure to be settled by a statistical calculation does not make them
unknowable in principle. Reasons, principles, objections, and reflection
can support practical judgments. The empirical boundary gives the
analyst no automatic answer about which pricing rule is permissible. A
defended account of respect and justification remains necessary.

An exclusive focus on reducing uncertainty can obscure these
differences. Some questions need another observation; some need a
changed research design; some require recognition of a limit; and some
require a better argument about ends. When a proposal depends on
knowledge its method cannot supply, the analyst should revise the claim,
change the decision rule, or defend proceeding under that acknowledged
limit. Adding a speculative latent variable supplies no substitute for
that justification.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-a-spectrum-of-ontological-adequacy}{%
\section{A Spectrum of Ontological
Adequacy}\label{M09-a-spectrum-of-ontological-adequacy}}

\noindent \noindent A manager deciding whether to deploy personalized prices needs
an account of the people and relations the policy changes. A purchase
record describes a transaction. A demand model describes responses under
specified conditions. The decision also concerns who sets those
conditions, who can refuse, and whose reasons count. Ontological
adequacy concerns whether the account preserves the objects and
relations needed for its stated claim. A precise answer to a narrow
question becomes inadequate when it acquires authority over a broader
decision without examining those additional objects.

\hypertarget{M09-from-recorded-outcomes-to-persons-and-institutions}{%
\subsection{From Recorded Outcomes to Persons and
Institutions}\label{M09-from-recorded-outcomes-to-persons-and-institutions}}

\noindent \noindent The following spectrum orders the questions an interpretation
admits. Each position describes a claim or decision argument. A paper
can contain arguments at several positions, and a small model can
support an adequate answer to a small question. The positions have no
numerical distances and supply no overall score of a researcher,
institution, or philosophical tradition.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Position & Account Admitted by the Interpretation & Question That
Exposes Its Scope \\
\midrule

A. Measurement as reality & A recorded outcome is treated as exhausting
the relevant object. & Has purchase become consent, or average price
become household welfare? \\
B. Behavioral representation & Response variation, latent preferences,
and prediction enter the account. & Does fitting behavior explain its
formation, authority, or value? \\
C. Institutions and procedures & Contracts, dependence, timing, decision
rights, and feasible alternatives enter. & Who controls the process, and
which burdens occur outside the recorded outcome? \\
D. Agency and reasons & People can endorse, refuse, delegate, contest,
and offer reasons for different ends. & Can the proposed principle be
justified to those affected? \\
E. Acknowledged limits and justified scope & The argument distinguishes
empirical knowledge, its limits, and practical justification. & Which
conclusion is warranted, which remains open, and what ought to be done
under that condition? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_ontological_spectrum.tex}
\caption{Five positions extend an interpretation from measurement as reality through behavioral representation, institutions, agency, and acknowledged limits.}\label{fig:M09_ontological_spectrum}
\end{figure}

The upper row names the five positions. The lower row connects
household-cost reassurance, purchase targeting, and cancellation to the
questions their interpretation must answer. The direction represents
broader explicit scrutiny. It does not assert that adding entities,
variables, or philosophical vocabulary improves an argument. A concept
earns inclusion by changing the question, the supported inference, or
the justification of the decision.

``Ontological laziness'' identifies a specific failure here: convenience
of measurement substitutes for an argument about what matters. Its
strongest form dismisses a person's claim because the analyst has no
column for it. The criticism should name the substitution and show why
the omitted object changes the decision. A study confined openly to
forecasting purchases can be excellent for that purpose. An assertion
that the forecast exhausts welfare or legitimates targeting carries
additional obligations that predictive success cannot discharge.

\hypertarget{M09-place-the-cases-inference-on-the-spectrum}{%
\subsection{Place the Case's Inference on the
Spectrum}\label{M09-place-the-cases-inference-on-the-spectrum}}

\noindent \noindent Electricity costs and public reassurance. The study's measured
utility outcomes supply empirical evidence within their design and
uncertainty. The inference from an insignificant average-price result to
the absence of household harm falls at A: it changes both the
evidentiary claim and the object of concern. Household bills, fixed
charges, cost allocation, income, recovery timing, and participation
rights extend the account through C and D. The arguments in §§9.26--9.33
establish particular reporting and interpretation problems; hypothetical
project cancellation remains a mechanism to investigate. A revised
conclusion at E reports what the design resolves, what risks remain, and
why proposed guarantees or further inquiry are proportionate. The
strongest criticism targets the unsupported reassurance while preserving
the paper's positive estimates and acknowledged restrictions.

\textbf{Personalized pricing and AI experimentation.} Flexible demand
estimation generally belongs at B when its claim concerns behavior. Dubé
and Misra's reported consumer-surplus comparison already goes beyond a
revenue-only assessment; the AI experimentation studies also contain
safeguards that should retain their stated scope. The problematic
extension is that an accurate estimate of willingness to pay authorizes
extracting it, or that a flexible latent preference explains away every
objection to the procedure. Neither conclusion follows from model fit.
Moving through C and D requires examining how evaluations form,
permission to use information, practical refusal, essential need, and
whose ends the system serves. At E, the recommendation defends its
normative premise and retains the restrictions supporting its welfare
calculation. The findings and safeguards in §§9.14--9.18 and
§§9.34--9.39 remain part of that assessment.

\textbf{Cancellation and the marketing of dynamic pricing.} A retained
subscription or accepted price can be accurately recorded while leaving
the conditions of acceptance unresolved. Treating the transaction as
sufficient evidence of endorsement places the interpretation at A or B.
Information, cancellation effort, urgency, and available alternatives
belong at C. Authority to reconsider and reasons for objecting belong at
D. Favorable language about flexibility or convenience must preserve
those distinctions. A defensible statement at E explains the actual
rule, relevant alternatives, and customer consequences without
converting commercial acceptance into moral permission. These are
proposed inferences for assessment; source attribution requires the
particular quotation and context.

The same standard constrains criticism of these cases. An unmeasured
burden remains a question until supported. A model's inability to
establish metaphysical freedom establishes no metaphysical unfreedom.
Labeling every omitted object noumenal would exempt ordinary empirical
claims from investigation. The critical conclusion becomes stronger when
it identifies exactly which omission invalidates the broader
interpretation and which further claim still requires evidence.

\hypertarget{M09-agency-beyond-a-behavioral-representation}{%
\subsection{Agency Beyond a Behavioral
Representation}\label{M09-agency-beyond-a-behavioral-representation}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose an automated purchasing service reliably chooses the
same product a person would have selected. Agreement can establish
useful predictive performance under the comparison used. The service's
authority to commit the person, the person's understanding of its
mandate, and the ability to withdraw delegation remain separate
questions. A person may value delegation and have good reasons to avoid
repeated choices. Preserving agency therefore requires attention to the
terms of delegation and the person's reasons, rather than an assumption
that more manual decisions always improve their position.

A representation of response frequencies by deterministic plans also
leaves the actual production of deliberation unspecified. Randomness
alone establishes no authorship, and predictability alone establishes no
absence of control. Experiments can examine defined aspects of
comprehension, reconsideration, and response to reasons. They require
operational conditions and provide correspondingly bounded conclusions.
Their success cannot convert a mathematical representation into
theoretical cognition of a noumenal self.

Kant's limiting concept gives this boundary philosophical importance.
Persons need not become completely identifiable empirical objects before
questions about respect and authority can arise. The negative concept of
noumenon supplies no description of a hidden decision mechanism.
Practical arguments explain why an actor ought to respect another
person's standing despite the incompleteness of behavioral
representation. A useful analysis retains both the empirical inquiry and
the independent demand for reasons.

\hypertarget{M09-easy-measurement-and-the-object-claimed}{%
\subsection{Easy Measurement and the Object
Claimed}\label{M09-easy-measurement-and-the-object-claimed}}

\noindent \noindent The electricity case separates an accurately recorded variable
from a valid measure of the claim being made. The paper explicitly uses
realized revenue per MWh and explains that choice on pp.~14--16. The
question is whether an interpretation preserves that object. Household
expenditure, affordability, and project-related financial exposure
require additional quantities and relations. Adcock and Collier
distinguish the concept, its operational indicators, and the resulting
observations when assessing measurement validity. Reliable collection
alone leaves the adequacy of that connection to be justified.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055401003100}{Adcock and Collier,
2001, pp.~529--531}.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Recorded Object & Broader Claim to Examine & Evidence Needed for the
Connection \\
\midrule

Realized revenue per MWh & Household bills or affordability are
unchanged. & Matched charges, quantities, billing periods, household
resources, and the relevant counterfactual. \\
Capacity entering operation & A utility has no project-related exposure
before entry or without entry. & Service requests, investment
commitments, cancellations, recovery decisions, and their dates. \\
Four named developers & An ownership category identifies a leasing or
operating business model. & Facility-level classifications and evidence
about the proposed business-model mechanism. \\
A utility or customer-class average & Each affected household is
protected from a material burden. & Distributional incidence, justified
burden criteria, and protection for differently situated households. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The first row requires an accounting bridge even before a causal
argument. At a matched customer class and period, average revenue per
unit multiplied by average units sold per customer gives revenue per
customer. The average-price ratio alone leaves that quantity unresolved.
Household affordability additionally involves resources and essential
needs. Sections 2.28.1 and 6.35 reproduce the bill arithmetic with
complete Python, including a case with unchanged average price and
higher expenditure. A higher observed bill in turn requires a credible
counterfactual before being attributed to the data center.

The second and third rows concern classification. An operating-capacity
record can be accurate while classifying a financially exposed utility
as having no operating addition. A developer label can also be accurate
while failing to identify a contractual form. The institution determines
whether the available indicator answers the research question. These are
concrete reasons to inspect project histories and contracts, rather than
treating finer statistical estimation of the existing indicator as a
complete remedy.

The fourth row adds the scope of the population claim. Perfect precision
for an average still leaves variation across households unresolved.
Calling an outcome harmless then introduces a further judgment about
relevant burdens. The defects should be named separately: the indicator
may fail to represent the intended construct, the comparison may fail to
identify its causal change, or the reported result may fail to justify
the practical conclusion. A study can satisfy one requirement and fail
another.

The strongest supported criticism is therefore precise: the broader
reassurance is unwarranted wherever its conclusion depends on these
unvalidated connections. The paper's stated outcome and design should
remain visible beside that criticism, as should its positive findings
and institutional discussion. Ease of data access supplies a possible
reason for selecting an indicator; it establishes neither the authors'
motive nor the indicator's adequacy for every later use.
\href{../01_Resources/41_Statistical_Claims_and_Decisions/INSTITUTIONAL_ASSESSMENT.md}{Paper
and measurement assessment}.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-philosophical-critiques-of-empiricism-and-reduction}{%
\section{Philosophical Critiques of Empiricism and
Reduction}\label{M09-philosophical-critiques-of-empiricism-and-reduction}}

\noindent \noindent A firm may ask a narrow empirical question, such as whether a
proposed price increases revenue. The decision to impose that price
raises additional questions about explanation, permission, and
worthwhile ends. Philosophical critiques of empiricism help examine the
authority claimed for the evidence. Empiricism includes diverse
positions; reliance on observation alone does not commit a researcher to
every doctrine criticized below. The relevant target is the particular
inference that grants measurement an authority it has not earned.

\hypertarget{M09-kant-conditions-and-limits-of-cognition}{%
\subsection{Kant: Conditions and Limits of
Cognition}\label{M09-kant-conditions-and-limits-of-cognition}}

\noindent \noindent Kant defends empirical knowledge while examining the
conditions under which it is possible. His critical philosophy also
challenges speculative claims exceeding those conditions. Sections
9.41--9.42 apply this discipline to behavioral representations that
become complete accounts of persons. A rich response model can improve
an empirical answer while leaving theoretical cognition of things
independently of sensible conditions unavailable. The practical account
of persons as ends requires its own argument. Neither a regression nor
the announcement of its limits settles that argument.
\href{../01_Resources/15_Marketing_Dialectics/01_Kant_Primary_Texts/README.md}{Kant,
\emph{Critique of Pure Reason}, B306--B311; \emph{Groundwork}, sections
II--III}.

\hypertarget{M09-sellars-observation-and-justification}{%
\subsection{Sellars: Observation and
Justification}\label{M09-sellars-observation-and-justification}}

\noindent \noindent Sellars criticizes the idea that observational knowledge
possesses an independent, self-authenticating authority. Describing a
claim as knowledge places it within practices of giving and assessing
reasons. His argument preserves empirical inquiry and its capacity for
correction. For marketing analysis, recording an event as consent
already requires concepts and grounds connecting the record to that
classification. Sensor accuracy or a perfectly reproduced transaction
count cannot independently validate the interpretation. State those
grounds and make them open to challenge. This application concerns the
justification of classifications; it does not equate Sellars's
epistemology with Scanlon's moral theory.
\href{https://www.ditext.com/sellars/epm8.html}{Sellars,
\emph{Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind}, §§32--38}.

\hypertarget{M09-bhaskar-being-and-knowledge-of-being}{%
\subsection{Bhaskar: Being and Knowledge of
Being}\label{M09-bhaskar-being-and-knowledge-of-being}}

\noindent \noindent Bhaskar's critique of the epistemic fallacy rejects reducing
questions about what exists to questions about our knowledge of it. He
distinguishes causal structures from observed event patterns and allows
fallible inquiry into mechanisms beyond immediate observation. A flat
price series can coexist with contractual obligations or cost-recovery
mechanisms requiring separate investigation. Establishing such a
mechanism requires evidence about the institution and its operation.
Bhaskar's realism therefore supports inquiry beyond measured
regularities; it does not certify whichever hidden mechanism a critic
proposes. Its account of knowable causal structures differs from Kant's
negative noumenon.
\href{https://internationalcentreforcriticalrealism.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/07-1-bhaskar-theorising-ontology-2007.pdf}{Bhaskar,
``Theorising Ontology,'' 2007, pp.~192--194}.

\hypertarget{M09-husserl-intentionality-and-the-meaning-of-experience}{%
\subsection{Husserl: Intentionality and the Meaning of
Experience}\label{M09-husserl-intentionality-and-the-meaning-of-experience}}

\noindent \noindent Husserl criticizes an account of mental life that treats it as
an accumulation of psychic data while neglecting intentionality, the
directedness of consciousness toward something. The marketing
application asks what a person's acceptance, refusal, or evaluation is
about. The same recorded click can concern a desired purchase, an
attempt to dismiss a screen, or a misunderstood authorization.
Investigating meaning requires attention to the person's situation and
understanding. Such inquiry concerns experience and should not be
relabeled knowledge of Kantian noumena.
\href{https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/philosophy/works/ge/husserl.htm}{Husserl,
\emph{The Crisis of European Sciences}, §22}.

\hypertarget{M09-scanlon-normative-reasons-and-ontological-restraint}{%
\subsection{Scanlon: Normative Reasons and Ontological
Restraint}\label{M09-scanlon-normative-reasons-and-ontological-restraint}}

\noindent \noindent Scanlon challenges the assumption that accepting normative
reasons requires rejecting a scientific understanding of the natural
world. He proposes assessing claims through reasoning appropriate to
their domains, reconciling them where their implications conflict. The
resulting position permits serious moral argument without requiring a
numerical observation for every reason. A customer's objection to
unauthorized purchasing can therefore warrant assessment even when the
system predicts their product choice correctly. Empirical claims within
that objection remain answerable to evidence. Reasons receive no
immunity from criticism simply because they are normative.
\href{https://media.philosophy.ox.ac.uk/assets/pdf_file/0008/25856/Lecture_2.pdf}{Scanlon,
\emph{Being Realistic about Reasons}, 2009 John Locke Lecture 2,
pp.~1--7}.

\hypertarget{M09-publication-incentives-and-the-choice-of-questions}{%
\subsection{Publication Incentives and the Choice of
Questions}\label{M09-publication-incentives-and-the-choice-of-questions}}

\noindent \noindent If researchers anticipate greater rewards for readily
estimated effects or technically elaborate models, they may choose
questions that fit those methods. Important problems concerning
authority, dependence, or worthwhile ends may then receive less
attention. This is a plausible selection mechanism. Its prevalence in
marketing journals, its causal determinants, and its consequences
require evidence about proposed, completed, submitted, and published
research. A count of published computational papers alone would leave
the missing comparison unresolved.

Evidence for one form of publication selection comes from Franco,
Malhotra, and Simonovits's study of 221 TESS survey experiments. The
authors report that strong results were more likely than null results to
be written up and published. That finding concerns selection by result
strength in the studied population. It does not establish a journal
preference for computational sophistication or the exclusion of
ontological inquiry.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1255484}{Franco, Malhotra, and
Simonovits, \emph{Science}, 2014}.

The decision consequence is to justify the research question before
rewarding its computational execution. A study should identify which
person's problem it addresses, why the selected outcome represents that
problem, and which consequences remain outside its scope. An
intellectually demanding calculation can still pursue a poorly defended
end. A careful account of agency or institutional authority can be
valuable even when its conclusion resists a single numerical estimate.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-personalization-and-the-learners-authority}{%
\section{Personalization and the Learner's
Authority}\label{M09-personalization-and-the-learners-authority}}

\noindent \noindent An educational platform can predict which explanation a
student prefers while leaving open whether the explanation helps the
student reason independently. The institution choosing the platform must
defend the learning objective and the authority given to
recommendations. Convenience, engagement, and measured performance are
relevant reasons. The student's ability to inspect, question, and reject
an explanation also matters to the proposed principle.

A Kantian assessment asks whether the system supports the learner as a
person capable of deliberating about reasons. A Scanlonian assessment
asks whether a principle governing its use can be justified to affected
learners. A student could reasonably object to a system that hides
consequential assumptions, prevents access to the original argument, or
treats disagreement as a defect to be corrected. The strength of that
objection depends on the circumstances, feasible alternatives, and
burdens of the rule. These are course applications of the philosophical
arguments in §§9.30--9.32 and §§9.40--9.43.

Personalization can preserve a common analytical objective while
offering different cases, levels of detail, and ways to inspect a
result. Students should be able to change their selection and
investigate an explanation beyond the system's recommendation. A record
of earlier answers gives evidence of particular responses under
particular conditions. It supplies no complete account of the student's
capacity, aspirations, or future reasons. Calling an unmeasured
educational outcome noumenal would obscure opportunities to investigate
it; Kant's limiting concept concerns a distinct boundary of theoretical
cognition.

The electricity case provides a concrete test. A student first predicts
a bill change, then inspects the accounting identity, and then
challenges a causal or normative inference. Feedback can explain the
denominator while leaving a reasoned disagreement about a policy open. A
strong response identifies what the study measures, preserves its actual
findings, and explains which additional premise would support broader
reassurance. Agreement with the instructor's conclusion alone supplies
an inadequate measure of this achievement.

The same standard applies to the course's own critique. Ask students to
formulate the strongest supported reply, identify evidence that would
change the criticism, and transfer the argument to an unfamiliar
setting. A learning tool earns support when it helps students produce
