and examine reasons under a defensible educational objective. Its
capacity to adapt content makes that objective consequential before
optimization begins.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-conflicts-of-interest-and-the-analysts-judgment}{%
\section{Conflicts of Interest and the Analyst's
Judgment}\label{M09-conflicts-of-interest-and-the-analysts-judgment}}

\noindent \hypertarget{M09-identify-the-duty-before-naming-the-conflict}{%
\subsection{Identify the Duty Before Naming the
Conflict}\label{M09-identify-the-duty-before-naming-the-conflict}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing analyst is asked to recommend a feed design. The
employer rewards advertising contribution, while some users want to
finish a task and leave. The analyst's recommendation affects both
parties, and the employer controls the budget for measuring
consequences. The first question is which responsibilities govern the
analyst's judgment. Accurate reporting, faithful execution of a
consumer's instruction, and impartial evaluation of a customer-benefit
claim can each create a responsibility that an engagement target
threatens.

Valsan distinguishes opposing interests in a transaction from an
interest that interferes with judgment owed to another. On this account,
the latter requires a duty-bearing relationship. The Institute of
Medicine likewise treats a conflict as a risk to judgment concerning a
primary responsibility; the conflict can exist before biased conduct is
demonstrated. These accounts explain why sincerity alone provides an
inadequate safeguard.
\href{https://lawjournal.mcgill.ca/article/fiduciary-duties-conflict-of-interest-and-proper-exercise-of-judgment/}{Valsan,
2016, §§III--IV};
\href{https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK22926/}{Institute of
Medicine, 2009, Summary}.

Three situations need different arguments. A seller seeking a high price
and a buyer seeking a low price have divergent interests. An analyst
paid for favorable findings while responsible for a sound evaluation
faces an interest that can compromise that responsibility. An adviser
undertaking to serve a consumer while receiving commissions for steering
purchases faces a conflict tied to the undertaking. The source of the
duty must be stated in each case. An employment relationship does not
automatically make every analyst a legal fiduciary to every customer.
Ordinary commercial dealings remain subject to moral scrutiny concerning
deception, manipulation, and imposed burdens.

\hypertarget{M09-incentives-enter-before-the-estimate}{%
\subsection{Incentives Enter Before the
Estimate}\label{M09-incentives-enter-before-the-estimate}}

\noindent \noindent A bonus need not change a regression coefficient to influence
a recommendation. It can affect the outcome selected, the alternatives
funded, the follow-up period, or the people invited to explain a burden.
A team may estimate watch time accurately while leaving unwanted
continuation outside the evaluation. The numerical result can be correct
even when the decision process systematically excludes reasons against
deployment.

The analyst should identify who sets the question, pays for the work,
chooses the comparison, approves publication, and can require a
redesign. Financial compensation, continued access to data, promotion,
reputation, and commitment to an earlier recommendation can create
different pressures. Their existence warrants an assessment of the
procedure. A claim that a particular researcher concealed evidence still
requires evidence of concealment.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_conflict_judgment.tex}
\caption{Commercial rewards and duties can pull on the same analytical judgment. Consumers need a route to challenge the objective and the decision.}\label{fig:M09_conflict_judgment}
\end{figure}

The upper path connects the employer's reward to the analyst's choices
about measurement and recommendation. The lower path connects those
choices to responsibilities and affected users. A consumer's ability to
challenge the objective changes who can demand an answer when the
commercial measure omits a burden. Independent review needs access to
the relevant records and authority to alter the decision; its value
depends on how it operates.

\hypertarget{M09-disclosure-and-control-address-different-problems}{%
\subsection{Disclosure and Control Address Different
Problems}\label{M09-disclosure-and-control-address-different-problems}}

\noindent \noindent Explaining that a service earns more when a user stays longer
can improve understanding of its incentive. The explanation leaves
separate questions about stopping, appeal, and the analyst's rewards.
Cain, Loewenstein, and Moore's laboratory studies identify circumstances
in which disclosure encourages adviser exaggeration or moral licensing
while recipients insufficiently adjust. Their fourth study examines
jointly presented unconflicted advice. These findings support evaluating
the remedy's operation in its setting; they establish no universal
effect of disclosure.
\href{https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/WhenSunLightFails.pdf}{Cain,
Loewenstein, and Moore, 2011}.

A useful response combines truthful disclosure with changes to decision
rights and incentives. An evaluator can have a fixed budget and
compensation independent of the deployment result. A review process can
require reporting customer outcomes and preserve the ability to publish
adverse findings. Users can retain a stopping control that the growth
team cannot silently disable. A conflicted decision maker may need to
recuse when independent judgment cannot be secured within the role. Each
measure should address a specified pressure rather than serve as
evidence of ethical quality by its mere existence.

\hypertarget{M09-benevolence-and-dependence}{%
\subsection{Benevolence and
Dependence}\label{M09-benevolence-and-dependence}}

\noindent \noindent A platform may currently honor user preferences while
retaining unilateral power to alter the terms of assistance. Lovett and
Pettit's republican account directs attention to a capacity for
interference that is not subject to the affected person's effective
control. Its commercial application asks whether protection depends
entirely on a provider's continuing goodwill. An enforceable stopping
instruction, meaningful appeal, and viable alternatives can address
different sources of dependence. A symbolic opt-out with substantial
costs can leave the practical relation largely intact.
\href{https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/sites.wustl.edu/dist/6/3556/files/2017/02/2009.-Neorepublicanism-2bzyex8.pdf}{Lovett
and Pettit, 2009, pp.~13--16}.

Whether platforms should acquire fiduciary duties is a further
institutional question. Balkin develops an information-fiduciary
proposal; Khan and Pozen challenge its capacity to reconcile platform
incentives and competing obligations. These are legal and normative
arguments, not a statement that all platforms already owe an identical
fiduciary duty. For a marketing recommendation, identify the undertaking
actually made and defend any additional obligation proposed.
\href{https://lawreview.law.ucdavis.edu/sites/g/files/dgvnsk15026/files/media/documents/49-4_Balkin.pdf}{Balkin,
2016, §§III--V};
\href{https://harvardlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/497-541_Online.pdf}{Khan
and Pozen, 2019}.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-infinite-scroll-reward-learning-and-consumer-purposes}{%
\section{Infinite Scroll, Reward Learning, and Consumer
Purposes}\label{M09-infinite-scroll-reward-learning-and-consumer-purposes}}

\noindent \noindent A feed can remove natural pauses, select appealing content,
and repeatedly invite continuation. An advertising-funded provider may
gain from additional exposure even after a user has accomplished the
purpose that brought them to the service. The ethical concern becomes
sharper when the design frustrates a stated stopping intention or
exploits a demonstrated difficulty in leaving. Greater use alone leaves
the value of that use unresolved.

Reward learning provides one relevant empirical mechanism. Lindström and
coauthors analyze posting behavior and manipulate social rewards in an
online experiment with 176 participants. Their findings support a
reward-learning account of posting. The study measures behavior rather
than dopamine release, and it does not isolate an infinite-scroll
interface. Schultz, Dayan, and Montague connect dopamine-neuron activity
to reward prediction in a distinct neuroscientific setting. Moving from
those results to a claim that a specific feed causes clinical addiction
requires additional evidence.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19607-x}{Lindström et al.,
2021};
\href{https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/papers/sdm97.pdf}{Schultz,
Dayan, and Montague, 1997}.

Allcott, Gentzkow, and Song provide separate experimental evidence:
temporary incentives to reduce social-media use have persistent effects,
and allowing people to set future limits reduces use. Their estimate
that self-control problems account for 31\% of use is conditional on
their economic model and study population. It is neither a clinical
prevalence measure nor an estimate of an infinite-scroll feature's
effect.
\href{https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20210867}{Allcott,
Gentzkow, and Song, 2022}.

A responsible evaluation would compare feasible feed designs using
outcomes chosen before observing results. These could include completion
of a user-stated purpose, compliance with a requested stopping point,
unwanted continuation reported later, and displacement of other
activities. Survey missingness matters when dissatisfied users leave
before responding. Report outcomes over the eligible population and
assess selective follow-up. Qualitative accounts can clarify what users
meant by a stopping request, while an appropriately designed experiment
identifies effects of the assigned design.

The analyst must also consider users who value sustained entertainment,
social contact, or accessible browsing. Automatically restricting all
use could burden them. A design that allows informed continuation while
honoring revocable stopping instructions provides a concrete alternative
to examine. Its consequences require evaluation, and its justification
requires reasons that affected people can challenge. The absence of a
neural measure supplies no permission to disregard an expressed refusal.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-from-commercial-incentives-to-an-ought-conclusion}{%
\section{From Commercial Incentives to an Ought
Conclusion}\label{M09-from-commercial-incentives-to-an-ought-conclusion}}

\noindent \hypertarget{M09-state-the-principle-and-its-alternative}{%
\subsection{State the Principle and Its
Alternative}\label{M09-state-the-principle-and-its-alternative}}

\noindent \noindent Consider a hypothetical platform that knows a group of users
wishes to stop after a chosen duration. Its analyst can predict which
prompts prolong their sessions. The proposed principle permits
overriding that boundary whenever expected advertising contribution
increases. A feasible alternative preserves useful recommendations and
lets users deliberately revise the boundary. The comparison concerns who
has authority over continuation as well as what each design produces.

A Kantian assessment examines a maxim that treats a person's difficulty
in carrying out a considered intention as a commercial opportunity.
Deliberately defeating that intention to obtain additional exposure can
subordinate the person's capacity to set ends to the firm's objective.
Prediction accuracy strengthens the firm's ability to implement the
practice; it supplies no justification for the end or the means. A user
who knowingly revises a goal presents a different case from a system
that quietly defeats it. The relevant facts concern understanding,
authority, and how continuation occurs (§§9.4 and 9.16).

Scanlonian reasoning compares the objections a person could reasonably
raise to the governing principles. A time-limited user can object to a
rule permitting a provider to override an expressed boundary for
revenue. Other users can object to unnecessary restrictions on valued
entertainment. Workers and creators can raise reasons concerning
livelihoods and a viable service. Assess the burdens each principle
imposes from these positions, including the costs of the feasible
alternative. A larger total of small commercial benefits does not
automatically answer an individual's serious objection. Neither a
majority vote nor a weighted engagement score performs this reasoning
(§9.30).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_engagement_reasons.tex}
\caption{An ought conclusion requires supported facts, a defended principle, and comparison with objections to a feasible alternative.}\label{fig:M09_engagement_reasons}
\end{figure}

The empirical premise concerns whether a request is defeated and whether
an alternative can work. The normative premise concerns the authority of
a person's revocable instruction. Challenges can change either premise:
an ambiguous signal may fail to establish refusal, and a necessary
protective interruption may call for a narrower principle. A defensible
conclusion states the circumstances in which the platform ought to honor
the boundary and what exception, if any, can be justified to the
affected person.

\hypertarget{M09-the-analysts-responsibility-within-the-organization}{%
\subsection{The Analyst's Responsibility Within the
Organization}\label{M09-the-analysts-responsibility-within-the-organization}}

\noindent \noindent The analyst can document the outcome omitted by a growth
target, preserve adverse findings, and compare an alternative that
serves the user's purpose. If management requests a claim of consumer
benefit from engagement alone, the analyst ought to decline that claim
and explain the missing premise. Where the evidence shows that a feature
defeats valid stopping instructions for commercial gain, the
recommendation should oppose that feature under the defended principle.
The proposed responsibility concerns the work the analyst controls and
the reasons for it.

Confucian remonstrance adds an institutional question: can an employee
challenge a profitable proposal without being punished for disloyalty? A
firm that rewards the appearance of agreement while suppressing relevant
objections weakens the judgment on which its recommendations depend
(§9.11). Protecting dissent, funding independent assessment, and
assigning authority to respond to affected users give professional
responsibility an organizational basis. Requiring individual courage
while retaining incentives to conceal burdens leaves the structural
pressure in place.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-a-synthetic-evaluation-of-feed-policies}{%
\section{A Synthetic Evaluation of Feed
Policies}\label{M09-a-synthetic-evaluation-of-feed-policies}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose four designs serve the same hypothetical population of
1,000 adult user-days, including 800 leisure users and 200 users with a
stated time limit. The finite feed provides stopping points. The endless
feed continues despite the requested boundary. A disclosed endless feed
adds information about the firm's incentive while holding behavior
fixed. A user-controls design honors the boundary and permits deliberate
continuation. The inputs are exact scenario totals rather than sampled
observations or estimated effects.

Platform contribution is revenue less variable operating cost in USD per
user-day. Goal completion uses a purpose specified before exposure.
Regret is a next-day report of unwanted use, with complete follow-up
assumed for the constructed population. Excess time sums positive
deviations from intended duration; a person who finishes early
contributes zero. Excess time may follow an authorized revision, so it
alone does not establish an overridden refusal. The two groups retain
their original denominators under every policy.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.15}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}@{}}
\toprule
Synthetic Design & Contribution per User-Day & Goals Completed & Regret
Reports & Excess Minutes per User-Day \\
\midrule

Finite feed & USD 0.200 & 88.0\% & 4.0\% & 2.4 \\
Endless feed & USD 0.314 & 85.6\% & 12.2\% & 6.4 \\
Disclosed endless feed & USD 0.314 & 85.6\% & 12.2\% & 6.4 \\
User controls & USD 0.236 & 91.8\% & 3.4\% & 1.2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The endless feed raises contribution while reducing overall goal
completion relative to the finite feed. Leisure users' goal completion
rises from 90\% to 92\%, while time-limited users' completion falls from
80\% to 60\%. Within the latter group, regret rises from 8\% to 45\%.
The result depends on whose outcomes enter the comparison. These
constructed differences do not estimate real-platform harms.

A manager could assign a monetary penalty to reported regret. Define the
score per user-day as

\[
S_p(\lambda)=\pi_p-\lambda r_p,
\]

where \(p\) indexes the design, \(\pi_p\) is contribution in USD per
user-day, \(r_p\) is the fraction reporting regret, and \(\lambda\) is a
hypothetical USD penalty per report. At \(\lambda=0.50\), the endless
designs remain the maximizers. At \(\lambda=2\), user controls maximize
the score. The analyst's weight changes the recommendation without
changing the evidence. A measured regret rate does not establish which
weight is justified.

Now impose a separately defended requirement that a design honor a valid
stopping instruction. Both endless designs become infeasible. User
controls have the highest contribution among the remaining designs at
each displayed weight. This restriction represents the normative premise
in §9.47. Its justification must be assessed through reasons and
feasible alternatives; the calculation supplies its commercial
consequence.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Conflicts_of_Interest/evaluate_policies.py}{evaluate\_policies.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Compare synthetic feed policies, incentive weights, and refusal rights."""
import csv
import json
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
INTEGER_FIELDS = (
    "n", "contribution_cents", "goals_completed", "regret_reports",
    "excess_minutes", "respects_stop", "discloses_incentive",
)


def load_rows(path):
    with path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(handle))
    seen = set()
    for row in rows:
        for name in INTEGER_FIELDS:
            row[name] = int(row[name])
        key = (row["policy"], row["group"])
        assert key not in seen, key
        seen.add(key)
        assert row["n"] > 0
        for name in ("goals_completed", "regret_reports"):
            assert 0 <= row[name] <= row["n"]
        assert row["contribution_cents"] >= 0
        assert row["excess_minutes"] >= 0
        for name in ("respects_stop", "discloses_incentive"):
            assert row[name] in (0, 1)
    return rows


def summarize(rows):
    by_policy = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
        by_policy[row["policy"]].append(row)
    composition = None
    result = {}
    for policy, group_rows in by_policy.items():
        current = {r["group"]: r["n"] for r in group_rows}
        if composition is None:
            composition = current
        assert current == composition, "Policy populations differ"
        n = sum(r["n"] for r in group_rows)
        totals = {
            k: sum(r[k] for r in group_rows)
            for k in ("contribution_cents", "goals_completed",
                      "regret_reports", "excess_minutes")
        }
        result[policy] = {
            "n": n, **totals,
            "contribution_usd_per_user_day": totals["contribution_cents"] / (100 * n),
            "goal_completion_rate": totals["goals_completed"] / n,
            "regret_rate": totals["regret_reports"] / n,
            "excess_minutes_per_user_day": totals["excess_minutes"] / n,
            "respects_stop": all(r["respects_stop"] for r in group_rows),
            "discloses_incentive": all(r["discloses_incentive"] for r in group_rows),
            "groups": {
                r["group"]: {
                    "n": r["n"],
                    "goal_completion_rate": r["goals_completed"] / r["n"],
                    "regret_rate": r["regret_reports"] / r["n"],
                } for r in group_rows
            },
        }
    return result


def best(policies, penalty, require_stop=False):
    """Penalty units: hypothetical USD per additional regret report."""
    scores = {
        name: p["contribution_usd_per_user_day"] - penalty * p["regret_rate"]
        for name, p in policies.items()
        if not require_stop or p["respects_stop"]
    }
    assert scores, "No policy meets the stated condition"
    maximum = max(scores.values())
    return sorted(name for name, score in scores.items()
                  if abs(score - maximum) < 1e-12)


def main():
    policies = summarize(load_rows(HERE / "policy_inputs.csv"))
    weights = [0, 0.5, 2]
    decisions = [
        {"regret_penalty_usd": weight, "require_stop": stop,
         "maximizers": best(policies, weight, stop)}
        for stop in (False, True) for weight in weights
    ]
    output = {"status": "synthetic exact scenario; no estimated effects",
              "policies": policies, "decisions": decisions}
    destination = HERE / "results"
    destination.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (destination / "policy_comparison.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(output, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    for policy, values in policies.items():
        print(policy, f"USD {values['contribution_usd_per_user_day']:.3f}",
              f"goals {values['goal_completion_rate']:.1%}",
              f"regret {values['regret_rate']:.1%}")
    for decision in decisions:
        print(decision)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

Run
\texttt{python3\ 03\_Data\_and\_Code/Conflicts\_of\_Interest/evaluate\_policies.py}
from the repository root. The program reads the companion CSV through a
path relative to its own location and writes
\texttt{results/policy\_comparison.json}. It checks counts, distinct
policy-group rows, and common population composition. The separate
verification script reproduces totals and decision comparisons from
hand-calculated expectations.

The unchanged disclosure scenario isolates a logical point: information
about a financial incentive can coexist with an unchanged opportunity to
override a user's instruction. Its behavioral equality is stipulated, so
it supplies no evidence that real disclosure is ineffective. The model
also contains no complete welfare measure. User purposes, retrospective
reports, and institutional authority remain distinct objects even when
they support the same recommendation in this example.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-conflicts-of-interest-across-marketing-dialectics}{%
\section{Conflicts of Interest Across Marketing
Dialectics}\label{M09-conflicts-of-interest-across-marketing-dialectics}}

\noindent \noindent The same discipline applies to pricing, cancellation, mHealth
targeting, and public claims about electricity development. Begin with
the affected person's decision and the analyst's responsibility. Then
examine how compensation, access, reputation, or organizational
commitments could influence the question and the interpretation. A duty
to communicate evidence accurately can be compromised even when the
analyst has no authority over the underlying product.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.25}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.25}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.25}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.25}}@{}}
\toprule
Case & Incentive to Examine & Judgment or Authority at Stake &
Substantive Response \\
\midrule

Engagement design & Contribution from additional exposure & A user's
revocable stopping instruction and the assessment of benefit & Measure
completion and unwanted continuation; preserve control \\
Personalized pricing & Margin from targeting willingness to pay & The
move from demand fit to customer welfare and permissible treatment &
Examine incidence, access, alternatives, and reasons for the pricing
rule \\
Cancellation & Revenue retained after a request to leave & The
customer's withdrawal and accurate reporting of its completion & Record
charges, requests, completion, and refusal costs \\
mHealth targeting & Revenue from continued use or additional purchases &
The person's purposes and authority over sensitive information &
Separate logging from benefit; require appropriate authorization \\
Electricity reassurance & Attention, reputation, or commercial support,
where documented & Accurate claims about household burdens and
opportunities to contest them & Preserve uncertainty, examine bills and
cost recovery, and include affected residents \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

For the electricity case, scrutiny of the price-to-bill inference stands
independently of any unverified claim about an author's motives or
funding. A disclosed financial relationship would justify additional
examination of procedures; it would not, by itself, refute an estimate.
Conversely, an absence of a disclosed financial tie would not repair a
missing premise. The logical and institutional assessment must survive
either incentive story.

Marketing Dialectics asks how an observed result acquires authority to
settle a broader question. Treating engagement as benefit, demand as
welfare, or a price average as household affordability can conceal the
very interests that should be examined. The analyst must identify the
bridge premise and explain why the affected person has reason to accept
it. If the person cannot effectively challenge the question, favorable
measured outcomes can coexist with a substantial loss of authority.

A consumer's practical standing exceeds the variables used to predict
their behavior. Unknown intentions and unmeasured burdens invite further
empirical inquiry. Kant's noumenal limit concerns a different question
about the reach of theoretical cognition (§9.41). Neither category
permits an analyst to infer authority over the person from a successful
forecast. A defensible recommendation states what the firm ought to do,
whose objection it answers, and which evidence or reason would require
revision.
